INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this  Three Hundred Sixty -Ninth Report on the Action Taken by the 
Government on the recommendations/ observations of the Committee contained in its Three 
Hundred Fifty- Second Report on Functioning of Major Ports in the Country. 
2. The Three Hundred Fifty- Second Report of the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the Parliament on 
10th August, 2023. 
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its 
Three Hundred Fifty- Second Report were received from the Ministry of Port, Shipping & 
Waterways on 24th January, 2024. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the  6th 
February, 2024.

REPORT 
  
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping and Waterways  on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three 
Hundred Fifty Second  Report on “Functioning of Major Ports in the Country ” which was 
presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 10th August, 2023.  
  
2.         The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways on 24th January, 2024  in respect of all the observations/ recommendations 
contained in the Report. The replies have been categorized as follows:- 
  
Chapter-I: 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry:  
Paragraph Nos.:22, 27, 30, 33, 34, 43, 44, 52, 53, 63, 70, 73, 94, 96, 97, 98, 99, 102, 
103, 120, 136, 153, 174, 180, 186, 214,

77, 81, 82, 95, 100, 101, 104, 109, 110, 112,121,122, 123, 124, 138, 149, 150, 151, 
152, 154, 169, 170, 172, 173, 175, 187, 200, 201, 202, 203, 204, 208, 210, 211, 
212,213, 215,  
Total: 55 
  
Chapter-III:

been accepted by the Committee:

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Capacity of Major Ports 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that of all the Major Ports, only the JNPA has achieved a 
world-class Turn Around time of 24 hours for Containers. The Committee commends the 
JNPA for this seminal achievement and exhorts the other Major Ports to follow the good 
practices of the JNPA to improve their respective Turn Around times. 
 (Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee also notes that the Average Ship Output Per Berth Day, like the TRT, 
shows only a marginal increase for many ports, and some ports have even shown a decline in 
output. Though the Paradip Port has crossed the threshold of 30,000 tones, yet unless all 
Major Ports project discernible increase in their performance parameters, the efforts of 
individual Ports would not help achieve the objectives. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry takes special efforts towards monitoring the ground situation at ports that impede 
the performance progress.. 
(Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. Several mechanization projects 
are currently underway at various stages in t he Ports. The completion of these mechanization 
projects will contribute significantly to the overall improvement of OSBD. These projects are 
monitored at both the port and ministry levels, ensuring effective oversight and successful 
implementation. Additionally, the Ministry is focusing on enhancing the OSBD through an 
increased share of Public -Private Partnership (PPP) berths, which will not only improve 
operational efficiency but also boost OSBD. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee observes that mechanization of berths, minimum dwell time, skilled 
labor, and port connectivity for reduction in evacuation time are essential to reduce the 

3 
 
Turnaround time and recommends that the Ministry may make efforts toBring in greater PPP 
partnerships for mechanization of berths. 
 (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      Noted. 
 
DRAFTS OF INDIAN PORTS VERSUS FOREIGN PORTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee observes that the world over, the shipping industry is moving towards 
mega-size vessels with ships of 20,000 TEU and above. While a Capesize vessel requires 
upwards of 18m draft, the draft at Indian ports is in the range of 14 -16 metersonly, owing to 
siltation. The Committee observes that the geographical and topogra phical limitations being 
are identical for both the public and private ports inIndia, how but the private ports have 
been able to develop drafts matching with world class ports whereas the public ports have 
lagged behind. The Gujarat Pipavav port has a dra ft of 18.5 metres and plans to extend it to 
20.5 metres. The Committee, while acknowledging the high dredging costs, underscores that 
the ports drafts must be in sync with the growing size of the ships in the interest of 
maximizing the benefits of large ships in cargo handling. 
 (Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Most of the Major Ports have achieved a draft depth of 14 meters, while other Major 
Ports i.e. Kamarajar, Paradip, Deendayal, and Cochin, are working towards achieving even 
deeper drafts of up to 18 meters. Furthermore, the development of Vadhavan Port into a 
Mega Port, boasting an impressive draft depth of 20 meters, is a strategic move aimed at 
further bolstering the capabilities and competitiveness of maritime infrastructure. To make 
the major ports more competitive with Global Ports, the Ministry is exploring the possibility 
of treating the channel as a national asset and also examining the feasibility of funding the 
entire dredging cost, after studying the extant practices followed by the  other countries in the 
world. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.        Ports must increase draft according to the respective cargo profile. Indian container 
terminals must target an 18m+ draft. With the evolving ship types andIncreasing port parcel 
sizes, loading and discharge rates must be enhanced. The Committee also emphasizes that 
greater ship sizes and container loads need increased mechanization at Indian ports to 
improve the loading and unloading ecosystem. Dual cycle cranes and Automated Guided 
Vehicles (AGVs) may be introduced in ports to ensure incremental productivity. 

4 
 
 (Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. 
 
 
 Recommendation/Observation 
6.        The Committee notes the huge pension liabilities of the Mumbai port. However, it feels 
that such liabilities did not emerge in a day and are known from the time it got accumulated. 
Necessary contingency planning should have been effected and due mechanism put in place. 
The Committee appreciates that the  port has now limited induction to technical and 
professional posts but notes that the present sanctioned strength of port employees at 7,462 is 
still much higher than JNPA and private ports of Mundra and JSW Jaigarh. 
 (Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1      The observations of the Committee are well noted. During the fiscal year 2022 -23, the 
port has contributed ₹ 825 crore to bridge the gap. The shortfall in the pension fund 
investments and actuarial valuation as of 31.03.2023 is ₹2108.57 crore which is a reduction 
as compared to previous years. Considering the trend in the coming years the gap is expected 
to reduce further. Furthermore, the port is wholeheartedly committed to addressing this gap. 
The Mumbai Port Authority has formulated a plan, as ev ident in the commitment to 
contribute 90% of the amounts received from land monetization proposals. In the fiscal year 
FY 2023-24, an amount of ₹520 crore has already been contributed (up to 31.08.2023) to the 
Pension Fund as a commitment towards meeting t he pension liabilities. Current working 
strength of employees is 3327. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7.        The Committee observes that automation being critical to productivity enhancement is 
also necessary to reduce the staff strength of the port. But, the Digitalization process is still 
ongoing in the port with Port Enterprise Business System, GIS -based Estate Operations 
Management System, and Integrated Access Surveillance System. The Committee 
recommends that the Port implements the digitization and a utomation programme in a time 
bound manner without any further delay. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1      The suggestion is well noted. 
 Recommendation/Observation 
8.The Committee observes that the iron ore in Goa is of low -grade material for which 
beneficiation needs to be done before it is exported. Moreover, a grade of only up to 62.5 per 
cent can be exported. The Committee observes that the Mormugao port relied hea vily on the 

5 
 
revival of iron ore export for its sustenance. As dependence on one commodity is laden with 
risk for any port, the Committee suggests that the port explores the possibility of other 
commodities, like bauxite, gypsum etc. from Goa and other neig hboring States for 
transportation. The Committee observes that the Mormugao Port authorities had informed 
that transportation of iron ore cargo from Karnataka could be a possible alternative in case 
the iron ore mines in Goa were not  revived. The Committee feels that as there are ports like 
Krishnapatnam, Kakinada and Vishakhapatnam which can handle the cargo, it is unlikely 
that interstate cargo would come to Mormugao port unless attractive rates and concessions 
are offered by the Port. The Committee recom mends that the Mormugao Port may put in 
place, proactive strategies to attract cargo from neighboring states. 
 (Para 52) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1      Mormugao Port has set up a Business Development Cell which is actively working in 
line with the recommendations of the committee. Further the Port is offering concessions to 
attract cargo on case to case basis. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        Regarding the development of the cruise terminal, at the meeting in Goa with the 
Mormugao Port Authori ty, the Ministry of Tourism, the State Government of Goa and 
various Tour Operators, the Committee was informed that there are only day cruises 
operating at present. The Committee had enquired about media reports on Goa port being 
dropped from the cruise c ircuit of three top cruise liners. The Committee was informed that 
there had been an incident with one cruise liner due to an altercation with taxi drivers at the 
port gates. As such, the issue had been taken up with the Goa government. There was now 
better coordination with all parties, including the taxi drivers. The Committee observes that 
globally, the cruise industry was dominated by a few companies and such incidents would 
mar the prospects of Goa in the international cruise circuit. The Committee obs erved that the 
long and beautiful coastline of Goa presents huge potential for cruise tourism. The success of 
the cruise industry would depend on having an ideal ecosystem in which local conveyance 
plays a major role.  
(Para 53) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1      Mormugao Port Authority has taken up the issue directly with Department of Tourism, 
Government of Goa for compliance of the parliamentary committee. 
 
 ISSUES IN OTHER MAJOR PORTS 
KANDLA PORT 
 

6 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.        The Committee also  recommends that the Ministry makes every effort to implement 
the Landlord Port Model in the Major Ports. 
 (Para 63) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1      Noted. 
 
PORT MECHANIZATION AND MODERNIZATION 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.        The Committee finds it difficult to appreciate the position of the Ministry that all 
berths in the Major Ports would be mechanized by 2030, i.e. in a span of seven years. The 
Maritime Vision Plan is to position India as a top maritime nation. For this, the Ministry 
should make all efforts for mechanization and automation of all the Major 
Ports by that year.  
(Para 70) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. The Ministry is regularly 
monitoring the progress of mechanization projects. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      Mechanization of berths remained at the core of the measures taken by the JNPA in 
reducing its Turn Around Time from 52 hrs to 28 hours in a span of 05 years. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry as also the Major Ports take expeditious action for the time -
bound implementation of the 31 mechanization projects and also draw up actionable plans 
for the mechanization of the remaining berths at the earliest. The Committee also 
recommends that the Major Ports may take th e initiative to replace the old, outdated 
equipment at the old berths with modern equipmentsso as to enhance their productivity.  
 (Para 73) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1    This Ministry, vide its letter No. PD -13/98/2023-PPP/e-362935 dated 4th December, 
2023 has shared the recommendation of the Committee with all Major Ports for necessary 
action and compliance. 
  
DEVELOPMENT OF TRANSHIPMENT HUBS 

7 
 
VOC 
Recommendation/Observation 
13.      The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry but feels that the distance between two 
ports should be a matter of consideration as it impacts the overall productivity of both the old 
and also the upcoming ports. The Committee recommends that the distance between an 
upcoming port and another port in the region serving th e same hinterland should form a part 
of the study before establishing the need for a new port.  
 (Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1    In this regards, it is pertinent to mention that a new Major port i.e. Vadhavan port is 
under development stage and will be jointly implemented by JNPA and Maharashtra 
Maritime Board with a shareholding of 74% and 26% respectively. 
Further, the recommendations of the committee are well noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
14.      The Committee notes that one of the main  problems obstructing the development of 
Transshipment in India emanates from the lack of deep drafts of Indian ports, Especially 
those on the Eastern Coast and Southern coast. While dredging is necessary to deepen the 
drafts, the costs of dredging are charged to the shipping lines, adding to the cost of port calls 
in India compared to the foreign ports, thus, discouraging big ships from coming to Indian 
ports. The Committee has been informed that foreign ports do not bear the costs of dredging, 
which are borne by respective Government.  
 (Para 96) 
 
15.      Upon enquiry by the Committee, the Ministry acknowledged that the Syama Prasad 
Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, receives a dredging subsidy from the Government. But, the other 
Major Ports are responsible for their dredging expenditure, both capital and maintenance. 
The Committee desires to know why only the Kolkata port receives a dredging subsidy from 
the Government. The Committee would like the Ministry to give a comparative data on the 
number of foreign gov ernments which bear the cost of dredging and the number of foreign 
ports which bear the cost of dredging themselves without any government help. 
 (Para 97) 
 
16.      If the former is a practice worldwide, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
may explore the possibility of government support for dredging in Major Ports so that a 
globally uniform practice is followed so as to make our ports cost effective and competitive. 
 (Para 98) 

8 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1    Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, being a riverine port, is located in a unique and 
challenging environment. The Hooghly River on which it is located has a high rate of 
siltation. This means that the port needs to be dredged more frequently and at a higher cost 
than other ports. Therefore, dredgin g subsidy is given to the Port to maintain its draft and to 
continue to operate efficiently. 
 
16.2 To make the Major Ports more competitive with global ports, the Ministry is 
exploring the possibility of treating the channel as a national asset and also ex amining the 
feasibility of funding the entire dredging cost, after studying the extant practices followed by 
the other countries in the world. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
17.      The Committee also notes that solutions like Floating Cranes, which unload the cargo 
from Capesize Ships anchored in mid -sea into barges that take the cargo to the port, have 
helped ports like Kandla, a low draft port, to improve productivity and increase cargo 
volumes. The Committee desires to know if such solutions can be appli ed at other ports. In 
particular, it recommends that the Ministry looks into the solutions where dredging costs are 
prohibitive. 
 (Para 99) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1    The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. Ports like Deendayal and 
Mormugao currently use floating cranes for mid sea barge operations whereas ports such as 
JNPA, KPL, VPA and ChPA do not have a need for this service due to their cargo profile, 
draft availability and adequate berthing facilities. Some of the ports are exploring th e 
possibility of using floating cranes for mid sea barge operations in the future. 
 
DPA 
As far as DPA is concerned, yes the port users have the option of utilizing floating cranes 
available for mid sea barge operations at its port limits at O.T.B. (Outer Tuna Buoy), for 
handling Dry cargo ships. 
 
JNPA 
JNPA is predominantly a container port. Other than containers, JNPA handles small amount 
of Liquid and break bulk. JNPA do not handle bulk cargo. 
 
KPL 

9 
 
KPL is a deep draft Port which can handle larger vessels with a draft of 16m. 
KPL has initiated action for becoming the Cape Compliance Port to handle Cape size vessels. 
Hence, Barge operation at anchorage is not necessarily felt at this juncture. 
 
MoPA 
At Mormugao Port Floating cranes / Transhippers are used to unload/ load 
cape size vessels at outer anchorage through/into barges by taking advantage of natural deep 
water draft available at Outer anchorage. 
 
NMPA 
The Port  is  exploring  the  possibility  of  handling  cape  size  vessels  at 
Anchorage to handle iron ore. 
 
VOCPA 
Deploying floating crane for Anchorage operations & lightering from higher capacity vessels 
would augment the cargo handling potential of the Port. 
 
At VOC Port, floating crane was deployed from 15.02.2015 to 27.10.2016, for lightering at 
Anchorage using FC and barges and Subsequently handling the deeper draft vessel at berth. 
However, the Operator discontinued the services 
 
VPA 
At VPA there are adequate    berthing facilities in outer harbour  to accommodate cape size 
vessels with a permis sible draft of 18.10 mtrs. and LOA 390 mtrs. &in inner harbour to 
accommodate Babycape vessels with a permissible draft of 14.50 mtrs. and LOA 260 mtrs. 
 
As such the trade is not felt to handle cargo by floating cranes at ships anchored in mid sea by 
barges as the Port is equipped with international standards of Navigational and cargo 
handling facilities. 
 
MbPA 
Mumbai Port is also low draft port especially in the Dock Basin which cannot accommodate 
mother vessels. About 23.50 % of cargo of Mumbai Port is handled at anchorages where dry 
bulk cargo is discharged from Mother vessels to barges and these barges carry the cargo to 

10 
 
nearby ports like Dharamtar, PNP and Karanja. This cargo is discharged by Ships own 
cranes. 
 
ChPA 
There is no such requirement for deployment of floating cranes at ChennaiPort considering 
its cargo profile, volume and draft availability. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
18.      The Committee recommends that the digitization of ports be given utmost priority so 
that automation would reduce transshipment cost. 
 (Para 102) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1    The recommendation of the Committee has been well noted. The Major ports have 
already taken various initiatives in port digitalization and automation such as the 
implementation of Single Window Platform –NLP Marine (Sagarsetu), 100% RFID -based 
tracking and tracing, Standard ERP system, e -DO and e -BoL for shipping lines, automation 
of weighbridges etc. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
19.      The Committee also recommends that involving the private sector by way of 
investment in infrastructure, provision of ancillary services and streamlining of Immigration 
and Customs formalities, would be crucial for developing Transshipment Hubs. 
 (Para 103) 
Reply of the Ministry 
19.1    Various fiscal incentives and other support measures such as longer concession period, 
discounted tariffs, waivers in custom duties and GST etc are proposed in the draft DPR to 
encourage private participation and the investments to make ICTP an attractive destination 
for transshipment. 
  
PRIVATE PUBLIC SECTOR PARTNERSHIPS IN THE PORTS SECTOR 
Recommendation/Observation 
20.      The Committee notes that the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, in their 2015 
Performance Audit report on the Public Private Partnership Projects in Major Ports, had 
commented that the PPP mode of implementation suffered delays mainly due to protrac ted 
time taken for finalization of tenders, time taken for obtaining security clearance of 
shortlisted bidders, time taken for the signing of Chartered Accountant (CA) and litigations 

11 
 
by bidders during the tender process. The Committee observes that with 6 9 projects yet to be 
awarded, the Ministry needs to ensure that there is timely implementation of the projects to 
achieve the targeted timeline. TheCommittee understands that one of the primary objectives 
of resorting to PPP is for faster development of in frastructure, and delays in implementation 
of PPP projects defeat this very objective. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
takes efforts to increase the percentage of PPP investments in major ports and speed up 
theImplementation of PPP projects in t he Pipeline which are still in the under 
development/Inter-ministerial Consultation/Bidding stage.. 
 (Para 120) 
Reply of the Ministry 
20.1    Noted. It has been experienced, delays are mostly observed in getting security 
clearance which is under purview of  MoD, MHA & MEA. MHA furnish clearances 
sometimes get delayed, depending on case to case basis. Ministry of PS&W is not directly 
engaged and has no role to play in the process. However, the Ministry regularly follows up 
and approaches competent authority f or intervention, as and when required.  Moreover, in 
some cases the market response to the tenders is extremely poor leading to restructuring of 
the projects. 
  
LOGISTICS AND EASE OF DOING BUSINESS 
Recommendation/Observation 
21.      The Committee observes  that since it is the older ports which have legacy pension 
issues and most of the newer ports have mainly contractual employees and a fewer regular 
employees, pension liabilities cannot be cited as a universal contributory factor for high 
operating expens es. Besides, salary payments are obligation of every organization and 
cannot be a reason for high VRC. The requirement of 50% discount on cruise tourism is 
relatively recent and does not explain why the VRC has always been high in Indian ports. The

Agreements are generally made for 30 years an d with the rapidly changing market scenario, 
every change cannot be anticipated at the bidding stage in contractsspanning three decades. 
In fact private players are now looking for even longer concession periods in the port sector. 
The Adani Ports and Spec ial Economic Zone (APSEZ) has won a bid to build a Greenfield 
port in Tajpur, West Bengal for aConcession period of 99 years. The MCA, 2021 also has

47.1    Reply already given at para 200.

Reply of the Ministry 
48.1    Noted.

Concession Agreements can be avoided by adopting the right models for the project from the

CAPACITY OF MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that while port capacity is considered to be saturated at 70 -
75% of capacity, some of the Major Ports are functioning far below the mark. Mormugao 
operates at only 27% capacity, while Chennai and VoCA operate just at 32%.. 
 (Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The capacity of Major Ports has been re -rated with respect to global bench marks as 
per Berthing Policy 2016. The actual usable capacity of the ports is lower than the re -rated 
capacity. Hence, the utilization percentage against actual usable capa city is higher in these 
ports. However, a number of factors contribute to the low capacity utilization at these ports, 
including restrictions imposed by Goa State Pollution Control Board for handling cargo at 
Mooring Dolphins and other berths, single Railw ay line from Vasco to Tinaighat, challenges 
due to common hinterland and competition from other ports. The ports are taking steps to 
improve their capacity utilization, such as mechanizing berths, converting berths into 
container terminals, and promoting the use of oil jetties. 
1.2 Marmugao Port Authority (MoPA): Mormugao Port operates at 68% of its Usable 
Capacity, and 27% of its Re -rated capacity. The capacity as per CTO at Mooring Dolphins is 
only 4.75 as against re -rated capacity of 18.50 Milliontones. A lso seen from the table the 
rerated capacity of berth no 6, 7 and 8 is 17.40, 13.70 and 5.20 respectively as against usable 
capacity of 6.50, 5.20 and 1.00 Milliontones. Thus due to the restrictions imposed by Goa 
State Pollution Control Board for handling  cargo at Mooring Dolphins and other berths, Port 
is unable to handle cargo beyond the prescribed limit by GSPCB. Due to single Railway line 
from Vasco to Tinaighat, Mormugao Port is unable to evacuate cargo effectively through 
rakes. This affects the disc harge of vessel as it cannot discharge the cargo in stockyard, 
unless the cargo from the yard is evacuated. Details may be seen at Annexure-1. 
 
1.3 VO Chidambarnar Port Authority (VOCPA)

The Capacity Utilization of Chennai Port during the last 3 years ending FY2022 -23

Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that there is still much untapped potential to be harnessed so 
as to increase the capacity of most of the Maj or Ports. The Committee points out that the 
capacity utilization of the Non -Major Ports in India has remained at 64%, which is much 

55 
 
higher than the average capacity utilization in the Major Ports and recommends that the 
Major Ports may set targets to incre ase the utilization of their existing capabilities to an

2.1      Major ports have experienced remarkable traffic growth of approximately 10% during 
the fiscal year 2022 -23. Recognizing the importance of accommodating future demand in 
light of this substantial growth, it has become imperative to ensure spare capacity. To address 
this need, we are focusing on capacity expansion on two fronts: firstly, by introducing new 
berths, and secondly, by optimizing o ur existing infrastructure through the mechanization of 
berths, deepening of channels, and enhancing evacuation capacity. These strategic initiatives 
are vital for not only sustaining our current momentum but also for effectively meeting the 
increasing demands of the future. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation

Ministry and the Major Ports but the Ministry has not commented on the much higher 
capacity utilization in the Non -Major Ports, pointed out by the Committee. The

capacity utilization in Non -Major Ports and incorporate the same if possible, in their 
initiatives for capacity expansion.

mechanization of berths, deepening of draft, and digitalization of processes and procedures to 
further improve the TRT.

ISSUES ARISING OUT OF THE PROSPECTIVE APPLICATION OF THE 
NEWMODEL CONCESSION AGREEMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        The Committee had requested the Ministry to give its comments on the issue of 
extending the benefits of the MCA, 2021 to both the existing as well as newConcessionaires. 
The Ministry has put forth the arguments that the PPP projects are executed through 
Concession Agreements which are legally binding and are governed by the policies that are 
applicable in that time period. Any post - bid changes in theConcession Agreement is open to 
litigation. The Ministry has also informed that a Committee consisting of the Chairmen of 
VoCPA, ChPA& JNPA was constituted in May, 2023 for deliberation on whether the 
provisions of MCA, 2021 can be made retrospective and the report of that Committee is 
awaited. 
 (Para 191) 
10.      The Committee observes that the within the past two decades, the Model 
Concessionaire Agreement has been changed thrice, in 2008, 2018 and 2021 
(Comparative statement of the provisions of the three MCAs placed at Annexure XIV). The 
first revision came after a decade and brought only minor changes in a few of the provisions. 
The second revision came within 03 years and brought about a major overhaul in existing 
regulations, with the introduction of market based tariff fixation, abolition of the authority of 
TAMP, provisions for change in cargo, etc. It is not surprising that the existing 
Concessionaires find themselves in a disadvantageous position vis -a-vis the new 
Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021.  
 (Para 192) 

62 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1    Noted. The proviso clause to Section 27(1) of the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, 
provides freedom to the Concessionaire to fix tariff based on the market conditions.  
10.2 The existing PPP concessions would be governed by the respective signed Concession 
Agreement and tariff provisions contained in respective signed Concession Agreement and 
tariff guidelines, if any, stipulated at the time of the Concession agreement. Government of 
India requires the Project sponsors (Major Ports) to award PPP projects through a transparent 
open competitive bidding process, due diligence through DPR, research and analysis for both 
short and long term business continuity during concession period are part of this process. 
This is also to ensure greater transparency and consistency to the bid process and terms of 
contract, level playing field to all players, throughout the project life cycle and market 
discovery of rates.  Hence, saying existing Concessionaires are in a disa dvantageous position 
vis-a-vis the new Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021 does not seem correct in full merit. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
10.3    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.   
  
Recommendation/Observation 
11.      The Committee also observes that the new Agreement was issued with the purpose of 
countering the lukewarm response of the private sector in PPP projects and to provide a 
framework to increase PPP participation to boost p ort performances. The Committee 
observes that in 2019, on the issue of periodic revision of SoR (Schedule of Rates) for land, it 
had been decided not to apply revision of SoR for land every 05 years for PPP projects as it 
may not be in the overall interest  of the Major Ports. TheCommittee feels that the 
retrospective application of the MCA, 2021 should be examined in the same spirit. The 
Concessions given to the private operators generally are passed on to exporters/importers by 
leveraging costs and therefo re the general public can only benefit by these measures. The 
Committee feels that the Ministry may take these concerns into account while examining the 
requests of the existingConcessionaires.  
 (Para 193) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1    In MCA 2021, the Concessionaire shall, as consideration for the use, in its capacity as 
a bare licensee of the Project Site and the equipment comprised in the Port‟s Assets, made 
available in accordance with Article 2.4, pay to the Concessioning Authority ₹ 1 (the 
“License Fee”). 
11.2 On the aspect of making enabling provisions to provide option to the existing PPP 
Concessionaires for migration to the market determined tariff regime, as has been done for 
the prospective bidders / concessionaires for new PPP projects, the majority of the  Major 

63 
 
Ports Chairpersons opined that such an arrangement would be desirable as it would provide a 
level playing field to the Concessionaires, presently being governed under different tariff 
norms, operating at a Port. However, considering the procedural c omplexities involved in 
drafting a workable solution within the framework of the existing rules and regulations, a 
detailed comprehensive study of the whole issue, including legal, financial and contractual 
aspects, would be advisable. 
11.3 Based on the vi ews expressed by Chairpersons of the Major Port Authorities during 
the meeting, the Ministry has decided to constitute a Committee of Chairpersons, to study the 
whole issue in a holistic manner. Report of the committee is yet to be received.. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
11.4   The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.    
  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      The Committee notes that the issue is under examination by a Committee consisting of 
the Chairmen of various Major Ports and desires that the Ministry may update the Committee 
on its outcome. 
 (Para 194) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1    The Committee has not yet submitted its recommendations. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Achievements, Programmes and Initiatives of the National Akademis 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Akademis in organizin g various 
cultural programmes and events to achieve their mandate to preserve and promote the diverse 
cultures and art forms of the country. 
(Para 6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Ministry places high regard to the appreciation given by the august Committee.  
 
Budgetary Allocation and Issues  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee recommends the Akademis to explore the option of CSR (Corporate 
Social Responsibility) Funds available for "protection of national heritage, art and culture 
including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance and works of art; setting up 
public libraries; promotion and development of traditional arts and handicrafts;" as provided in 
clause (v) of Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 135. The Committee 
recommends that some portion of the CSR Fund may be mandatorily earmarked for the 
development and promotion of Culture and Cultural Institutions. Government can think of 
making such amendments in the legislation related to CSR. 
 (Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The autonomous bodies are encouraged to garner CSR funds, funds from other Ministries 
and also from Non-Government Sources. An SOP is being issued to all in this regard. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. In Committee's view a long -term guarantee of sustained funding will go a long way in 
creating a stable environment to implement ambitious plans. Artistic excellence can flourish 
only in good cultural infrastructure. Thus, Committee feels that Private partners can also 
provide financial support t hrough sponsorships, grants, donations, or investments under PPP 
mode. 

 
3 
  
(Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The recommendation of the Committee has been communicated to all autonomous 
bodies under Akademi division of Ministry of Culture . Ministry has, other wise also, been 
directing its bodies to increase their sustainable internal revenue through sponsorships,  
collaborations and investments under PPP.  A comprehensive SOP is being issued in this regard. 
 
Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Committee, further, suggests that one Member of Parliament should be included on the 
Governing Board of each of the Institutions on the lines of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
and other such institutions to assist the working of Akademis and to provide ground reports to 
the Akademis. 
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Akademis invite the nominations from States and Union Terr itories for its General 
Council. I t is purely a prerogative of Stat es and UTs to nominate legislature or Member of 
Parliament. The recommendation of the Committee will be placed for approval while 
formulating new constitutions and governing boards. 
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Akademis must work towards increasing cultural public infrastructure such as 
affordable workspaces and easy access to cultural centres and cultural hubs across the country. 
They should bring activities closer to people and increase outreach through different means such 
as the EAST (Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely) principle. 
 (Para 70) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Different Akademis have devised programs and events which are closer to the public 
viz., gramlok by Sahitya Akademi, theatre training workshops by NSD and SNA , outreach 
training programs by Kalakshetra and CCRT. The suggestion of the Committee would be taken 
seriously and all Akademis will be directed to enlarge the domain of their activities bringing the 
public closer and to build new audiences. 
Technological Advancements/Digital accessibility  

 
4 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. Akademis should develop online learning platforms or learning management systems that 
offer courses, workshops, and educational resources. These platforms can provide a range of 
content, including video lectures, interactive modules, downloadable materials, and assessments. 
 (Para 86) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The institutes employ online learning management systems to offer courses, workshops 
and educational resources. The Vedic Heritage Por tal of the Indira Gandhi National Centre for 
Arts (IGNCA) in an online portal that is serving as a  one-stop solution for the user, for any 
information regarding the Vedic heritage. 
6.2 The suggestion of the esteemed Committee has been informed to all Akademis and they 
are working on developing such modules. 
 
Protection of rural and tribal culture 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee also believes that it is important to prioritize the voices and perspectives 
of tribal communities, while also providing platforms for them to share their culture with a wider 
audience. Akademis should develop educational outreach programs that   promote tribal and 
rural culture in schools, colleges, and local communities. There is also a need for collaboration 
with tribal organizations, NGOs, and tribal development agencies to jointly support initiatives 
for the promotion of tribal culture. Further, Akademis must promote rural stays and tribal stays, 
especially among the younger generation to acquaint them with the cultural  heritage of the 
country. 
 (Para 118) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The Committee's recommendation is noted for compliance. 
 
Leveraging G20 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee recommends that Akademis should collaborate with tourism authorities 
and G-20 stakeholders to promote cultural tourism in India. Akademis should also encourage G -
20 delegates to explore Indian cultural treasures beyond the conference venues, thus promoting 
tourism and economic opportunities. Akademis can initiate collaborative pro jects between 
National Akademis and cultural institutions from G -20 member countries. This can involve joint 
exhibitions, performances, artist residencies, or cultural exchanges. Digital platforms like social

Budgetary Allocation and Issues  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the overall budget allocation for the Ministry of Culture is only 
0.075% of the total budget, which is grossly inadequate. In particular, the combined budgetary 
allocation (2023 -24) for the National Akademis is just Rs. 401 crore. The Committee in this 
regard, recommends that the Ministry of Culture should increase the budgetary allocation to the 
National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions in order to increase their efficiency and 
outreach. 
 (Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The budget allocated to the Minis try is distributed among the stakeholders in accordance 
with the programmes/activities planned during the year. The total budget allocation to the 
Ministry for 2023-24 was Rs. 3399.65 crore. Out of which funds allocated to the Akademis was 
Rs. 401.27 crore  i.e. about 11.8% of the total allocation of the Ministry. Whenever, additional 
fund requirement is requested by the Akademis, during the year, the same is considered 
generously by the Ministry based on merits and required funds are made available through 
supplementary grants. 
  
Recommendation/Observation

spend roughly 2%-5% of their budget on the promotion of art and culture and a majority of the

which is not the case in India. 
 (Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry

Government Sources as well, wherever feasible.

CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE 
MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that only the Chairman of Sahitya Akademi is elected. The process 
for appointment of the Chairman/President as also their tenure varies between the Akademis. 
The tenure of the Governing Body is also different for the different Akademis, ranging between 3 
years for Lalit Kala Akademi to 10 years for Kalakshetra Foundation. There are no fixed 
guidelines with regard to the number of me mbers of the Governing Council, the number of 
meetings to be held, etc. Also, there are no people's representatives in the Governing Council of 
the Akademis. 
 (Para 17) 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee observes that there are different parameter s for different Akademis. In 
Committee's view, this lack of uniformity is not desirable as it leads to administrative and 
organisational inconsistencies among the various Akademis and Institutions. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends Government to formula te a policy emphasizing uniformity among all the 
Akademis in terms of the tenure of the Chairman/President, representation and election of the 
General Council, and the minimum number of meetings to be held each year. If required, 
legislation governing the Akademis/ Institutions may be amended to ensure uniformity among the 
Akademis and their functionaries. 
 (Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 It is submitted that the Memorandum of Association (MoA)/Constitution of each 
Akademi has the set guidelines for app ointment of Chairman / President, tenure of the General 
Council, number of members of the General Council and number of meetings to be held. 
Ministry is making efforts to bring uniformity in appointment and governance structure across 
all the Akademis. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.2 The Committee notes the Ministry’s reply and reiterates its recommendation for 
establishing a uniform policy regarding appointment and governance structure across all 

 
28 
  
the Akademis. It believes that having fixed guideli nes will promote  parity and  effective 
functioning within the Akademis and will also aid the Ministry in exercising administrative 
control.  Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry to consider the inclusion of a  
Member of Parliament (MP) on the Governing Councils of each Institution.   
 
Regional Centres and Zonal Cultural Centre (ZCCs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee takes note of IGNCA's reply that the opening of Regional Centres in more 
number of States would be feasible subject to the a llocation of more funds for staff as well as 
establishment costs. The Committee takes note of the fund constraints faced by the Institutions. In 
this regard, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should seriously consider 
enhancing the budgetary allocation for the Akademis. The Committee also noted the suggestion 
from the National School of Drama, requesting Hon'ble MPs to contribute funds from MPLAD 
funds which could be used in the enhancement of art and culture education. 
(Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The total budget allocation to the Ministry for 2023 -24 is Rs. 3399.65 crore an d the 
allocation to the Akademis is Rs. 401.27 crore which is about 11.8% of the allocation.  In order 
to meet the additional requirement, if any, during the year, funds ar e made available to the 
Akademis through supplementary grants. It may kindly be appreciated that the grants allocated 
to the Ministry is decided by the Ministry of Finance. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.2 The Committee feels that sufficient budget is crucial for the Akademis growth. In 
the light of the repl y of IGNCA regarding establishing of new Regional Centres, the 
Committee  emphasizes that the Ministry should re assess the budgetary requirements  at 
the RE 2024-25 stage and at BE s tage in subsequent financial years. Also, Ministry should 
prepare a consolidated proposal for additional budget, keeping in view  the expansion 
requirements of each Akademi and the same may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance  
for approval.  
  
Administrative Staff and Vacancies 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee observes that the Government's Cultural Institutions are affected by 
vacancies and a lack of trained manpower. Lack of manpower not only affects the working of 

 
29 
  
these organizations but also hinders their efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry of Culture should urgently take measures to fill up the said vacancies at each level 
since manpower is the backbone of these organizations. The Committee also emphasizes that the 
Ministry must conduct the recruitment process in a fair and transparent manner, adhering to 
equal opportunity for all and non -discrimination principles. The Committee may be apprised of 
the recruitment process being followed in the Akademis and Cultural Institutions to fill in posts. 
(Para 37) 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee desires the Ministry to complete the recruitment process and fill up all the 
vacancies within a fixed period. The Ministry may also apprise the Committee of the status of the 
matter. 
(Para 38)

5.1 As per Ministry of Finance guidelines dated 05.01.2024 regarding creation / revival /

abolished, and to f ill these posts administrative M inistry needs to revive these posts by taking 
Ministry of Finance‟s approval. Ministry of Culture is making continuous efforts to revive these 
posts. Further, the posts which are lying vacant for less than 5 years, the recruitmen t process for 
these vacancies are undergoing expeditiously in all the academies. 
5.2 The current sanctioned / vacant strength of each Akademi is enclosed at Annexure III. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation

in-position strength across all  seven Central Akademis. Specifically, three Akademis viz.,

5.4 The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for such meager working strength in 
the Akademis and urges the Ministry to make concentrated effo rts to streamline the

Segregation of Functions 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that segregation of functions is also an important concept to 
internal control frameworks , financial reporting and regulatory compliance. The overall 

 
30 
  
effectiveness of the organization depends on an effective internal administration, adequate 
division of responsibilities, and the requirement of a sufficient number of staff who are 
adequately trained. Separation of functions is an important mechanism to help reduce the risk of 
fraud, error and other financial misconduct. In addition, it helps to promote accountability, 
transparency and ethical behaviour within the organization. The Committee, the refore, 
recommends segregation of the purchasing, provisioning, financing and policy -making functions 
within the Akademis. 
(Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 There are various verticals  under each A kademi to handle internal frameworks. As per 
the Memorandum of Associations / Constitutions of th ese Academies, the Governing Board / 
Society is the supreme authority in each Akademi which formulates policies as per the mandate. 
Further, General Financial Rules (GFR) is applicable to all Autonomous Bodies of the  Ministry 
and hence follows all purchasing, financial policies as per GFR. Administration Unit of each 
Akademi is responsible for hiring manpower as per approved RRs. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.2 The Committee is of the opinion that , given their distinct frameworks and mandate, 
each Akademi should have its own  dedicated functioning authority. The Committee notes 
the Ministry’s reply and reiterates that the administrative sections responsible  for tasks 
such as hiring manpower, purchasing, HR issues, and budget management  should be 
clearly defined in each Akademi and be empowered to ensure efficient functioning.  
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee feels that the National Akademis need to enhance its outreach, both  
within urban and rural areas, to make the arts more accessible and inclusive. Without effective 
outreach programmes, Akademis may struggle to reach a broader audience, beyond their 
immediate surroundings. A lack of outreach can reinforce existing cultural  hierarchies and 
exclude cultural practices that are not adequately represented or recognized. This exclusion can 
lead to marginalization of certain art forms, traditions or communities, thereby, limiting cultural 
diversity and stifling creativity. There i s also a risk of losing intangible cultural heritage, as 
there may be insufficient engagements with communities, artists and practitioners who are the 
custodians of these traditions. 
(Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 

 
31 
  
7.1 All the Akademi s through their  various regional centres try their  best to reach out to 
artists who are unaware of the functions and activities of t he Akademis. Also, some Akademis 
have project offices in different states for  particular art form. Further, Ministry of C ulture has 
set up seven Z onal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) in the country to protect, promote and preserve 
various forms of folk art & culture throughout the country and also to set up mechanism for 
development of the cultures of various regions. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2 The Committee feels that to enhance outreach and awareness, Ministry should issue 
directives to all the Akademis to implement specific measures.  Akademis could leverage  
social media platforms, radio stations, local newspapers , and other channels to enga ge 
communities, art practitioners and artists from across the country and tap into their full  
potential.  Additionally, t he Akademis should explore ways to publicize  their events, 
seminars and workshops through various platforms to reach a wider  audience a nd 
encourage greater participation.  
 
Infrastructure and Facilities  
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee observes that investing in infrastructure for cultural Akademis is essential 
for supporting the growth, development, and sustainability of arti stic and cultural practices. 
Committee recommends that informal education may also be imparted through these Institutions. 
Ministry should provide the necessary funds and also promote synergy among the Institutions for 
sharing of infrastructural facilities. Committee also suggested Akademis to explore CSR funds to 
mobilise the resources for infrastructure developments including auditoriums, classrooms, 
studios, rehearsal halls and exhibition areas.  
(Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 This Ministry envisage s to  strengthen regional presence to facilitate the people of 
different region s and promote synergy among the Akademis for sharing of infrastructural 
facilities. All Akademis are autonomous in nature and they are free to obtain CSR funds. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.2 The Committee is of the opinion  that CSR funding could serve  as an additional 
budget source for the dev elopment and growth of Akademis.   The Committee may be 
apprised of the steps being taken by both the Ministry and the Akademis to secure and 

 
32 
  
utilize this funding.  The Committee also seeks information on the CSR funds received by

Returning of Awards  
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee notes the i nstances of recipients of awards, given by Akademis (such as 
Sahitya Akademi Awards), returning their awards in protest of certain political issues which are 
outside the ambit of the cultural realms and the autonomous functioning of the concerned 
Akademi. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of the other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. 
(Para 92) 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. A Member of the Committee opined agains t the view that artists, authors and other 
intellectuals and performers who have been recommended for awards must sign a commitment 
that they will not return the awards as a form of protest at any point in the future before they are 
able to receive it. He was of the view that India is a democratic country, and our Constitution 
has provided to every citizen the freedom of speech and expression and also the freedom to 
protest in any form. Returning of awards is only a form of protest. The Member added that th e 
Committee must strongly recommend to the Government to look into the actual issues in protest 
of which such awards have been returned and work towards resolving them. He was seconded by 
another Member. 
(Para 93) 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee questioned the re-engagement of such awardees who joined the Akademi 
after insulting it. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. The Member again submitted that the Akademis and the other Institutions should 
continue to work together with these artists and not shun them. 
(Para 94) 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee observes that the awards given by each Akademi con tinue to be top 
honors for an artist in India. The Committee emphasizes that Sahitya Akademi or other 
Akademis are apolitical organizations. There is no place for politics. The Committee, therefore, 
suggests that whenever an award is given, the consent of the recipient must be taken, so that 
he/she does not return it because of political reasons; as it is disgraceful to the country. The 
Committee recommends prior concurrence of short -listed candidates for awards before 

 
33 
  
finalization. A system may be put in p lace where an undertaking is taken from the proposed 
awardee citing acceptance of the award and that the awardees cannot dishonour the award at 
any point of time in future. Awards may not be given without such an undertaking. In the event

in the future. 
(Para 95)

12.1 The Ministry agrees with the Committee's perspective and would like to avoid 
controversies in all regards. However, obtaining a  signed commitment from the writer prior to

Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2 The Committee acknowl edges the  Ministry’s reply  and understands its concern

the North -East Region. It also reiterates the need for special emphasis on providing

Recommendation/Observation

management of the digital files it produces. 
(Para 129{iii})

manuscripts are available online for research purpose without download/ print facility. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
15.2 The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s reply and applauds the Ministry for its 
efforts in preserving, documenting and disseminating the country’s rich  manuscript 
heritage. The Committee  seeks information on  the numbe r of manuscripts still pending

CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE 
MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions  
The Committee notes the Ministry’s reply and reiterates its recommendation for 
establishing a uniform policy regarding appointment and governance structure across all 
the Akademis. It believes that having fixed guidelines will promote parity and effective 
functioning within the Akademis and will also aid the Ministry in exercising administrative 
control.  Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry to consider the inclusion of a  
Member of Parliament (MP) on the Governing Councils of each Institution.   
(Para 2.2) 
 
Regional Centres and Zonal Cultural Centre (ZCCs) 
The Committee feels that sufficient budget is crucial for the Akademis growth. In the light 
of the reply of IGNCA regarding establishing of new Regional Centres, the Committee  
emphasizes that the Ministr y should reassess the budgetary requirements at the RE 2024 -
25 stage and at BE stage in subsequent financial years. Also, Ministry should prepare a 
consolidated proposal for additional budget, keeping in view the expansion requirements of 
each Akademi and the same may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance for approval.  
(Para 3.2) 
  
Administrative Staff and Vacancies 
The Committee is concerned about the huge difference between the sanctioned and in -
position strength across all seven Central Akademis. Spe cifically, three Akademis viz., 
Sangeet Natak Akademi, CCRT, and Lalit Kala Akademi, are functioning with less than 
40% of their sanctioned strength. National School of Drama has approximately 48%, and 
IGNCA has around 36% vacancies against their sanctioned strengths.   
(Para 5.3) 
The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for such meager working strength in the 
Akademis and urges the Ministry to make concentrated efforts to streamline the processes 
and initiate the recruitment process at the earliest.   
(Para 5.4) 

 
39 
  
 
Segregation of Functions 
The Committee is of the opinion that, given their distinct  frameworks and mandate, each 
Akademi should have its own dedicated functioning authority. The Committee notes the 
Ministry’s reply and reiterates that the admin istrative sections responsible for tasks such 
as hiring manpower, purchasing, HR issues, and budget management should be clearly 
defined in each Akademi and be empowered to ensure efficient functioning.   
(Para 6.2) 
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
The Committee feels that to enhance outreach and awareness, Ministry should issue 
directives to all the Akademis to implement specific measures.  Akademis could leverage 
social media platforms, radio stations, local newspapers, and other channels to engage 
communities, art practitioners and artists from across the country and tap into their full 
potential.  Additionally, the Akademis should explore ways to publicize their events, 
seminars and workshops through various platforms to reach a wider audience and 
encourage greater participation.  
(Para 7.2) 
 
Infrastructure and Facilities  
The Committee is of the opinion that CSR funding could serve as an additional budget 
source for the development and growth of Akademis.   The Committee may be apprised of 
the steps being taken  by both the Ministry and the Akademis to secure and utilize this 
funding.  The Committee also seeks information on  the CSR funds  received by each 
Akademi in the last three years and how these funds have been utilized.  
(Para 8.2) 
Returning of Awards  
The Committee acknowl edges the  Ministry’s reply  and u nderstands its concern about  
confidentiality and legal implications related to obtaining signed commitment s. The 
Committee suggests that the commitment document should  include a non-disclosure clause 
to prot ect against  breach of confidentiality. Alternatively, the Ministry  should explore 
other measures to prevent similar issues i n the future. A dditionally, a policy should be 
established to monitor  artists who have returned their award s but remain affiliated with 
the Akademi.  
(Para 12.2) 

 
40 
  
 
Youth Engagement 
The Committee feels that given the vast number of traditional dance and music forms in 
the country, it is crucial to support and nurture the talents of the youth. A handful of 
institutions and centres may not  be adequate to address the diverge range of art forms. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry and concerned Akademis make dedicated 
efforts to establish additional teaching institutions and centres, particularly in the North -
East Region, hilly areas, and islands, to create more opportunities for the young children.  
(Para 13.3) 
 
Representation and promotion of culture of North East States of India  
The Committee notes the reply and urges  the Ministry to allocate a specific portion of the 
budget for eac h Akademi to the development and promotion of the rich culture of the 
North-East Region. It also reiterates the need for special emphasis on providing assistance 
to NER to ensure maximum support and cultural growth in the region.  
(Para 14.2) 
 
Handling, preservation and digitization of Manuscripts 
The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s reply and applauds the Ministry for its efforts 
in preserving, documenting and disseminating the country’s rich manuscript heritage.  The 
Committee seeks information on  the number of manuscripts still pending digitization and 
Ministry’s roadmap to achieve 100% digitization.   
(Para 15.2) 
Non-availability of information in Hindi or any other local language 
The Committee recommends the Ministry to take necessary steps to at le ast first make the 
various art forms available in Hindi and English languages in order to maximize reach and 
accessibility. Following this, the Ministry, should work on making the information 
available in scheduled and other local languages, based on regio nal requirements, in a 
phased manner.  
(Para 16.2)

Construction of ROBs and RUBs 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee apprecia tes the increase in annual average progress in the number of 
Level Crossings (LCs) replaced with Road -Over-Bridges and Road -Under-Bridges. However, 
it also notes that the target of replacement of 1100 LCs set for 2023 -24 is lower than the 
annual average of  1207 progress achieved during 2014 -2023. The Committee is of the view 
that the target should be increased and the pace of replacement of LCs with ROBs/ RUBs 
should be expedited in the interest of greater safety and seamless mobility of the commuting 
public. 
(Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 As per the policy of the Ministry, all LCs on National Highways are to be replaced by 
ROB/RUB. Construction of ROBs/RUBs on NHs are taken up either on standalone basis or as part 
of improvement/ upgradation project of  a section of NH. The  recommendations of the Committee 
are noted and construction of ROBs/RUBs in replacement of existing LCs on NHs  will be 
expedited.

4. Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) should be used to penetrate the ground or structure, 
allowing for subsurface inspection of ROBs/RUBs. It can identify hidden defects, such as 
voids, delamination, or corrosion in concrete or steel elements. GPR can provide va luable 
information on the internal condition of the structure without the need for invasive 
investigations. 
Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) Systems should be adopted to involve the installation of 
sensors and monitoring devices on ROBs/RUBs to continuou sly monitor their structural 
behaviour. These sensors can measure parameters like vibrations, strains, and deflections, 
providing real-time data on the performance and health of the structure. SHM systems enable 
early detection of structural abnormalities and help in proactive maintenance and 
intervention. 
(Para 49) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Ground Penetrating Radar is being widely used to assess underground utilities. Foundation 
of ROBs/RUBs are generally not distressed as they are not located on river bed . Ministry has 
recently used guidelines for structural health monitoring on real time basis of bridges and structures 

4 
 
including ROBs and RUBs based on span length, location such as in coastal/highly polluted areas, 
age and history of previous rehabilitation/retrofitting measures using various kinds of sensors. 
 
Recommendation/Observation

particle testing, and radiographic testing, can be employed for ROB/RUBs inspection. These  
techniques assess the integrity of structural components, detect cracks, weld defects, or 
corrosion, and identify potential failure points. NDT methods are typically used in 
combination with visual inspections to provide a comprehensive assessment of the structure's 
condition. 
(Para 50)

5.1 Schmidt Hammer Test, Ultrasonic Pulse Velocity Test and other NDTs are carried out for

Environment clearances and land acquisition 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways in addressing the most important issue of land acquisition in fast tracking the 
ROB/RUB projects. The Bhoomira shi portal has undoubtedly expedited the process of land 
acquisition for National Highways. However, the Committee urges upon the Ministry and 
NHAI to accord continued priority to the land acquisition issue and fails to appreciate as to 
why huge Government  funds are parked with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition 
(CALAs). 
    (Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1  The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has launched Bhoomi Rashi Portal as a 
single point platform for online processing of Land Acquisit ion notification and payment of 
compensation to accelerate Highways infrastructure in India. The portal is a new mile stone in the 
nation’s journey towards digitization and transparency. The objective of the portal is to fast track the 
process of Land Acquisition notifications and to obviate the necessity of parking of huge amount of 
government fund with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition. 
6.2  The Ministry has made it mandatory for payment of compensation of Land Acquisition 

5 
 
through Bhoomi Rashi Port al for the projects of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highway and 
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The Ministry is continuously impressing upon the 
NHAI to make payment only through Bhoomi Rashi portal. The efforts has also been made for on -
boarding of National Highways Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited (NHIDCL) for 
payment of compensation through Portal. 
 6.3  The Present system of payment of compensation in respect of Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways does not allow park ing of any fund with CALA. In case of NHAI, limit is 
created/fund is deposited for particular projects in CALA account up to which CALA can make 
payment through PFMS directly into account of the beneficiary. Therefore, the present system in 
NHAI inherently does not allow parking of Government funds with CALA. However, in some cases 
CALA could not be able to release compensation due to litigations in Courts, non -acceptance of 
award by beneficiaries, mismatch of beneficiaries’ details, arbitration awards etc. and the funds/limit 
remain parked/unpaid in CALAs Accounts.  
6.4  NHIDCL deposits the LA compensation amount with the concern CALA after passing of 
award under section 3G of National Highways Act, 1956 so as to enable them to distribute the 
compensation amount to beneficiary. No payment is deposited to concerned CALA’s account prior 
to 3G Award. In addition, NHIDCL has opened Zero balance accounts for the CALAs with only 
drawing rights so that money gets placed with the CALA for disbursement only. However,  in some 
cases, the CALAs are in the process of shifting to Zero balance accounts system.  
6.5  It is anticipated that once all the Implementing Agencies are completely on - boarded on 
Bhoomi Rashi Portal, there would be no parking of government funds with CALAs in any manner.

Use of technology for inspections 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. Modern technology for periodic inspection of ROBs/ RUBs can help in the early 
detection of damage, minimize human errors and lower maintenance costs.  The Committee, 
therefore, feels that more steps should be taken to adopt modern technology for inspection of 
ROBs/RUBs. Drones equipped with high -resolution cameras and sensors can be used to 
capture aerial imagery of ROBs/RUBs, providing a detailed visual assessment of th e 
structure's condition. The images can be analysed further to identify any signs of damage, 
deterioration, or structural weakness. Drones are particularly useful for accessing hard -to-
reach areas and can significantly reduce inspection time and costs. 
(Para 47) 
  

30 
 
8.1 Laser scanning technologies, such as LiDAR, can be used to generate accurate 3D 
models of ROBs/RUBs. LiDAR sensors emit laser pulses and measure the reflected light,
