6.3.     However, with the exponentially increased NH network length and the proposed 
development of NHs under various schemes, there is a need to increase the intake of CES  (Roads) 
officers. Further, 20% of the technical posts of NHAI are fitted by CES (Roads) officers. 

48 
 
6.4      In order to address the shortage of CES (Roads) officers in the Ministry and its 
implementing agencies, cadre review of CES (Roads) has been undertaken from time to time. 
Consequent to the last cadre review in 2017, the cadre strength of CES (Roads) was increased from 
242 to 328. Presently, a fresh proposal for cadre r eview for increase in number of posts of CES 
(roads) cadre from 328 to 425 is under consideration after the recommendation of Cadre Review 
Committee under Cabinet Secretary. Further, NHAI has also identified 518 vacancies in the various 
grades under differ ent recruitment modes, deputation and di rect recruitment, to fill up under 
Mission Recruitment Mode during the year 2023-24. 
6.5  The Ministry has revived 17 posts of Senior Technical Assistant and 04 posts or of 
Technical Assistants of Subordinate Technic al Staff of General Central Services Cadre in the year 
2022 with the approval of the Department of Expenditure. 
6.6  As regard to consultant in the Ministry, it is stated that the consultants are engaged in the 
Ministry based on their administrative requir ement which changes time to time after following the 
duty procedure prescribed by Department of Expenditure & GFR Rules, 2017. 
6.7  In order to enhance the skill of the CES (Roads) officers, the Ministry had established an 
institute namely Indian Academy o f Highway Engineers which provides the intensive trainings to 
these officers on the latest evolving technologies in the Road Sector on regular basis. 
6.8 As regard NHAI, 72 no of External Professionals has been engaged by NHAI from April 
2018 to till date based on the norms for engagement of External Professionals have been approved 
by the Authority in its 113th meeting held on 15.06.2017.As regards staff requirement, status of the 
recruitment process has been indicated in Annexure-I. 
Further recommendation/observation 
6.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should expedite the recruitment process 
and fill up the vacancies for smooth working and expansion of road infrastructure. Further, 
the cadre review with provision for capacity building should be taken undertaken as early as 
possible keeping in mind the five R’s recommended by the Committee. 
Budgetary Allocation 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes that the provisioning and utilization of funds for the construction of 
ROBs/ RUBs could be made better. There needs to be more co-ordination between the Railways and 
the State Governments in providing a budget and executing the works. Further, the large chunk of unspent amount 

49 
 
under the Setu Bharatam programme is an overarching concern. There  is a need for proper channelization and 
utilization of the earmarked funds. 
(Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 There is no separate funds allocation for ROB/RUB work  under Setu Bharatam or any other scheme /program 
and expenditure are incurred from the overall allocation of the State/UT. 
Further recommendation/observation 
7.2 The Committee recomm ends that a separate allocation must be provided to States for construction of 
RoBs/RuBs so that the process is expedited and there are no delays in the construction. 
 
(ii) Road Safety related issues 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee notes that the Motor Vehicles Amendment Act (MVAA), 2019 creates adequate 
accountability framework to ensure that road -owning agencies, contractors and concessionaires are he ld 
accountable for faulty road design and construction. To operationalise this at the State level, the Act provides 
discretionary powers to States to create Rules under  Section 210D.  The Section 210 D authorizes State Governments 
to make rules for design,  construction and maintenance standards for National Highways and roads other than 
National Highways, respectively. 
(Para 84) 
 
8.1 The Committee, therefore, recom mends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should persuade 
State Governments to fr ame such rules under Section 210D of the MVAA Act at the earliest.  The Committee may also 
be kept apprised of the matter.   
(Para 85) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.2 The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is the principal instrument through which road transport sector is  regulated in 
the country.  Ministry deals with various rules and regulation framed under the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and Central 
Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 pertaining to Transport Sector.  
8.3 The Section 210D of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 provides as under:- 
                  210D. Power of  State Government to make rules - The State Government may make rules for design, 
construction and maintenance standards for roads other than national highways, and for any other matter which is, or 
may be, prescribed by the State Government.” 
Further recommendation/Observation 
8.4 The Committee reiterates that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should persuade State 
Governments to frame such rules under Section 210D of the MVAA Act to create adequate accountab ility 
framework to ensure that road -owning agencies, contractors and concessionaires are held accountable for 
faulty road design and construction.  
Absent Pedestrian and Cyclist Facilities 
9. The Committee recommends including  pedestrian and bicycle facilit ies as a mandatory and integral part of 

50 
 
bridged sections to accommodate the requirements of all road users, promoting safety, accessibility, and sustainable 
transportation options. Moreover, the mandatory inclusion of pedestrian and bicycle facilities on b ridges promotes 
social equity, providing equal access to all members of the community, regardless of their mode of transportation 
or physical abilities.  
(Para 117) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Footpaths are provided on Major bridges and ROBs for pedestrians. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
9.2 The Committee notes that there are many roads where pedestrian and cycling facilities are not 
available. The Ministry should identify such roads and provide pedestrian and cycling facilities at the earliest. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee recommends that the Government should establish a Central Coordinating Body or a 
Committee comprising representatives from key ministries involved in road development, namely, the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highway s, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change, and Ministry of 
Railways. This body will facilitate regular communication, coordination, and decision -making among the Ministries. 
Such a step will also help overcome the delay in construction due to waiting in approval of clearances. 
(Para 132) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Group of Infrastructure Committee is the body at highest level that address es policy level 
issues for faster implementation of infrastructure projects including N H projects. The Committee 
also reviews and take effective action to ensure that pending approvals for infrastructure projects 
are expedited. There is one to interaction/coordination with concerned Ministries at executive levels 
to expedite decision making. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
10.2 The Committee would like to know how frequently the Group of Infrastructure 
Committee meets . The Committee also suggests to include Public Representatives in this 
Group of Infrastructure Committee for better communication and functioning.  
Recommendation/Observation 
11. With reference to encroachments, the Committee recommends that the Ministries should 
conduct a comprehensive survey and mapping of the ROB/RUB area to identify encroachments and 
unauthorized structures by using modern surveying techniques, such as drones or satellite imagery 
so that proper remedial measures can be taken to get rid of encroachments around the infrastructure. 

51 
 
(Para 142) 
 
11.1 The concerned authorities must ensure to take legal actions ag ainst encroachers in accordance with relevant 
laws and regulations. They should initiate eviction proceedings and enforce penalties for unauthorized occupation. 
Adequate humanitarian support and assistance should be provided to those affected by encroachme nt- induced eviction. 
(Para 143) 
 
11.2 Further, the Committee recommends that the engagement with the local community and stakeholders should be 
strengthened to obviate any future encroachments. The relevant NGOs, advocacy bodies and local opinion of leade rs 
may also be roped in to create awareness about non-encroachment of the public infrastructure spaces. 
(Para 144) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.3 Encroachments on National Highways including the locations around ROBs and RUBs are identified during 
physical inspections of NHs as well as captured in surveys conducted with Network Survey Vehicle.  
11.4 As per National Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002, the Ministry has notified Highway Administration to 
implement provisions of this Act including   removal of encroachments/unauthorized occupations and encroachments on 
NHs including locations around ROBs and RUBs are removed through such provisions.  
Further Recommendation/Observation 
11.5 The Committee recommends that removal of encroachments must be a priority for  improving the 
accessibility and safety of road users. The details of steps taken till now to remove encroachment must be shared 
with the Committee. 
 
Fund allocation and support to IRC 
12. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider deputing so me officers having 
interest and inclination toward standardization, R&D to work in the IRC.  Also, the Ministry may 
consider providing a reasonable amount of corpus seed fund to the IRC to manage the function of 
its Secretariat, the modalities of which may be worked out in consultation with the IRC.  
(Para 166) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 As of  today, IRC Secretariat has  staff of 38 (3 Technical & 35 Non - Technical) against total sanctioned 
strength of 64 personnel to manage routine activities of the IRC to achieve its objective. Four retired officers from 
MORTH/ CRRI are also working as Technical Consultant in IRC.IRC has its own revenue from membership, sale of 
publications, accreditation of materials, sponsorships etc. Ministry also provide funds to IRC fo r specific activities as 
and when required but R&D works are primarily carried out by academic / research institutes for which Ministry 
sanctions research projects to such institutes. The outcomes of such research projects are utilized by Technical 
committees of IRC for framing new guidelines / revising existing guidelines. 
 
Further recommendation/Observation 

52 
 
12.2 The Committee feels that the Ministry should evolve some alternative to provide a reasonable amount of 
corpus seed fund to the IRC to manage the functions of its Secretariat, the modalities of which may be worked 
out in consultation with the IRC. 
 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) technologies can be integrated 
into ROBs/RUBs to enhance road safety and better traffic management. These include systems for automated traffic 
control, real -time monitoring of road conditions, traffic signalling, and vehicle detection. ITS can improve the 
efficiency of traffic flow, reduce congestion, and enhance overall safety. 
(Para 180) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 Intelligent Transport System is being adopted in Expressways and high speed corridors.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
13.2 The Committee recommends that the Intelligent Transport System must also be launched in National 
and other State Highways to enhance road safety and better traffic management.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
14. Smart Sensors embedded in ROBs/RUBs can continuously monitor the structural health, detecting and 
alerting to any anomalies or signs of deterioration. SHM systems provide real -time data on the structural integrity, 
stress, vibrations, and deformation of the infrastructure, facilitating proactive maintenance and preventing failures.  
(Para 181) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 Structural health monitoring on real time basis using sensors is carried out in some very  important 
bridges. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
14.2 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should identify the bridges showing signs of 
deterioration and thereafter structural health monitoring should be done of all those bridges on a regular basis.  
 
Private Sector Participation 
15. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should conduct comprehensive feasibility studies to assess the 
viability of implementing PPP models for ROB/RUB development. The Ministry should evaluate factors such as 
project size, revenue potential, market conditions, and potential private sector interest. Feasibility studies will provide 
valuable insights into the suitability of PPP and help in making informed decisions. 
(Para 184) 
 
15.1 The Committee recommends that an assessment of legal and regulatory framework should be pursued to 

53 
 
evaluate the existing legal and regulatory framework and to identify any barriers  or limitations to implementing PPP 
in ROB/RUB development.  The Ministry should also identify necessary amendments or new legislations required to 
facilitate PPP arrangements, ensure transparency, and provide a favourable business environment for private 
partners. 
(Para 185) 
Reply of the Committee 
15.2 Economic and Financial viability of all NH projects including ROBs and RUBs are determined as a rule. 
However, ROB/RUB as stand alone projects are generally not viable / practicable on PPP mode considering s ize and 
therefore these stand alone projects are implemented on EPC mode. Corridor projects including ROBs and RUBs are 
implemented either in EPC mode or PPP mode depending on overall project viability.  
Further Recommendation/Observation 
15.3 The Committee would like to know about these stand alone projects which are being implemented on 
EPC mode and the present status thereof. 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. The Committee also suggests that the Ministries should establish transparent and competitive 
procurement processes to attract capable private entities. They should also implement a fair and competitive 
bidding process that encourages multiple private sector players to participate.  
(Para 186) 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1     Procurement of contractor and c onsultant are taken up using Standard RFP document and through e -tender 
procurement mode (Central Public Procurement Portal - CPPP). 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
16.2 The Committee would like to know how these modes are impartial enough to provide a fair and 
competitive bidding process. 
 
Sustainable and environment-friendly roads 
Recommendation/Observation 
17. The Committee appreciates the innovative efforts made in the direction of construction of environmentally 
sustainable roads. However, it feels that given the national aspirations to gradually move towards a zero -waste 
circular economy, more measures should be taken in this regard. The Committee suggests that the Ministries should 
adopt features like rain gardens, bioswales, and permeable pavement s to manage stormwater runoff and improve 
water quality. Green infrastructure can help recharge groundwater, reduce the load on drainage systems and help 
enhance biodiversity in roadside areas. 
(Para 192) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1 Rain Water Harvesting St ructures are constructed as part of Highway Development Project. Ministry has 
issued policy guide lines for use of municipal waste, industrial waste, recycling of road reclaimed materials etc. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 

54 
 
17.2 The Committee feels tha t there is an urgent need to explore more viable options other than Rain 
Water Harvesting Structures  alone. The Committee reiterated that the Ministries should adopt features like 
rain gardens, bioswales, and permeable pavements to manage stormwater runoff  and improve water quality. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
18. The Ministries should also implement Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS) to manage surface water runoff 
from roads. SuDS techniques include infiltration basins, constructed wetlands, and detention  ponds that mimic 
natural hydrological processes. SuDS can reduce the risk of flooding, promote groundwater recharge, and improve 
water quality by removing pollutants. 
(Para 193) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1 Adequate drainage measures as per hydrological ana lysis/site requirements are provided. For the efficient 
design of drainage system, the  RFP document for preparation of DPR, Consultancy  Service has been 
recently strengthened.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
18.2 The Committee enquires that even after adequate drainage measures are provided, there are problems 
of water logging at many places. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should focus on SuDS to 
manage surface water runoff from roads. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
19. The Committee also recommends that the Ministries can explore opportunities to integrate renewable energy 
sources into road infrastructure. This can include incorporating solar panels into noise barriers or utilizing solar -
powered lighting along roads. Renewable energy integrati on can help reduce dependence on fossil fuels and 
contribute to a more sustainable transportation network. 
(Para 195) 
Reply of the Ministry 
19.1 At some NH sections (particularly rural areas), solar energy is being used for lighting. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
19.2 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make all efforts to utilise solar energy for 
lighting purposes all across NH stretches in the country.

on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundred F ifty-Seventh 
Report on ‘Development of Niche Tourism (including Spiritual Tourism), Theme -based

respect of all the observations/ recommendations contained in the Report. The replies have 
been categorized as follows:-

CHAPTER-I 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Rural Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee while appreciating the Best Village Compe tition initiated by the 
Ministry, is dismayed to note that in the past one year, only one Model Rural Cluster has 
been identified, without any action being taken on the ground. The Committee notes that the 
villages to be covered in the Vibrant Villages pro gramme are located in far -flung areas, and 
close to borders, often in difficult terrains. The Committee feels that the State of Uttarakhand 
has a number of border villages with rich traditions and local culture and recommends that 
the Ministry may make con certed efforts to develop the Model Rural Cluster inUttarakhand 
within a targeted time schedule. 
. 
(Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Suggestion of the Committee is noted. The Ministry of Tourism has now revamped 
the SwadeshDarshan scheme as SwadeshDarshan 2. 0 with the objective to develop 
sustainable and responsible tourism destinations. For this purpose, the Ministry of Tourism 
has also identified 55 destinations in the country for development under the scheme. In 
addition to creating essential and basic inf rastructure at the destinations, the Ministry is 
focusing on creating and curating tangible and intangible experiences so that the destination 
can be holistically developed. As part of this endeavor, the  Central Sanctioning 
and Monitoring Committee (CSMC) in its meeting dated 13.09.2023 has in - principally 
approved an experience ‘Vibrant Village Cluster Experience at Gunji’ in the State of 
Uttarakhand. The State Government has been provided the essential technical support by 
providing ‘Project Development a nd Management Consultant (PDMC)’ under this scheme 
and the state has been asked to get the DPR prepared accordingly for further consideration. 
 
Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, And Exhibitions (Mice) & Wedding Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee notes that India has less than 1% share in the Global MICE business 
despite being one of the fastest growing economies. India was ranked 28th with 158 meetings  

3 
 
in 2019 International Congress and Convention Association (ICCA) ranking of cou ntries. 
Indian cities are ranked poorly in the international ranking of cities by ICCA in terms of the 
number of international associations meetings. There are only 07 cities of India in the top 
475 cities, the topmost being Delhi at the 75th position with 37 meetings held and Ahmedabad 
at the bottom at the 424 th position with 04 meetings. Even Goa, which is one of the country’s 
top tourist destinations, is ranked at the 307 th position with 08 meetings. The Committee also 
notes that India’s outbound MICE market is one of the fastest growing markets globally. 
 (Para 50) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      Observations of the Hon’ble Committee has been Noted. 
 
Wedding Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.      The Committee recommends that apart from development of infrastructure and facilities 
to support the growth of wedding tourism, the Ministry may also facilitate easy and uniform 
process of registration of marriages in every state of India even for couples belonging to 
other states. 
. 
 (Para 58) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The matter has been taken up with all State Governments/ UT Administrations. 
  
Cruise Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee observes that prior to Covid, there was a 35 per cent year -on-year 
growth of cruise traffic in  the country. Post -Covid, from 2021 onwards, there has been an 
increase in cruise traffic but the pre -Covid growth has still not been achieved. Prior to 
Covid, there were 4.7 lakh passengers on cruises and now, about 3 lakh passengers have 
been on cruises. 
 (Para 62) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Observation of the Hon’ble Committee has been Noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 

4 
 
5.        The Committee has been informed about five projects sanctioned under the Assistance 
to Central Agencies Scheme for promot ion of Cruise Tourism in Kerala (Annexure -III) 
from2016-17to2019-20.TheCommittee desires to know if similar assistance has been given 
for promotion of CruiseTourism in other States. 
(Para 64) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      The list of Central Financial Assistance sanctioned under the Scheme of Assistance to 
Central Agencies for promotion of Cruise Tourism in other States is at Annexure-II 
  
Medical And Wellness Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
6.        The Committee observes that lack of regulation on qu ality of service is a major 
concern and appreciates that the National Strategy is to encourage registration of all 
medical tourism facilitators with the Government. The Committee, however, recommends that 
such registration should    be mandatory as standard isation of services is the biggest 
impediment affecting medical tourism in India. The Committee recommends that while NABH 
accreditation may be highlighted in various source markets, the Ministry should encourage 
major Indian hospitals to obtain the JCI accreditation. 
. 
 (Para 72) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1      Since the matter relates to regulation of health services, it has been taken up with 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
  
Golf Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
7.        The Committee further observes that   though   the   Ministry   has drafted the National 
Strategies and constituted National Boards for most areas of Niche Tourism, developed 
websites and published newsletters yet, coordination with the concerned Ministries and 
formulation of pr oject schemes under the various niche areas seem to be wanting. The pace 
of implementation on the ground appears sluggish. Most of the  National Boards and Task 
Forces have held only 2-3 meetings in a year. Most of the websites for Niche Tourism do not 
provide complete and detailed information, necessary for the tourists.  The Ministry’s 
interactions with the stakeholders and State Governments appear sporadic. The growing gap 
between the strategic  vision and implementation needs to be bridged and the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may take necessary action for the same. 
 (Para 83) 

5 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1      Observation of the Hon’ble Committee has been noted for compliance. 
 Spiritual Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
8.      The Committee notes that of 23 Spiritual Circuits, 05 are yet to be completed out of 
which 02 circuits of Kerala are lagging much behind schedule.The work on the Sabarimala – 
Erumeli – Pampa-Sannidhanam circuit in Pathanamthitta district in Kerala had been 
initiated in 2016-17 while the SivagiriSreeNarayana Guru Ashram circuit had been initiated 
in 2018 -19. At the time of the Demands for Grants 2023 -24, the Committee had been 
informed that the reason for delays in these two Kerala Circuits was due to lack of clearance 
from the Temple Authorities. The Committee has been informed during its Study Visit to 
Kerala in September, 2023 that the status of physical completion of the two projects is 76% 
and 51%, respectively. The Committee is disappointed to see the slow progress on these  
important projects which have a target completion date of June, 2023 and October, 2023 
respectively. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should develop a clear  cut 
Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) and  obtain prior clearances and approvals from 
relevant authorities for future compliance in the interest of timely completion of projects. 
 (Para 95) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1      Observations of the Committee is noted. The Ministry of Tourism is regularly 
reviewing the progress of the referred delayed  projects and is providing necessary guidance 
so that the projects are smoothly completed. 
  
Prashad Scheme  
Recommendation/Observation 
9.      The Committee observes that the PRASHAD scheme was launched in 2014 -15 and 
completion of 21 projects out of 45 is certainly not a significant achievement, even taking into 
account the Covid years. The Committee points out that spiritual circuit projects were taken 
under SwadeshDarshan Scheme 1.0 also and the Ministry has had adequate experience of the 
kind of problems that ordinarily come up while dealing with construction and development at 
pilgrimage sites. The Committee calls upon the Ministry to be mindful of the potential 
problems and calibrate suitable response at the DPR stage, so that the projects are not hel d 
up at later stages, causing both time and cost overrun. 
 (Para 100) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1      Noted for compliance. 
 

6 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.        The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has taken the initiative to amend 
guidelines and f unding pattern midterm where necessary  and recommends that the Ministry 
may revise the timeline of the delayed projects and ensure that the projects under this scheme 
are completed within the revised timeline. The Committee also recommends that the 
PRASHAD Dashboard when online may be monitored on a real time basis at the level of a 
senior functionary in the Ministry to ensure the completion of all pending projects.. 
 (Para 102) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
10.1      Observation/ recommendation has been Noted. 
  
Promotion of Swadesh Darshan Schemes  
Recommendation/Observation 
11.        The Committee appreciates the Utsav Portal website and the Tourist Train initiatives 
of the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should study the impact of the 
projects completed under the Swadesh  Darshan 1.0 scheme on the tourism and analyse the 
shortcomings so that the same could be improved in SD 2.0. 
(Para 115) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1      The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
  
Potential Tourist Spots  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      In the meetings with the stakeholders, the    Committee was informed about various 
potential tourist spots in the country which have been placed at Annexure – IX. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may examine t he concept of Greenfield Tourism 
where new locations can be developed as potential tourism spots with the participation of 
Government of India and the concerned State Government with private investments for 
creation of modern tourist infrastructure, hotels  and all tourist            facilities          and 
connectivity by air, rail and road. The Statue of Unity near Kevadia in Gujarat is a classic 
example of Greenfield Tourism, being a man -made tourist destination which has earned a 
formidable reputation as a popular tourism spot. Another example is tourism on the sand 
dunes near the  Salasar Balaji Temple in the Churu District of Rajasthan where hotels and 
restaurants have come up to cater to the tourists who visit the temple and stay to enjoy the 
sand dunes in the desert. The Committee observes that development of such Greenfield tourist 
spots would take the pressure off the already established tourist spots which sometimes suffer 
from the adverse effects of over tourism.. 

7 
 
(Para 134) 
Reply of the Ministry         
12.1    The suggestion of the Committee is noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
13.      The Committee recommends that the Ministry may while promoting destinations in 
Arunachal Pradesh or Lakshadweep or such areas which require special permits, highli ght 
the requirement in its campaigns so that tourists are aware of the rules and are able to plan 
their schedule accordingly. 
(Para 135) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1    Ministry acknowledges that incorporating permit - related information in promotional 
campaigns for destinations, will help in enhanced tourist awareness, enabling better planning 
for their visits to these areas. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
14.      The Committee further observes that the Ministry had formulated the Draft National 
Tourism Polic y in July, 2022 incorporating key recommendations of NITI Aayog, Sectoral 
Group of Secretaries, global best practices from organizations such as UNWTO and policies 
and strategies formulated by other countries after multiple rounds of consultations and 
feedback from Central Ministries, State Governments and Industry Stakeholders. More than a 
year later, the policy, however, has still not been finalized. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry may make every effort to ensure that all concerns of the stakeh olders in the 
tourism and hospitality sector are addressed and the National Tourism Policy is put in place 
in a time-bound manner. 
 (Para 136) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1    The suggestion of the Committee is noted.  Ministry of Tourism is following the 
necessary procedure for seeking approval of the Competent Authority for draft National 
Tourism Policy.  
  
 Promotion Of Tourism Abroad By Indian Missions 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
15.      Upon enquiry by the Committee on the background of these Tourism Offi cers and 
whether they have been imparted training in promotion of tourism, it has been informed that 

8 
 
these officers were already dealing with the subject of promotion of Indian culture and

17.      The Committee observes that films can h ave a massive impact on destination 
marketing as visitors are often inspired to visit filming locations featured in popular films.

Rural Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that in  a predominantly agrarian and rural economy like 
India, rural tourism has immense potential for boosting employment a nd income for villagers 
while offering opportunities to the city dwellers to take a break from the hectic pace of urban 
life to experience nature and local culture at a much slower pace. India is home to a diverse 
range of unique villages, each with its own cultural, architectural and historical significance. 
Unique villages such as ‘Mattur’ in Karnataka where all the residents speak only Sanskrit 
and many others offer a glimpse into India’s rich traditions and culture. The Committee, 
however, observes that the Rural Tourism website does not provide details as to how to travel 
to the unique villages nor details regarding rural home  stays for most of the villages. Even 
the Khonoma village page does not provide any useful details for the tourists. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the Rural Tourism website has all details of 
rural homestays, travel connectivity and tourist spots in respect of every village featured for 
the convenience of the tourists. 
. 
 (Para 26) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The Rural Tourism India website is integrated with the NIDHI+ portal and the content 
and the details related to the home stays are directly fetched from www.nidhi.tourism.gov.in 
Also the website is continuously upgrading the content on it. However, due to the excessive 
amount of data the time taken to upload the data varies. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 


44 
 
1.2      The Committee appreciates the Ministry's ongoing efforts to integrate the Rural 
Tourism India website with the NIDHI+ portal and its commitment to upgrading the 
website's content.  
1.3 The Committee recommends for the implementation of regular content audits to 
ensure that the information on the Rural Tourism website is accurate, up -to-date, and 
user-friendly.  
1.4 The Ministry should create a schedule for these audits, prioritizing villages that 
are likely to attract a significant number of tourists. 
 
1.5 While recognizing the challenge s of handling large volumes of data, the 
Committee recommends the Ministry to explore more efficient methods for uploading 
and integrating data from the NIDHI+ Portal. This may include technological upgrades 
or the use of advanced data management tools to minimize delays and ensure that the 
latest information is easily accessible to tourists. 
 
1.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry collaborate  and work  closely with 
local authorities and tourism boards in the featured villages  to ensure the accuracy and 
comprehensiveness of the information provided . T his collaboration will help capture 
and present all relevant details, including lesser -known travel routes and homestay 
options, accurately on the website. 
 
Adventure Tourism  
 Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee notes that there have been a n increasing number of accidents in 
Adventure sports, especially in paragliding, which has claimed the lives of a number of 
tourists in the last few years. As per media reports, even “soft adventure” sports like trekking 
have led to casualties in certain situations. The Committee has been informed by stakeholders 
that 3 Gs - Guidelines, Guides and Gears – are critical in risk mitigation. The Committee has 
also been informed that the Ministry has released guidelines for safety and quality norms for 15 Land B ased, 07 
Air Based and 07 Water Based adventure tourism activities, which cover the entire range of thrilling activities. 
Besides, some States have also adopted various regulatory measures and safety protocols to address the 
inherent concerns of adventure tourism. ISO 21101:2014 and BIS have laid down safety management standards 
for compliance by adventure activities service providers that act as benchmarks for safe adventure activities. 
The Committee desires to know about the impact of such safety guidelin es    on    reduction    of accidents in 
adventure tourism. The Ministry may give data on the number of accidents as also the casualties which have 
taken place in adventure tourism in the country in the last five years. The Committee has also been informed  
that while testing and certification of PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) kits is necessary, it is difficult for 
small Indian manufacturing enterprises to obtain the universally accepted international certifications like UIAA 
(French) (International Cli mbing and Mountaineering Federation). The Committee recommends that testing 
labs where certification is done by the BIS may help small enterprises in this field.  
. 

45 
 
(Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The Ministry is committed to continuous improvement  and enhancement of safety standards in 
adventure tourism. In order to provide impetus to the development of adventure tourism in the country, the 
Ministry of Tourism has notified a National Strategy for adventure tourism. The Strategy focuses on 
developing adventure destinations, promoting safety in adventure tourism, skill development, capacity building 
and marketing.  
2.2 As part of implementation process of the aforesaid strategy document, Ministry of Tourism has 
drafted a “Model Adventure Tourism Safet y Law” after consultations with States, Line Ministries and various 
industry stakeholders. The final draft of the “Model Adventure Tourism Safety Law” has been circulated to 
Stakeholders and State/UT’s Governments for inputs.  
   
 Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.3      The Committee acknowledges the reply of the Ministry but reiterates its request for detailed data 
on the number of accidents and casualties in adventure tourism over the last ﬁve years. This information 
is essential for evaluating the e ﬀectiveness of the safety guidelines and standards in mitigating risks 
associated with adventure sports. The Committee urges the Ministry to provide this data at the earliest, 
including a breakdown by speciﬁc activities (e.g., paragliding, trekking) and th e locations where these 
incidents occurred. The Ministry address the Committee's identified safety gaps.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee feels that strict adherence to safety guidelines and implementation of safety protocols can 
be possible only if responsible and licensed/ certified adventure tour operators handle the activities. Licensed 
tour operators play an important role in promotion of adventure tourism as they conduct thorough risk 
assessments, implement safety measures, and pro vide high quality safety gears, besides engaging experienced 
and professional guides to handle emergency situations. The Committee has been informed that presently, 
adventure tour operators‟ licenses are issued by either the Centre or the States and there are still a lot of 
unlicensed tour operators in the country’s adventure tourism sector who operate without requisite permits, 
certifications and regulatory approvals to meet the requirements of safety,quality and also the law in thefield. 
The Committee desires to know what action has been taken or is proposed to be taken by the Ministry on the 
unlicensed adventure tour operators. The Committee has also been informed that the Ministry has circulated a 
draft model adventure tourism law to all the States/UTs f or feedback. The Committee stresses that high risk 
adventure sports cannot be regulated only by guidelines and recommends that the Ministry may make all efforts 
to come out with laws soon so that only licensed and responsible operators who adhere to the la id down safety 
norms remain in business to provide adventure tourism services. 
. 
 (Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The Ministry of Tourism under its voluntary scheme only accords approval/recognition to Tour 
Operators, including Adventure Tour Oper ators, under the category of Tourism Service Providers, through 
NIDHI+ portal. It is not under the purview of the Ministry to issue licenses to Adventure Tour Operators or to 
maintain the list of license holders. However, during application, in order to ob tain recognition from the 
Ministry, Adventure tour operators are required to specify the specialization of activity like trekking, water 
sports, aero sports, scuba diving, safaris, etc. The field staff must obtain an Adventure Certificate from 
specialized organizations including State Govt. Institutes like NIM (Uttarkashi), JIM (J&K), AB Institute of 

46 
 
Mountaineering (Manali), HMI (Darjeeling), SonamGyasto Institute (Sikkim), NIMAS (Arunachal Pradesh) etc. 
for Mountaineering and NIWS (Goa) for Water/Aero Sports. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.2      The Committee observes that the Ministry's approval/recognition scheme is voluntary and does 
not enforce compliance with safety regulations or mandatory certification. This approach is inadequate 
for manag ing high -risk activities, as it does not ensure that all operators adhere to necessary safety 
protocols, thereby leaving tourists vulnerable. The Committee recommends that the Ministry implements 
centralized licensing framework for Adventure Tour Operators    at the national level. Despite the 
jurisdictional complexities, the Committee believes that a uniform licensing system is crucial for ensuring 
that all operators adhere to the required safety, quality and regulatory standards. The Ministry should 
collaborate with State/UT Governments to develop this framework, making licensing a mandatory 
requirement for operating in the adventure tourism sector. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.  Regarding the standardization of safety gears, the Committee ha sbeen    informed   that   presently, 
there is no single system of certification of adventure equipments in our country. The Bureau of Indian 
Standards (BIS) is working towards setting standards for adventure equipments that can demonstrate proven 
track record of reliab ility to help ensure a safe adventure experience. The Committee expresses its displeasure 
that India does not have standardized safety gears even for high risk adventure sports and recommends that the 
Ministry may expeditiously implement a uniform standard  across the country for all adventure tourism 
verticals, prepared by Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).. 
(Para 36) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Recognizing the importance of ensuring safety in high -risk adventure sports, particularly  through 
standardized equipment, the Ministry is actively working towards developing a framework.    
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
4.2      The Committee seeks an update on  the progress made in develop ing a framework that emphasizes 
the importance of ensuring safety in h igh-risk adventure sports, particularly  through the use of 
standardized equipment.

Promotion of Tourism Abroad By Indian Missions 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        The Committee notes the events and programmes organised by the Indian Missions abroad to promote 
tourism and the budgets for the same. The Committee has been informed that the Tourism Officers posted in 
Indian Missions have tourism prom otion as additional charge. The Committee recommends that as 
responsibility for tourism promotion abroad now rests solely with the Indian Missions in all countries, the 
Tourism Officers may be given sole charge as far as possible as it is necessary for the  transitional change from 
the Overseas Tourist Offices to the Missions in many countries and to create confidence among the stakeholders 
that the Missions are attaching top priority to tourism promotion.    The Tourism Officers were designated by 
MEA in Oct ober, 2021. The Committee has been informed that since then the Tourism Officers have had only 
one meeting with  the Indian stakeholders a year back and desires to know how many meetings have been held 
with them as also the foreign tourism agents and B2B players since their appointment. 
(Para 149) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
9.1    5 meetings were held between Indian Missions and Ministry of Tourism officials for 
discussions relating to promotional activities for promotion of India as a preferred tourist 
destination and promotional activities including fairs and exhibitions. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
9.2    The Committee is concerned  about the limited number of meetings held by the 
Tourism Officers with Indian stakeholders and foreign tourism agents/B2 B players 
since their appointment. The Ministry should ensure that regular and frequent 
meetings are scheduled to foster better communication and collaboration.

CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
Rural Tourism  
The Committee appreciates the Ministry's ongoing efforts to integrate the Rural 
Tourism India website with the NIDHI+ portal and its commitment to upgrading the 
website's content.  
(Para 1.2) 
 
The Committee recommends for the implementation of regular content audits to ensure 
that the information on the Rural Tourism website is accurate, up -to-date, and user -
friendly.  
(Para 1.3) 
 
The Ministry should create a schedule for these audits, prioritizing villages that are 
likely to attract a significant number of tourists. 
(Para 1.4) 
 
 
While recognizing the challenge s of handling large volumes of data, the Committee 
recommends the Ministry to explore more efficient methods for uploading and 
integrating data from the NIDHI+ Portal. This may include technological upgrades or 
the use of advanced data management tools to minimize delays and ensure that the 
latest information is easily accessible to tourists. 
(Para 1.5) 
 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry collaborate  and work closely with local 
authorities and tourism boa rds in the featured villages  to ensure the accuracy and 
comprehensiveness of the information provided . This collaboration will help capture 
and present all relevant details, including lesser -known travel routes and homestay 
options, accurately on the website. 
(Para 1.6) 

52 
 
Adventure Tourism  
The Committee acknowledges the reply of the Ministry but reiterates its request for 
detailed data on the number of accidents and casualties in adventure tourism over the 
last ﬁve years. This information is essential for evaluating the e ﬀectiveness of the safety 
guidelines and standa rds in mitigating risks associated with adventure sports. The 
Committee urges the Ministry to provide this data at the earliest, including a 
breakdown by speciﬁc activities (e.g., paragliding, trekking) and the locations where 
these incidents occurred. The Ministry address the Committee's identified safety gaps. 
(Para 2.3) 
The Committee observes that the Ministry's approval/recognition scheme is voluntary 
and does not enforce compliance with safety regulations or mandatory certification. 
This approach is inadequate for managing high-risk activities, as it does not ensure that 
all operators adhere to necessary safety protocols, thereby leaving tourists vulnerable. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry implements centralized licensing 
framework for Advent ure Tour Operators   at the national level. Despite the 
jurisdictional complexities, the Committee believes that a uniform licensing system is 
crucial for ensuring that all operators adhere to the required safety, quality and 
regulatory standards. The Mini stry should collaborate with State/UT Governments to 
develop this framework, making licensing a mandatory requirement for operating in 
the adventure tourism sector. 
(Para 3.2) 
The Committee seeks an update on  the progress made in developing a framework tha t 
emphasizes the importance of ensuring safety in high -risk adventure sports, 
particularly through the use of standardized equipment.  
(Para 4.2) 
Golf Tourism  
The Committee desires that the Ministry provide the speciﬁc reasons for the delays and 
unsatisfactory progress in the Trivandrum Golf Club project. 
(Para 5.2) 
 
Further, it is recommended that the Ministry establish a more robust monitoring 
mechanism to oversee the implementation of projects funded under this scheme. The 
Ministry should ensure that fu ture projects are completed on schedule, with regular 
progress reports and transparent communication among all stakeholders to prevent 
situations similar to those encountered with the Trivandrum Golf Club project.  The 
Committee also desires to  know  whet her  other  Golf clubs in the country have been 
given similar  assistance  under  the Scheme.  
(Para 5.3) 

53 
 
The Committee observes that current initiatives may not fully address the increasing 
demand for specialized skills in niche tourism sectors, which oft en require advanced 
and continuous training. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may broaden 
its training programs to include more specialized and advanced courses tailored to 
speciﬁc niche tourism sectors, such as adventure tourism, eco-tourism, wellness tourism, 
cultural tourism, and others. 
(Para 6.2) 
 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry introduce continuous skill 
development programs, rather than focusing solely on short -term courses. This could 
include periodic refresher courses, advanced certiﬁcations, and  on -the- job training 
opportunities to ensure that the workforce stays current with the latest trends and best 
practices in their fields. 
(Para 6.3) 
The Committee desires an update on the progress in granting industry status to the 
tourism and hospitality sector under the jurisdiction of State Governments and UT 
administrations. The Committee recommends that the Ministry intensify its e ﬀorts to 
advocate this industry status to the tourism and hospitality sector across all States and 
UTs. Such status is essential for providing incentives such as tax beneﬁts, utility 
subsidies, and improved access to ﬁnancing, which can encourage the development of 
more hotels in the Three Star and below categories. 
(Para 7.2) 
Swadesh Darshan 2.0  
The Committee desires from the Ministry a detailed explanation on how the additional 
50 destinations align with the scheme’s objectives of promoting sustainable and 
responsible tourism. The Ministry should conduct and present an impact analysis to 
illustrate how this increase in the number of destinations will inﬂuence the overall  
eﬀectiveness  and  success of the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 scheme. This analysis may 
include a comparative assessment with Swadesh Darshan 1.0 to evaluate any differences 
in outcomes. 
(Para 8.2) 
Promotion of Tourism Abroad By Indian Missions 
The Committee is concerned about the limited number of meetings held by the Tourism 
Officers with Indian stakeholders and foreign tourism agents/B2B players since their 
appointment. The Ministry sho uld ensure that regular and frequent meetings are 
scheduled to foster better communication and collaboration. 
(Para 9.2)

4.         The Committee further notes that while Inland Waterways is undeniably the 
most environment friendly mode of transport, development of waterways cannot be 
undertaken without its environmental costs as  development activities change a river’s 
hydrology and morphology. Indian rivers support much biodiversity and aquatic life, 
many of which are already endangered due to high levels of pollution. Dredging of the 
riverbed for providing requisite draft advers ely affects the ecology of the river 
systems and fish breeding activities. While river systems could play a crucial role in 
cargo transportation and reduction in logistics costs especially in landlocked States 
and thus, could be an economic gamechanger, th e concerns of environmental 
sustainability should also be given equal importance. A case in point is India’s 
national aquatic animal, the endangered Gangetic Dolphin. The NW -1 passes through 
the Vikramshila dolphin sanctuary, India’s only dedicated protect ed area for the 
Gangetic Dolphin, one of the only three surviving freshwater dolphin species in the 
world. The Gangetic Dolphins, essentially blind, rely heavily on echolocation, i.e., 
using sound to navigate and locate prey, and developmental activities s uch as capital 
dredging and construction interfere with their activities. The Committee observes that 
speed regulations, buffer zones and regulation of dredging were some of the measures 
proposed to be taken to minimize the deleterious impact on dolphins a nd other 
aquatic life and desires to know the status of implementation in this regard. 
(Para 23) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1       The inland transportation system of India aspires to become game changer for 
improving logistics performance for promoting trades to achieve five trillion economy. NW-1 

7 
 
(Ganga – Bhagirathi – Hooghly river system) from Varanasi to Haldia is prioritized for the 
development of river transportation with international benchmarking.  
4.2       The emphasis given on environment control m easures is highly monitored during 
development and operation phase of logistics movement along NW -1; the Environment 
Management Plan for NW -1 is already in place and its compliances are being regularly 
monitored.  
 State of the Art dredgers have been deploy ed for the dredging work. They are 
equipped with the noise reduction/ Masking equipment like AVP (Anti Vibration 
Pads) used in engine room foundation to reduce the noise generation inside water and 
outside, AVP is also bridged to reduce the high noise exposure to cabin crew.  
 Spill Kits are being placed on board containing Floating booms, socks, pads, pillows, 
Granular absorbent, PPEs and handling instruction. All necessary precautions are 
exercised to avoid oil spills of leakage. Daily weekly and monthly dredgers inspection 
checklist is maintained on board to ensure regular servicing and maintenance of 
dredgers to prevent any leakage of the equipment and machinery. Regular training is 
being imparted to the operation team and crew about the implementation of  
emergency response plan, handling of emergency response equipment. No spillage 
and accident to the dolphins recorded till date.  
 Dolphin deflector has been installed onboard dredgers to keep the dolphin away from 
the dredging areas. Dredging operation is halted in case of sighting of aquatic 
mammals.  
 Waste management plan is in place for the dredgers and vessels. Waste oil is stored & 
disposed as per the Hazardous and Other Waste Management Rules 2016. 
Authorization has also been obtained by contractor, a nd agreement with SPCB 
authorized vendor is also there.  
 STP/ Bio toilets are installed on board dredgers and no solid and liquid waste is being 
discharged in the river to follow the Zero discharge policy. Municipal waste is being 
segregated at the source and being stored in the color -coded bins and disposed as per 
the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 through municipal corporation/local body 
along with river banks. Bilge water is being stored in closed containers and disposed -
off through authorized recycler regularly.  
 Apart from this, bandalling is being done to concentrate the flow of water towards the 
river channel as well as to prevent the deposition of silt from outside the channel to 
reduce the requirement of dredging.  
 Dredging is being avoided durin g the rainy season, while during the normal days 
dredged materials are discharged close to surface of the water body to minimize the 
dispersal of sediments. Disposal is being done at approx. 100 -150 m away from the 
channel.

14.       The Committee notes that the number of accident cases due to boat capsizing has 
seen an increasing trend especially in the last two years, resulting in many deaths and 
injury to the passengers. With the increase in  the number of waterways, the number of 
accidents may also increase unless remedial measures are put in place to enhance boat 
safety and prevent accidents. The Committee observes that one of the main reasons for 
most boat accidents in India is overloading of passengers, imbalance due to lack of 
proper distribution of weight of the running boat, and dangerous working practices, 
followed by poor quality of vessels and unregistered vessels, violating rules, vessel 
traffic etc. In their deposition before the Co mmittee, the representatives of the IWAI 
had stated that a system is in place to survey and certify the vessels for balance and 
stability, fire safety and training of manpower manning the vessel, etc. before 
registration and certification. Accidents taking  place are registered by the State 
Government and feedback is taken for improvement. 
(Para 110)

proposed here would prove to be a game changer for the entire North Eastern Region as

regard.

with regular monitoring and reporting mechanisms to ensure adherence to timelines 
and to identify potential bottlenecks early. 
(Para 4.4) 
The IWAI and MEA should continue to strengthen bilateral cooperation with Myanmar 
to facilitate smooth implementation of the project. This includes resolving any logistical, 
regulatory, or operational challenges that may arise during the execution of the second 
phase. 
(Para 5.4) 
 
Along with th e completion of Phase -II, the Committee stresses the importance of 
regular maintenance of the infrastructure developed under the KMTTP. Ensuring the 
sustainability and functionality of the ports, terminals, and vessels will be crucial for the 
long-term success of the project. 
(Para 5.5) 
The Committee recommends that efforts be made to increase the number of Indian 
vessels operating on the IBP route. This could involve incentivizing private entities to 
invest in and operate vessels on this route, potentially  through subsidies, tax benefits, or 
low-interest financing options. 
(Para 6.5) 
 
To make Indian vessels more competitive, the Ministry should explore measures to 
reduce capital expenditure (Capex) and operational expenditure (Opex) for Indian 
vessel operators. This may include financial assistance, fuel subsidies, and streamlining 
regulatory processes to reduce administrative costs. 
(Para 6.6) 
 

44 
 
The Committee suggests that the Ministry, in collaboration with relevant trade bodies, 
work on promoting and facil itating bilateral trade via waterways. Identifying potential 
import cargo from Bangladesh to India and creating a balanced trade flow could 
significantly enhance the viability and utilization of Indian vessels on the IBP route. 
(Para 6.7) 
The Committee is concerned about the low expenditure relative to the allocated funds 
over the past five years. This underutilization of funds indicates potential inefficiencies 
in project execution and financial management. The Committee emphasizes the need for 
better planning, monitoring, and utilization of allocated resources to ensure the timely 
and effective development of the project. 
(Para 7.2) 
The Ministry should facilitate forums, workshops, and consultations to gather inputs 
from local communities, environmental gr oups, and industry stakeholders, ensuring 
that diverse perspectives are considered in the development process.  The findings from 
R&D activities, especially those related to environmental impacts and sustainable 
practices, should be documented and widely di sseminated. This will help in the sharing 
of knowledge, best practices, and technological advancements with relevant 
stakeholders and the broader community. 
(Para 8.2) 
Public-Private Partnership 
The Committee recommends expanding the scope of private secto r involvement in the 
inland water sector beyond terminal operations to include other critical areas such as 
vessel operations, maintenance services and infrastructure development. This broader 
engagement will enhance overall sector efficiency and innovation. 
(Para 9.3) 
Kochi Water Metro 
The Committee understands that IWAI’s role is primarily technical. The Ministry 
should support State Governments in planning and implementing similar projects by 
providing technical guidance, funding assistance, and recommen dations on best 
practices. This support will help ensure that new projects are developed with a solid 
foundation based on the Kochi Water Metro’s experience. 
(Para 10.2) 
 
River Cruise-Ganga Vilas 

45 
 
The Committee recommends launching incentive programs to enc ourage river cruise 
operators. These programs could include financial subsidies, tax incentives and 
streamlined regulatory processes to reduce operational costs and attract both domestic 
and international cruise operators. The Committee also recommends red ucing charges 
for domestic tourists to ensure inclusivity.

THE MINISTRY 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS - AT A GLANCE 
  
FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE POLICY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.         The Committe e observes that the earlier subsidy scheme of the Ministry of 5 
years offered shipbuilders 30% extra on building ocean -going merchant vessels that are 
more than 80 metres in length, if they are manufactured for the domestic market. For 
export orders, however, ships of all types and capacities were eligible for the subsidy. In 
the new ﬁnancial    assistance scheme, assistance will be given for all types of ships 
irrespective of size. In the new scheme, both state -owned and private yards will get the 
assistance only after they construct and hand over to the ship to the buyer to ensure 
timely delivery of ships. The new ﬁnancial assistance  scheme was therefore for double 
the period of the earlier subsidy scheme, the focus extended for all ships and ensured 
timely delivery which had been a constraint in the earlier scheme. The Committee also 
observes that when commercial orders dried up in the wake of the 2008 ﬁnancial crisis, 
Indian shipyards were focusing mainly on defence orders to stay aﬂoat. The 
Government’s ﬁnancial assistance policy was meant to help bring in more and major 
commercial ship building orders. 
(Para 13.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1       Comments of the Committee are agreed. Additionally, from the data available in the 
SBFAP scheme, about 88 vessel orders have been procured by 35 Shipyards during the last 5 
years from domestic as well as export orders and these orders are worth Rs. 8631 crore. 
Further, shipyards have delivered 128 vessels worth Rs. 1145 crore to domestic and 
international ship owners in last 5 years that have received assistance under SBFAP of about 
Rs. 327 Crore.   Also, with the latest Government of India initiative to provide higher SBFA 
funding to green fuelled ships and hybrid vessels, further shipbuilding orders are expected t o 
be received.

Recommendation/Observation 
2.         The Committee observes that skilled manpower is the most essential 
prerequisite in Ship Building industry. Ensuring proper education and training could 
bolster the effectiveness of the industry. The Committee observes that as per 
studies the labour p roductivity value for India is approximately 10 times lower than 
the major shipbuilding nations. All these translate to about 20 -25 per cent cost 
advantage for major shipbuilding nations vis -à-vis India. The Committee 
recommends that investments in automat ion should be encouraged in order to 
improve labor productivity and reduce costs. 
(Para 23) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1       In this regard Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways have already joined hands 
with Siemens and Indian Register of Shipping (IRS ) to build World Class Center of 
Excellence in Maritime and Ship Building (CEMS) in Mumbai and Vishakhapatnam under 
the ministry’s flagship Sagarmala Programme.CEMS aim is to provide industry -relevant skill 
development, equip students with employable engin eering and technical skills in the port and 
maritime sector and contribute to the Government of India’s ambitious Sagarmala 
Programme. This initiative also adds to the Make in India and skill India efforts in the 
Maritime sector.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.         One of the constraints of shipbuilding in India is the limited investment in 
R&D in ship design and innovation. The Committee recommends that the 
Government focus on skill development and developing an R&D base to increase the 
competitiveness of the Indian shipbuilding industry. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1       The aim of setting up of National Centre of Excellence for Green Port & Shipping 
(NCoEGPS) is to provide Green solutions to transform Ports & Shipping. India is also 
implementing IMO energy efficiency requirements for existing ships and carbon intensity 
requirements on all its vessels whether coastal or international in order to help achieve IMO 
GHG reduction targets. 

4 
 
 3.2      Ministry of shipping has already joined hands with S iemens and Indian Register of 
Shipping (IRS) to build World Class Center of Excellence in Maritime and Ship Building 
(CEMS) in Mumbai and Vishakhapatnam. 
3.3       CEMS aim is to provide industry -relevant skill development, equip students with 
employable engineering and technical skills in the port and maritime sector and contribute 
to the Government of India’s ambitious Sagarmala programme. This initiative also adds to 
the Make in India and skill India efforts in the Maritime sector.           
Recommendation/Observation 
4.         The MIV document also advocates creation of a Maritime Development Fund 
to provide easy access to working capital and long -term ﬁnance needs across marine 
sectors. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may implement the creation of 
the Fund which can give access to Indian ship owners to improve their capacity   and 
shipyards to improve the infrastructure 
(Para 25)  
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1       Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways organized two workshops involving the 
financial institutions, PSUs and Private Shipyards to deliberate on the ship and ship building 
and financing aspect s, Maritime Development Fund, risk insurance etc. Based on the 
workshops different aspects of ship building such as finances, lower insurance rates, long 
interest loans, building maritime clusters, potential investments in the shipping sector were all 
discussed. Necessary actions are being carried out by this ministry. 
 4.2      The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) is working on developing 
a Maritime Development Fund (MDF) to propel growth and sustainability within the 
maritime sector. 
 4.3      The concept of the MDF has featured in both the Maritime India Vision 2030 (MIV 
2030) and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 (MAKV 2047) documents. 
 4.4      Currently, MoPSW is actively engaging with stakeholders across the maritime 
industry to assess their needs, challenges, and expectations regarding the fund. 
4.5       These insights will be instrumental in shaping the mandate and structure of the MDF. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.         As per a FICCI report, Indian shipyards require about 25 -35% of the ship's 
cost as working capital during construction, with interest rates averaging 10 -10.5%. 
In contrast, overseas shipbuilding yards enjoy significantly lower rates along with 

5 
 
lower-interest export credit. The Committee, therefore, recommends that  measures to 
reduce interest rates on working capital for Indian shipyards be explored.  
(Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1       Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has taken initial actions/stakeholders 
discussions regarding setting up a specialized maritime development fund Also Risk 
insurance cover and various other financial instruments are being evaluated. Leasing/other 
financial instrument through GIFT city also is being discussed by Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping and Waterways. 
SHIP REPAIR 
Recommendation/Observation 
6.         The Committee notes that India is suitably located to offer repair services for the 
Indian Navy as well as the US Navy for its 5 th and 7 th Fleet deployed in the Indian 
Ocean and the Arabian Sea. It has also been seen that many contracts of the US Navy 
have been awarded to either private Indian Shipyards or to other foreign shipyards.   
Indian PSU Shipyards are not strong contenders for repair amidst global competition.   
The Committee has also learnt from media repo rts that the US Navy and L&T have 
signed a 5 year Master Ship Repair Agreement (MSRA) which shows that the US is 
committed to utilize ship repair facilities on a regular basis at the L&T shipyard in 
Katupalli in Tamil Nadu. The Committee understands that M azagon Docks 
Shipbuilders have also concluded an agreement with an entity of the US Navy. While 
appreciating the above -said achievements, the Committee feels that while other Asian 
countries, notably Singapore and Japan have bagged many foreign ship repair  orders, 
India has lagged behind due to inadequate infrastructural support services needed for 
ship repair. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may make efforts to 
improve the infrastructure to enable other shipyards to bag ship repair orders. 
(Para 53) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1       Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has already joined hands with Siemens 
and Indian Register of Shipping (IRS) to build World Class Center of Excellence in Maritime 
and Ship Building (CEMS) in Mumbai and Vishakha patnam under the ministry’s flagship 
Sagarmala Programme. 
6.2       CEMS aim is to provide industry -relevant skill development, equip students with 
employable engineering and technical skills in the port and maritime sector and contribute to 
the Government of India’s ambitious Sagarmala Programme. This initiative also adds to the 
Make in India and skill India efforts in the Maritime sector.  
Initiatives taken for reviving the Ship Recycling Industry 

6 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7.         The Committee apprec iates the steps taken by all agencies involved to resolve 
the issues arising out of the Basel Ban Agreement and that EU ships may start to 
arrive in India from April, 2024 which would restore much of the problems affecting 
the recycling industry.    Regarding the issue of TMT bars, the Committee has learnt 
from media reports that the Committee set up by the Steel Ministry to look into the 
issue of the manufacturing TMT bars from ship steel has reportedly been unable to 
devise an SoP ( Standard Operating Proc edure) for usage of ship plates without 
testing of chemical composition. Non -standardised offerings and the absence of wider 
data are seen as major reasons for the rejection of using ship breaking steel plates for 
making TMT bars. The Committee studying th e issue has also suggested that ship 
breakers can sell the plates along with grade certiﬁcate and chemistry. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry, GMB and Ship Recyclers may cooperate 
with the Committee and ensure that large size data is made availab le for long -term 
durability studies to settle the issue of use of TMT bars for structural purposes. The 
Committee also recommends that the industry may explore the possibility of making 
other forms of steel, apart from TMT bars, from ship scraps, like gril ls, strips and 
other bars which may not require the same standards as TMT bars. 
(Para 84) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1       Regarding exploring the feasibility of using ship breaking steel plates to produce 
TMT bars under the IS 1786,the Ministry of Steel, v ide letter dated 13.03.2024 has 
forwarded the final version of SoP (Standard Operating Procedure) to DG, BIS for 
consideration and further action. BIS have a working group especially for IS 1786, which 
gives the final recommendation to the main Committee b ased on the examination of reports 
and SoP. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
8.         While appreciating the efforts being made to establish India once again as the 
top country in ship recycling as the industry is an economic driver for India,    the 
Committee underlines the importance of strategic planning to ensure that 
environmental conditions and workers safety and health standards are not 
compromised in the pursuit of doubling the capacity of the industry by 2030. 
(Para 86) 
           
Reply of the Ministry 

7 
 
8.1       Gujarat Maritime Board is planning to prepare the Master Planning to double the 
capacity of Alang through the renowned consultant. The Master Planning will be done to 
comply all the health safety and environmental standard for the green ship recycling. 
8.2       Safety Training and Labor Welfare Institute at Alang 
 In the view of the safety of the worker, Gujarat Maritime Board has established the training 
institute in Alang in 2003; Gujarat Maritime Board has follow the policy that each worker 
should get required training before work at ship recycling yard i.e. "No Training No Work". 
The institute has been in operation for the last 20 years and has trained more than 156,000 
workers so far. The new workers are trained as per the National Skill De velopment 
Standards. Only after receiving certification from the Gujarat Maritime Board, workers are 
considered trained and fit for working in the plots. 
 8.3      Health facilities at Alang 
 Gujarat Maritime Board started the 15 bedded Multi Specialty Hos pitals in support of the 
Indian Red Cross Society at Alang since March 2019 which provides medical services to the 
workers. These services include Ortho, Physician, Skin, Dental, Pediatric, X -Ray, Patho-Lab, 
ECG etc with indoor facility at free of cost. This hospital is operationalized on 24 x 7 bases at 
free of cost and till date; more than 2.86 lakh patients have been treated. GMB has started the 
expansion work of this hospital with additional 20 beds and facilities like MRI, CT Scan, and 
Trauma Centre etc. to comply the European Union Ship Recycling Regulations. Moreover, a 
Primary Health Care Facilities with 20 beds has been also operationalized at Alang since

REPORT 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation plays a vital role in creating a safe, secure, 
affordable, and sustainable environment for air travel, catering to both passengers 
and cargo transportation. It establishes a comprehensive regulatory framework to 
ensure safety and security in air transport services while formulating policies to 
develop adequate infrastructure to accommodate the sector’s rapid growth. Given 
the global nature of civil aviation, the Ministry ensures adherence to international 
standards and norms. It supervises various attached offices and Public Sector 
Undertakings, ensuring effective governance. Additionally, it promotes ease of 
doing business and enhances passenger facilitation.  
2. The Ministry is responsible for implementing treaties and agreements related 
to civil aviation and administering the Aircraft Act, 1934, as well as the Airports 
Authority of India Act, 1994. Its remit includes the regulation of aircraft and air 
navigation, the provision and management of aerodromes, and the organisation of 
air traffic, excluding the sanitised control of air navigation. It also oversees the 
provision of navigational aids and other facilities related to air navigation. 
Furthermore, the Ministry is responsible for the carriage of passengers and goods 
by air, the development of commercial aero-related manufacturing and its 
ecosystem, and the issuance of technical licences, certificates, and approvals for 
civil aircraft operations. It also supports the growth of the private air transport 
industry, including cargo services, and handles matters related to Greenfield airport 
development by State Governments and private/joint-sector companies. 
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
3. The Outcome-Output Monitoring Framework (OOMF)/Outcome Budget for 
the Financial Year (FY) 2025-26 of the Ministry throws light on the Ministry’s 

2 
 
primary goalof bridging the regional connectivity gap, particularly in underserved 
and remote areas, while boosting economic growth through aviation sector 
development. Through itsRegional Connectivity Scheme (RCS-UDAN), it seeks to 
enhance regional air connectivity by focusing on infrastructure development, 
operational efficiency, and improved accessibility, particularly in underserved 
regions. The following key goals and objectives can be inferred: 
i. Expansion of Airport Infrastructure – The Ministry aims to upgrade and revive 
airport infrastructure in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) and State Governments to support regional connectivity. This includes 
the development of new airports, heliports, and water aerodromes to improve 
accessibility. 
ii. Enhancing Regional Air Connectivity – A major objective is to operationalise 
new Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) routes and increase the number of 
flights under the scheme, thereby making air travel more accessible to the 
general public. 
iii. Improved Air Connectivity in the North Eastern Region (NER) – Recognising 
the strategic and economic significance of the North Eastern region, the 
Ministry seeks to operationalise additional airports, heliports, and water 
aerodromes, and introduce new RCS routes and flights in the region. 
iv. Increase in Passenger Traffic and Flight Operations – A clear objective is to 
facilitate higher passenger movement on RCS flights, targeting 20 lakh 
passengers and 40,000 RCS flights in FY 2025-26.  
v. Development of Specific Air Infrastructure Projects – The Ministry has outlined 
targeted infrastructure projects, such as: 
 Heliports: Tuting, Daparizo, Nagaon, and Bageshwar. 
 Water Aerodromes: Long Island, Shaheed Dweep, Swaraj Dweep, and 
Prakasam Barrage. 
 Airports: Fursatganj (Uttar Pradesh), Rangeilunda (Odisha), 
Rairangpur (Odisha), Shivpuri (Madhya Pradesh), and Ratnagiri.

decade, has seen its allocation reduced by 32 percent to Rs 540 crore in the 
current budget. This reduction, coupled with the announcement to expand the 
scheme significantly, creates potential resource constraints that could affect 
implementation.The government has committed to expanding the UDAN 
scheme to 120 new destinations with a target of carrying 4 crore passengers in 
the next decade. This ambitious goal, coupled with the establishment of new 
airports and helipads in hilly, aspirational, and North Eastern regions, will 
require enhanced security protocols and accident response mechanisms that 
appear underfunded in the current allocation structure. In its view, it is 
imperative to assess whether these funds are adequate to strengthen security 
infrastructure and enhance investigative capabilities. As aviation expands to 
tier II and III cities under the modified UDAN scheme, security infrastructure 
and capabilities must be extended proportionally.
