AIR FARE REGULATION - THE NEED OF THE HOUR 
12.1 The Committee, while examining the Demand for Grants of the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation for 2025-26, recommends the establishment of a 
stringent airfare pricing regulation mechanism under the framework of an 
AI-powered predictive monitoring system, tentatively named “AirPrice 
Guardian.” This system should aim to address consumer grievances related to 
unpredictable and exorbitant airfare surges, particularly during peak travel 
periods and emergencies, while ensuring transparency and fairness in pricing 
practices. The Committee notes that the current regulatory framework under 
the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) lacks the capacity to 
proactively monitor and regulate airfare trends, necessitating a 
transformative approach leveraging advanced technology. 
12.2 The proposed “AirPrice Guardian” system will utilize machine learning 
algorithms and predictive analytics to forecast airfare trends based on 
historical data, demand patterns, fuel costs, seasonal fluctuations, and 
external factors such as festivals or emergencies. By establishing dynamic fare 
bands for each route, updated quarterly through predictive models, this 
system will empower regulators to monitor deviations in real-time and take 

10 
 
preemptive action against excessive pricing. The Committee recommends that 
DGCA be empowered with quasi-judicial authority to impose temporary price 
caps or penalties on airlines engaging in exploitative practices. Additionally, a 
Pricing Transparency Index should be developed to rate airlines on their 
adherence to fair pricing norms, with this information made publicly 
available through a consumer-facing portal. 
12.3 The Committee further recommends that the existing Tariff Monitoring 
Unit (TMU) within DGCA be revamped with AI-driven tools for real-time 
data analysis and anomaly detection.  
12.4 In alignment with the Ministry’s focus on regional connectivity under the 
RCS-UDAN scheme, the Committee underscores that airfare monitoring must 
extend to underserved routes to prevent excessive fares that undermine 
accessibility. A portion of the funds should be allocated for RCS and that 
should be utilized to integrate fare monitoring mechanisms into regional 
connectivity projects. This will ensure that affordable air travel remains a 
cornerstone of India’s aviation growth strategy. 
12.5 The Committee also highlights the need for public awareness campaigns 
to educate consumers about their rights under this new regulatory 
framework. The Committee recommends the development of a mobile 
application, “Airfare Vigil,” modeled on the Election Commission’s cVIGIL 
app, to empower citizens to report instances of arbitrary airfare pricing. This 
app will allow users to upload evidence such as screenshots of ticket prices 
and contextual details, with features like real-time geo-tagging, automated 
complaint tracking, and time-bound resolution mechanisms. Upon 
submission, users will receive a unique ID to track their complaint status, 
ensuring transparency and accountability. The app will also include 
safeguards against misuse, such as filtering duplicate or frivolous complaints, 
while allowing anonymous submissions to encourage wider participation. 

11 
 
12.6  “Airfare Vigil” will be integrated with the AI-powered “AirPrice 
Guardian” system, enabling citizen reports to complement predictive 
analytics in identifying exploitative pricing patterns. This initiative will foster 
participatory governance by involving citizens in airfare regulation while 
strengthening DGCA’s ability to address consumer grievances swiftly and 
effectively. 
12.7. Given the Ministry’s overall revenue expenditure allocation of ₹2,330.31 
crore and capital outlay of ₹70 crore for 2025-26, the Committee recommends 
reallocating from underutilized allocations (such as Air India liabilities) 
toward developing and implementing this airfare monitoring system. The 
timeline for implementation should span 18-24 months, with Phase I focusing 
on high-traffic routes within six months and nationwide rollout completed by 
2026. 
12.8 The Committee believes that implementing “Air Price Guardian” & 
“Airfare Vigil” will address long-standing consumer grievances regarding 
airfare volatility while fostering transparency and accountability in India’s 
aviation sector. By aligning this initiative with broader policy goals such as 
regional connectivity and sustainable aviation growth, it will not only protect 
consumer interests but also strengthen India’s position as a global leader in 
aviation innovation and regulation. 
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND SECURITY 
13. The Committee observes and appreciates the fact that the Directorate 
General of Civil Aviation (₹300 crore) and the Bureau of Civil Aviation 
Security (₹80 crore) have been accorded significant funding. However, the 
Commission of Railway Safety (₹22 crore) has received markedly lower 
funding, despite its critical role in ensuring passenger and freight safety in 
railway operations. The Committee advises a reassessment of this allocation, 
with a view to strengthening railway safety mechanisms. Simultaneously, it 

12 
 
urges regular performance evaluations of DGCA and BCAS funding to ensure 
that these resources translate into tangible improvements in aviation safety, 
regulatory efficiency, and security preparedness. The Committee also 
recommends that Ministry should establish an integrated safety oversight 
mechanism that promotes collaboration between transport safety regulators 
including DGCA, BCAS, and the Commission of Railway Safety, utilizing 
shared resources where appropriate and developing common standards for 
multi-modal transport safety. Further, Committee recommends for 
development of a sustainable funding mechanism for aviation oversight 
functions at both national and regional levels, potentially including air safety 
charges, to ensure regulatory bodies can fulfill their mandates effectively 
without complete dependence on general budgetary allocations. 
 
IMPROVING AIRCRAFT INTERIOR - ENSURING STANDARDS 
13.1 The Committee has taken cognizant of reports concerning premature 
deterioration of seating materials, ergonomic failures, and technological 
obsolescence plaguing multiple airlines. This urgent disparity demands 
ministerial intervention through a standardized regulatory framework to 
ensure Indian aviation maintains competitive parity with global leaders. The 
Committee proposes establishing the Aviation Interior Quality Commission 
with immediate effect to implement rigorous testing protocols, sustainability 
guidelines, and accessibility standards across all domestic carriers. The 
situation is particularly concerning given the considerable fleet expansion 
underway. With Air India alone having ordered 570 new aircraft—including 
the recent addition of 100 more Airbus aircraft comprising 10 wide-body 
A350s and 90 narrow-body A320 family planes—the potential scale of interior 
quality issues demands immediate ministerial attention. Sustainability must 
become a central consideration in interior design and material selection. The 
Commission would establish progressive environmental standards for cabin 

13 
 
interiors, including recyclability requirements, VOC emissions limits, and 
lifecycle assessment obligations. These standards would align with India’s 
broader environmental commitments while positioning Indian aviation as a 
leader in sustainable cabin design. 
REGIONAL CONNECTIVITY SCHEME  AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
EXPANSION 
14. The allocation of ₹540 crore to the Regional Connectivity Scheme, with 
₹240 crore earmarked for the North-Eastern Region, demonstrates the 
government's commitment to regional connectivity. However, the Committee 
notes that historical data shows significant variation in route sustainability 
and regional imbalances in performance. To enhance the effectiveness of this 
allocation, the Committee recommends:  
14.1 Institution of a tiered funding approach that prioritizes routes with 
proven passenger load factors exceeding 70% while providing targeted 
support for underperforming routes with high development potential, 
particularly in the Eastern, Northeastern, and Central regions where recent 
data shows promising growth trajectories. 
14.2 Development of comprehensive performance metrics beyond passenger 
numbers, including economic impact assessments, connectivity improvements 
for underserved communities, and operational sustainability of routes beyond 
the initial subsidy period. These metrics should inform quarterly reviews of 
fund disbursement. 
14.3 Creation of a dedicated infrastructure development component within 
the Regional Connectivity Scheme, targeting airports serving tourist and 
pilgrimage destinations which have demonstrated higher passenger traffic 
growth following route establishment. This approach would maximize 
economic returns on investment while enhancing sector sustainability. 

14 
 
 
INVESTMENT IN AVIATION EDUCATION AND TRAINING 
15. The Committee expresses serious concern regarding the inadequate 
allocations for the National Aviation University (₹10 crore) and Indira 
Gandhi Institute of Aeronautics (₹0.02 crore), which appear insufficient to 
meet the growing demand for aviation professionals. With pilot training costs 
ranging from ₹40 lakh to ₹1.5 crore per candidate, and the sector's projected 
expansion, the Committee recommends: 
15.1 Substantial enhancement of budgetary support for aviation education 
institutions with a minimum five-fold increase in allocation to the National 
Aviation University and a significant revision of IGRUA's funding to enable 
infrastructure modernization and curriculum enhancement aligned with 
international standards. 
15.2 Establishment of a National Aviation Scholarship Fund designed to 
support deserving candidates from economically weaker backgrounds and 
underrepresented regions to pursue aviation careers, addressing both talent 
gaps and regional imbalances in the aviation workforce. 
15.3 Development of a public-private partnership model for aviation training 
infrastructure, wherein government investments in educational institutions 
are complemented by industry contributions, creating centers of excellence 
that combine academic rigor with practical training facilities meeting current 
industry requirements.

fund allocation system with milestone-based disbursement mechanisms tied to 
project completion stages rather than time periods. This system should

making protocols that reduce procedural delays while maintaining financial

Aviation Stability Fund' with a guaranteed minimum corpus over a five-year 
period, insulated from annual budgetary fluctuations through legislative 
safeguards. Within this framework, the Committee suggests implementing a 
tiered subsidy structure that progressively reduces support based on route 
maturity metrics, thereby encouraging operational sustainability while 
maintaining essential connectivity. Additionally, the Ministry should develop 
a comprehensive 'Last-Mile Air Connectivity Index' for evaluating and 
prioritizing route development decisions based on quantifiable social, 
economic, and strategic parameters. The Committee further recommends

University received only ₹10 crore in 2025-26, while the Indira Gandhi

Committee recommends establishing an 'Aviation Excellence Fund', 
developed through a public-private partnership model where government 
contributions are matched by industry stakeholders. This fund should finance 
comprehensive curriculum modernization, faculty development programs, 
and infrastructure upgradation at aviation institutions. Furthermore, the 
Committee recommends developing specialized 'Centers of Aviation 
Technology' at existing educational institutions, each focusing on emerging 
areas such as sustainable aviation fuels, unmanned aerial systems, and next-
generation air traffic management. These centers should feature mixed-reality 
simulation environments that reduce training costs while enhancing learning 
outcomes. Additionally, the Ministry should implement an 'Aviation 
Scholarship Program' targeting students from underrepresented regions and 
economically disadvantaged backgrounds, with guaranteed industry 
placements upon graduation to address critical skill shortages in the sector.

Committee recommends restructuring the PLI disbursement mechanism to 
incorporate an accelerated reimbursement pathway for qualifying 
manufacturers, with monthly rather than annual claim processing to address 
working capital constraints of smaller enterprises. The implementation should

include a two-track approach: a 'Standard Track' for established 
manufacturers and an 'Innovation Track' with simplified compliance 
requirements for startups and MSMEs developing cutting-edge drone 
technologies. Furthermore, the Committee suggests creating specialized 
'Drone Application Zones' in each state where regulatory exemptions and 
infrastructure support are provided for real-world testing and demonstration 
of drone applications across sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, and 
disaster management. Additionally, the Ministry should develop a 'Drone 
Manufacturing Capability Index' to identify and address specific bottlenecks 
in the indigenous production ecosystem, with targeted interventions to 
develop domestic capacity for critical components currently being imported, 
including advanced sensors, precision navigation systems, and specialized 
battery technologies.

26. The Committee examines the response of the Ministry on the status of 
the working and implementation of the Regional Connectivity Scheme-Ude 
Desh ka Aam Naagrik. The Committee observes that the Ministry has 
reported a total expenditure of ₹4,309.34 crore towards the development of 
aerodromes under both Phase 1 and Phase 2, with 88 aerodromes developed 
and operationalised to date. While acknowledging the progress made, the 
Committee recommends implementing a multi-dimensional Return on 
Investment (ROI) assessment framework that measures outcomes beyond 
mere infrastructure development. The Ministry should establish a 
comprehensive digital monitoring system capturing granular data on 
economic multipliers, including tourism revenue increases, local employment 
generation, and supply chain expansion attributable to each aerodrome. The 
Committee further recommends instituting a tiered funding mechanism that 
recalibrates financial allocations based on a "connectivity impact score" 
derived from passenger volumes, operational consistency, and regional 
economic indicators. Additionally, the Ministry should develop a specialized 
Asset Utilization Optimization Model that identifies operational inefficiencies 

28 
 
at underperforming aerodromes and implements corrective measures, 
potentially including alternative aviation uses for facilities with persistently 
low passenger traffic. 
27. The Committee appreciates that 619 routes have been operationalised, 
including 90 routes in the North-Eastern region, and that 88 RCS airports are 
now connected, with 12 of these located in the North-East. To address regional 
imbalances, the Committee recommends developing a Geographic 
Information System (GIS)-based "Connectivity Gap Index" that quantifies 
accessibility deficits using multiple parameters including travel time to 
nearest operational airport, population density, economic activity centers, and 
existing transportation alternatives. This index should prioritize future route 
development with mandatory allocation of at least 30% of new routes to 
regions scoring above a defined threshold. The Committee further 
recommends implementing a "Hub-and-Spoke+" model specifically tailored 
for remote regions, wherein strategically located airports serve as regional 
hubs connected to smaller airfields through fixed-wing aircraft, while final 
connectivity to truly remote locations is provided through helicopter services. 
The Ministry should also introduce "Seasonal Route Flexibility" provisions 
allowing operators to temporarily redirect capacity to meet seasonal demands 
(such as festival periods, harvest seasons, or tourism peaks) while maintaining 
essential connectivity year-round. 
28. The Committee notes with appreciation that 149 lakh passengers have 
availed RCS flights, alongside the operation of 2,96,000 flights under the 
scheme. To enhance long-term financial sustainability, the Committee 
recommends implementing a graduated "Viability Transition Program" 
wherein routes beginning with full VGF support would transition through 
defined sustainability milestones—including load factor thresholds, 
operational reliability metrics, and ancillary revenue generation—with 
proportional reduction in subsidies linked to each milestone achievement. The 

29 
 
Ministry should develop specialized "Multi-Use Aerodrome" guidelines 
enabling operators to generate supplementary revenue through co-located 
facilities such as cargo operations, aircraft maintenance services, aviation 
training centers, and non-aeronautical commercial activities appropriate to 
local market conditions. Additionally, the Committee recommends 
establishing an "Aviation Enterprise Zone" framework offering tax incentives 
and streamlined regulatory processes for businesses establishing operations 
within defined proximity to RCS airports, creating economic ecosystems that 
generate passenger traffic organically rather than through fare subsidies. 
29. The Committee acknowledges the proposed extension of the modified 
RCS Scheme for 10 years with targets to connect 120 new destinations, 
particularly in hilly, aspirational, and North-Eastern regions. To address 
approval delays, the Committee recommends establishing a specialized 
"UDAN Fast-Track Clearance Cell" with dedicated representatives from all 
relevant ministries empowered to process approvals concurrently rather than 
sequentially. This cell should operate with defined decision timeframes and 
escalation protocols for unresolved matters. The Committee further 
recommends implementing a modular approval approach whereby the overall 
scheme framework receives principal approval while allowing dynamic 
adjustments to specific components through a streamlined modification 
protocol, thereby preventing total scheme paralysis when adjustments are 
needed. Additionally, the Ministry should institute a "Provisional Operational 
Authorization" mechanism allowing airlines to commence operations on 
approved routes with interim financial arrangements pending final EFC 
approval, supported by appropriate financial guarantees to protect both 
operator and government interests. 
30. The Committee notes the ongoing 5.5 round of bidding for helicopter 
and seaplane routes and recognizes their potential for enhancing connectivity 
in challenging terrain. To accelerate development in this sector, the 

30 
 
Committee recommends implementing a specialized "Waterway Aerodrome 
Development Program" that identifies and categorizes potential water landing 
sites based on multiple factors including water body stability, surrounding 
infrastructure, tourism potential, and connectivity needs. This program 
should include standardized floating infrastructure designs that can be 
rapidly deployed with minimal environmental impact. For helicopter 
operations, the Committee recommends developing modular, prefabricated 
heliport infrastructure kits specifically designed for rapid deployment in 
remote and challenging terrains, complete with standardized navigation aids 
and essential ground support equipment. The Ministry should also establish a 
"Mixed-Mode Operations Framework" enabling seamless passenger 
transitions between conventional aircraft, helicopters, and seaplanes with 
harmonized scheduling, ticketing, and baggage handling protocols, creating 
truly integrated multi-modal connectivity networks rather than isolated 
transport solutions. 
31. To a pointed query on how the Ministry plans to ensure timely completion of

32. The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s assertion that the Project

34. The Committee notes that while the Ministry has granted 'In-Principle'

recommends establishing a dedicated "Greenfield Airport Monitoring Portal" 
providing comprehensive project tracking with standardized milestone-based 
reporting requirements for all developers. This digital system should generate 
monthly progress alerts highlighting critical delays requiring ministerial 
intervention. The Committee further recommends creating a specialized land 
acquisition facilitation team within the Ministry to coordinate with state 
governments, offering technical assistance and standardized compensation 
frameworks to accelerate the historically problematic land acquisition 
process. Additionally, the Ministry should establish a "Strategic Airport 
Development Fund" specifically for greenfield airports in priority regions 
including the Northeast, island territories, and economically underdeveloped 
areas with high tourism potential. This fund should implement a matching-
grant model where Central government contributions increase proportionally 
in regions with limited fiscal capacity but strong connectivity needs. 

33 
 
35. The Committee appreciates the inclusion of smaller cities in expansion 
plans but notes with concern that the current allocation framework may not 
adequately address emerging air travel markets in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities. 
The Committee recommends implementing a "60-40 Development Ratio" 
wherein at least 40% of airport infrastructure investment is mandatorily 
directed toward non-metro airports serving cities with populations under 1 
million. To support this approach, the Ministry should develop a standardized 
"Regional Airport Viability Assessment Tool" incorporating five key 
parameters: current surface transport connectivity gaps, tourism potential, 
industrial development plans, population growth patterns, and estimated 
catchment area travel demand. This assessment should be conducted for all 
proposed airport locations with results published transparently to justify 
investment priorities. Furthermore, the Committee recommends creating 
"Airport Access Zones" extending 50km around each regional airport with 
coordinated development of connecting infrastructure including dedicated 
airport expressways, rail links, and regional bus networks through formalized 
agreements with respective ministries and state governments. These zones 
should include simplified land-use conversion processes specifically for 
transportation infrastructure development to reduce implementation delays. 
 
PRODUCTIVITY LINKED INCENTIVE (PLI) SCHEME FOR DRONES 
AND DRONE COMPONENTS 
 
36. The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Drones and Drone 
Components, notified on 30th September 2021, aims to promote domestic drone 
manufacturing and innovation. With a total outlay of ₹120 crore over three years, 
the scheme offers one of the highest PLI rates at 20% of value addition, providing 
strong financial incentives for manufacturers. Unlike other PLI schemes, the value 
addition threshold is set at 40% instead of 50%, and eligibility norms for MSMEs 
and startups are relaxed, ensuring broader participation. The scheme also includes 

34 
 
developers of drone-related software and caps individual manufacturers’ incentives 
at 25% of the total annual outlay, thereby ensuring a wider distribution of benefits. 
Furthermore, if a manufacturer fails to meet the eligibility threshold in a given year, 
they are allowed to claim the lost incentive in the following year upon meeting the 
shortfall. The Ministry further informed that amounts disbursed under the scheme

37. The Committee acknowledges the Liberalised Drone Rules, 2021 and the 
Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Drones and Drone 
Components, introduced with a ₹120 crore outlay over three years to boost 
domestic drone manufacturing. While the PLI rate of 20% of value addition is 
among the highest across PLI schemes, the Committee observes that 
disbursements have been slower than expected (₹29.43 crore in FY23, ₹28.76 
crore in FY24, and ₹13.59 crore so far in FY25) which seems to be indicative 
of possible implementation delays, industry participation hurdles, or 
challenges in meeting eligibility norms. The relaxed value addition norm of 
40% and MSME-friendly criteria are commendable, but the cap of 25% per 
manufacturer may limit scaling opportunities for key industry players. The 
Committee therefore recommends a review of participation levels to identify 
impediments in fund utilisation, alongside stronger industry engagement to 
encourage wider adoption, particularly among MSMEs and startups. In the 
opinion of the Committee, given drones' strategic and commercial potential, 
the scheme may be considered for extension beyond three years, allowing 
sustained scaling and R&D investment.

39. The Committee notes with serious concern the high number of 
vacancies across key aviation regulatory and operational bodies, particularly 
in the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), the Bureau of Civil 
Aviation Security (BCAS), and the Airports Authority of India (AAI). The 
DGCA, responsible for aviation safety and regulatory oversight, has a 
vacancy rate exceeding 53 percent, raising fundamental concerns about its 
capacity to enforce aviation safety standards effectively. Similarly, BCAS, 
which is tasked with maintaining aviation security, has nearly 35 percent of its 
sanctioned posts unfilled, posing risks to the robustness of security oversight 
at airports. AAI, managing critical airport infrastructure and air traffic 
services, has over 3,200 vacancies, representing nearly 17 percent of its 
sanctioned strength, potentially impacting operational efficiency and airport 
expansion. The Committee is deeply concerned that chronic understaffing in 
these institutions could undermine safety, security, and service delivery 
standards, particularly as air traffic volumes continue to rise.The Committee 
urges the Ministry of Civil Aviation to expedite the recruitment process to fill 
vacancies across DGCA, BCAS, and AAI, ensuring that regulatory oversight, 
security enforcement, and airport operations are not compromised. Given the 
rapid expansion of air traffic and aviation infrastructure, the Ministry must 

36 
 
adopt a long-term workforce planning strategy to ensure staffing levels 
remain to meet operational demands. 
 
GRANTS-IN-AID TO INSTITUTION IN CIVIL AVIATION FOR 
PROMOTION/DEVELOPMENT OF AERO SPORTS 
40. The budget for aero sports and allied activities was initially planned for 
Rs. 1 crore in the year 2022-23 but no expenditure was made. The following 
year 2023-24 the budget was reduced to Rs. 0.10 crore. Subsequent for the 
year 2024-25 has been kept to Rs. 0.10 crore. The committee takes note of the 
fact that the Government of India has formed the National Aero Sports 
Guidelines (NASG) to develop a robust aero sports ecosystem, which has a 
global potential to partner in $30 billion industry across the world. The 
government has consciously taken a call to create a strong ecosystem for aero 
sports, which includes Ballooning, Aeromodelling, Amateur Built and 
Experimental Aircraft, Drones, Gliding, Microlights, Para Motors, 
Parachuting and Rotorcraft. The Aero Club of India has been designated as 
the National Airsports Control (NAC) by the government for promotion of 
aero sports across all the states. In order to implement the policy in letter and 
spirit, ACI requires a hand holding through a budgetary support to create an 
ecosystem for aero sports. The Committee recommends that budgetary 
allocation as per the requirement of the Aero Club of India may be enhanced 
as to support Flying Training Organizations and aero sports across the 
country. The committee also notes that the Aero Club of India has been one of 
the oldest autonomous organization of the Ministry of Civil Aviation working 
to support development for flying training and has successfully established an 
ecosystem of flying training for last 50 years. The Aero Club of India 
headquartered at the Safdarjung Airport area, Sri Aurobindo Marg, New 
Delhi and it was managed and run as an autonomous organization to conduct 
aero sports and flying training by assets created by the budgetary funding of 

37 
 
the Government which intern created an ecosystem for pilots training in 
India. The Aero Club of India was dispossessed of its office building some 
years ago, which requires restorations as the office building constructed 
through its own resources which now has been turned into a Directorate of 
Licensing for Air Traffic Services (ATS) under Airports Authority of India 
(AAI). The Committee recommends that the Ministry prioritize spending on 
aero sports and allocate budgetary support, including restoring the 
administrative infrastructure of the Aero Club of India (ACI), to facilitate the 
fulfillment of the National Aero Sports Guidelines (NASG) issued by the 
Government. The Committee further recommends enhancing budgetary 
support for the ACI will strengthen India’s aero sports sector and Flight 
Training Organizations (FTOs), ensuring the sustainable growth of the sector. 
FLYING TRAINING ORGANISATIONS 
41. The Committee notes that with the growth of the aviation sector, the 
airlines in India would require over 30,000 pilots in the next decade or so. 
Presently, in the country there is an acute shortage of Flying Training 
Organizations, with the limited infrastructure and resources. The Committee 
is of the opinion that the ecosystem for Flying Training Organizations is 
inadequate to meet the growing requirements which results in large numbers 
of Pilots going abroad for training. The requirement of commercial pilots in 
the country is roughly a thousand every year. However, with the existing 
FTOs, the country can barely produce 300 Commercial Pilots and another 
300 pilots train abroad, leaving a large gap of the requirement for commercial 
pilots. The training of pilots who go abroad, result in large foreign exchange 
drain. The present ecosystem of flying training has several shortcomings 
including long duration of training, high cost with constraints of shortage of 
trainer aircrafts, trainers / instructors, institutional funding, aircraft 
manufacturing, spares and training infrastructures. The Committee notes 
that there is an urgent need to proliferate flying training across the country to 

38 
 
meet the Pilot requirements of the future. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry develop clear policy reforms to ensure strong partnerships with 
state governments, the Airports Authority of India (AAI), and other 
stakeholders. These reforms should also streamline the regulatory 
mechanisms of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) for flight 
training. To further promote flight training and establish India as a global 
hub, the Committee advises making budgetary provisions for this sector. 
GREENFIELD INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT 
42. In the Budget, it was mentioned about Greenfield Airport project in 
particular reference to Bihar. The Committee is of the opinion that to cater 
the requirement of the state, which does not have a single International 
Greenfield Project like Shamshabad (Hyderabad), Devanahalli (Bangalore) or 
MoPA (Goa) or for that matter Jewar (Uttar Pradesh), it would be essential to 
establish an International Greenfield Airport next to Patna for the futuristic 
requirement as desired by the state for next 50 to 70 years to meet the 
aspirational needs of 14 crore people of the State of Bihar. The Committee is 
of the opinion that an International Greenfield Airport like Jewar should be 
given a top priority for futuristic development and growth of aviation 
infrastructure along with other Greenfield projects across the country. The 
Committee also notes that, in order to match the anticipated growth in 
national and international air traffic across the country and to supplement 
RCS connectivity, greenfield infrastructure projects should be expedited to 
achieve overall greater connectivity and promote air travel.

Budget Analysis and Allocation 
1.   Imbalance in Capital Outlay: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation

investigation capabilities. The Committee recommends a balanced allocation 
across aviation bodies to address critical gaps in security and investigative 
resources .

32% to ₹540 crore despite ambitious expansion goals. The Committee 
recommends proportional enhancement of security protocols and accident 
response mechanisms to support the scheme's growth into tier II and III cities .

allocations to specific performance indicators and outcomes, supported by 
regular audits to ensure efficient fund utilization. 
Air India-Related Expenditure 
4.  Reduction Plan for AIAHL Liabilities: Establish a phased five-year plan to 
reduce financial obligations, monetize non-core assets, and implement cost-
sharing mechanisms for medical benefits to retired employees.

monitor expenditures and accelerate liability resolution to minimize long-term 
fiscal impact.

predictive airfare monitoring, dynamic fare bands, and real-time anomaly

report arbitrary pricing, integrated with "AirPrice Guardian" for participatory 
governance and swift grievance redressal.

for cabin standards, including environmental sustainability guidelines to align

factors while supporting underperforming routes in growth regions like the 
Northeast.

REASONS FOR VARIATIONS / UNDER UTILIZATIONS DURING, 2022-23, 
2023-24 AND CURRENT FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25: 
5. For 2022-23, the initial budgetary provision was ₹ 3009.05 crore, which was 
revised to ₹ 3363.07 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry incurred an expenditure of ₹ 
3284.12 crore, which is approximately 97.65% of the revised allocation. 
6. For 2023-24, the budget was set at ₹ 3399.65 crore, later increased by ₹ 60.35 
crore to ₹ 3460 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry's expenditure for the year was ₹ 
3406.90 crore, representing 98.46% of the revised estimate. 
7. For 2024-25, the budgetary provision is ₹ 3260.93 crore, including ₹ 190.01 
crore under the Capital section. Although the Ministry proposed an RE allocation of ₹ 
3756.55 crore, reflecting an increase of ₹ 495.62 crore, the RE allocation remained the 
same as the BE allocation. The Committee acknowledges that the Ministry has 
undertaken additional activities such as the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day 
tableau, which were not included in the RE stage. However, it is expected that the 

7 
 
allocated budget for 2024-25 will be utilized optimally as per the Ministry's planned 
activities. 
8. The Committee observes that there is a significant reduction in the 
Ministry's total budget from ₹ 3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 
crore (RE) in 2024-25 and an increase to ₹ 3,360.96 crore for 2025-26. The 
Committee further observes the reduction in the Ministry’s total budget from ₹ 
3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 crore (RE) in 2024-25 can be 
attributed primarily to the one-time expenditures related to the Azadi Ka Amrit 
Mahotsav (AKAM). The AKAM celebrations saw a substantial increase in 
expenditure, with a revision of the Budget Estimate (BE) from ₹ 185 crore to ₹ 
335 crore during 2023-24, resulting in an expenditure of ₹ 334.39 crore, which 
was more than 80% over and above the original BE allocation. 
9. The Committee acknowledges that the reduction in budget during the 
2024-25 fiscal year is a reflection of the conclusion of AKAM-related activities, 
which were exceptional in nature and not a recurring part of the Ministry's 
regular expenditure plans. However, the reduction in the budget allocation for 
2024-25 compared to 2023-24 highlights the need to ensure that the Ministry's 
cultural preservation and development initiatives are adequately funded, 
especially in light of long-term goals for heritage conservation.  
10. The Committee further notes that the budget formulation process for 
2024-25 did not adequately account for key national cultural commitments, 
including the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day tableau, leading to an 
additional request for funds mid-year. The omission of such significant 
expenditures at the BE stage does seem to indicate deficiencies in financial 
forecasting and contingency planning. The Committee recommends the 
implementation of a comprehensive Multi-Year Budgetary Framework (MYBF) 
for the Ministry of Culture that extends beyond the annual budget cycle. This 
framework should incorporate: 

8 
 
a) A five-year rolling budget projection with annual revisions to accommodate 
changing priorities while maintaining long-term vision. 
b) Categorization of expenditures into core recurring activities, planned 
development initiatives, and special events/commemorations with separate 
budgetary provisions for each category. 
c) Establishment of a Budget Stabilization Reserve of approximately 5% of the 
total annual allocation to account for unforeseen cultural activities or 
emergencies, preventing mid-year fiscal disruptions. 
This approach would mitigate the abrupt budgetary fluctuations witnessed 
between 2023-24 and 2024-25, and provide greater stability for cultural 
institutions dependent on Government funding. 
11. The Committee further notes that although overall budget utilisation 
remains high, expenditure patterns across various cultural schemes have been 
inconsistent. Programmes such as museum development, cultural mapping, and 
global cultural engagement have experienced fluctuating levels of fund 
disbursement, with some initiatives facing under-utilisation in certain years and 
excessive allocations in other.  The Committee strongly recommends the 
development of a Cultural Calendar-Based Budgeting system that: 
a) Maintains a comprehensive five-year cultural events calendar that identifies 
recurring festivals, commemorations, and international engagements with 
historical budget requirements. 
b) Integrates cyclical cultural events (such as Kumbh Mela, which occurs every 
12 years) into long-term financial planning through a dedicated cultural events 
fund. 
c) Implements quarterly budget review mechanisms to assess expenditure 
against planned activities and make necessary adjustments before the Revised 
Estimates stage. 

9 
 
d) Develops an AI-assisted forecasting model that analyzes historical expenditure 
patterns and predicts resource requirements for upcoming cultural activities 
based on past event costs, inflation factors, and attendance projections. 
This systematic approach would ensure that cultural events of national 
importance receive appropriate financial provisions at the Budget Estimate stage 
rather than relying on mid-year adjustments 
 
12. The Committee observes a pattern wherein the Ministry relies heavily on 
mid-year budgetary adjustments, seeking substantial increases at the RE stage 
instead of ensuring that BE allocations accurately reflect financial needs. In the 
opinion of the Committee, this approach introduces uncertainty into long-term 
financial planning and may disrupt the timely execution of projects. A more 
accurate and predictive budget estimation process is required to minimise 
dependency on RE-stage adjustments. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry strengthen its engagement with the Ministry of Finance to establish a 
more flexible, needs-based budget allocation framework, one that will ensure 
funding provisions are more effectively met with practical expenditure 
requirements. Also, the Ministry should establish a Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) engagement cell within the Ministry to facilitate 
partnerships between businesses and cultural projects, capitalizing on the 100% 
tax exemption available under Section 80G(ii) of the Income Tax Act

14. The Committee recommends a more robust allocation for the conservation, 
restoration, and maintenance of protected monuments, especially the World 
Heritage Sites. Considering the increasing pressure on ASI’s existing resources, 
the allocation need to be increased to ensure timely conservation and meet global 
standards for preservation. It is recommended to create a dedicated Heritage 
Conservation Fund with a corpus of ₹ 500 crore over five years, with 
contributions from tourism revenue, CSR initiatives, and matching government 
grants through the National Culture Fund framework. This fund would 
specifically address emergency conservation needs and climate vulnerability 
mitigation measures at protected monuments.  
14.1 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) manages 3,698 centrally 
protected monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites 
and Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958, encompassing temples, forts, tombs, and 
prehistoric sites. Despite recent efforts, including a 70% budget increase to ₹ 
443.53 crore in 2023–24 and the delisting of 18 untraceable monuments like 
Delhi’s Barakhamba Cemetery and Haryana’s Kos Minar No.13, challenges such 
as encroachment, climate threats, and resource gaps persist. To address these 
issues, parliamentary committees recommends a multi-pronged strategy. First, a 
GIS-based digital inventory with real-time monitoring and biennial audits 
should be prioritized to enhance accountability and prevent monuments from 
disappearing due to urbanization. Strengthening legal frameworks, including 

12 
 
stricter penalties under the AMASR Act and fast-track courts for heritage 
violations, would streamline enforcement against encroachments. 
14.2 Climate resilience measures, such as expanding Automated Weather 
Stations (AWS) and pollution monitoring labs to high-risk sites like Konark Sun 
Temple, must be scaled to mitigate environmental damage. Concurrently, 
integrating AI-driven predictive maintenance, 3D mapping, and drone 
surveillance—as seen in Tamil Nadu’s excavation projects and Mehrauli’s recent 
Supreme Court-mandated survey—can revolutionize preservation through early 
damage detection. Community engagement is equally critical; initiatives like a 
tax-incentivized “Adopt a Monument” program and training locals as heritage 
stewards would foster grassroots ownership. 
14.3 Finally, delisting protocols require reform. An independent panel should 
reassess criteria to ensure delisting occurs only after rigorous documentation and 
public consultation, paired with a relic repatriation policy for displaced artifacts. 
By combining technology, legal rigor, climate adaptation, and community 
participation, India can balance heritage conservation with developmental 
pressures, safeguarding its cultural legacy for future generations. These steps 
would align with ASI’s mandate while addressing systemic gaps in monument 
management. 
15. The Committee recommends addressing delays in ongoing Museum 
Projects like the Dholavira Museum and the Leh Museum as they have faced 
significant delays due to issues such as land allotments, extending timelines by 8–
12 months. The committee further recommends prioritizing the resolution of 
these delays, ensuring that land allotments are expedited and necessary 
clearances are streamlined. A dedicated task force or coordination mechanism 
should be set up to oversee and speed up the approval processes for critical 
infrastructure projects. 

13 
 
16. The Committee recommends comprehensive digitalization of heritage 
assets to enhance both preservation efforts and public engagement: 
a) Develop a phased implementation of "Digital Twin" technology for all 
World Heritage Sites and at least 100 nationally significant monuments by 
2028. This would involve creating precise digital replicas to monitor 
structural changes, simulate conservation interventions, and enhance 
visitor experience through augmented reality applications. 
b) Establish a centralized Heritage Monitoring System using remote sensing 
and IoT devices to provide real-time data on environmental conditions, 
structural stability, and visitor impact at critical monuments. This would 
enable predictive maintenance and early intervention, potentially reducing 
long-term conservation costs by 30-35%. 
c) Launch a Metaverse Heritage Initiative that creates immersive digital 
experiences of inaccessible or vulnerable monument areas, allowing for 
virtual tourism while reducing physical impact on fragile structures. This 
initiative should prioritize monuments facing access restrictions due to 
conservation concerns. 
d) Implement block chain technology for monument documentation and 
conservation history, creating an immutable record of interventions and 
condition assessments that ensures accountability and preservation of 
institutional knowledge across administrative transitions. 
16.1 Recommendation: Institutional Reforms for Museum Project 
Implementation: The Committee recommends fundamental reforms to the 
project implementation mechanisms: 
a) Implement a modular development approach for museum projects, enabling 
phased completion and partial operationalization while resolving issues with 
remaining components. This would allow for incremental public access and 

14 
 
revenue generation rather than complete closure during extended development 
periods. 
b) Develop a standardized pre-implementation framework for museum projects 
that mandates resolution of land acquisition, environmental clearances, and 
conceptual design before budget allocation and project announcement, 
minimizing mid-project disruptions. 
c) Create specialized project management units for each major museum 
initiative with representation from relevant stakeholders, including state 
governments, ASI, content specialists, and community representatives to ensure 
coordinated action and accountability. 
 
16.2 To address content finalization delays as observed in the Digital Museum 
project at Kanakakunnu Palace, the Committee recommends: 
 
a) Establish a permanent Museum Content Advisory Board comprising 
historians, cultural anthropologists, museologists, and digital content specialists 
to expedite content development processes across all museum projects. 
b) Implement concurrent content development alongside infrastructure creation 
rather than sequential processes, with rolling approvals for thematic sections to 
prevent complete project stagnation during content refinement. 
c) Develop a shared digital content repository for Ministry museums that enables 
efficient resource sharing and adaptation of existing content for new museums, 
reducing redundant research and development costs. 
d) Integrate emerging technologies such as AI-assisted curation, interactive 
installations, and personalized visitor journeys through mobile applications to 
enhance the museum experience and attract younger audiences.

development:

sites into broader regional development plans. This would involve creating 
archaeological tourism circuits with appropriate infrastructure, interpretation

ENHANCING EFFORTS FOR CULTURAL REPATRIATION 
29.1 The Archaeological Survey of India, operating under the Ministry of 
Culture, is spearheading this significant cultural recovery effort, which includes 
the Kohinoor and beyond it to encompass thousands of artifacts removed during 
British colonial rule. 
29.2 To strengthen India’s campaign for cultural repatriation, the government 
should consider establishing a specialized “Heritage Recovery Task Force” 
comprised of diplomats, legal experts, archaeologists, and art historians. This 
multidisciplinary team would be dedicated exclusively to identifying, 
documenting, and pursuing claims for stolen Indian artifacts worldwide. The 
task force could develop comprehensive dossiers on priority items, including 
detailed provenance research, legal arguments for restitution, and cultural 
significance documentation to bolster India’s claims. 
29.3 India should leverage its growing economic and diplomatic influence to 
negotiate cultural property agreements with more countries, similar to the recent 
pact with the United States. These agreements should establish clear mechanisms 
for identifying looted artifacts, resolving disputes, and facilitating returns. 
Special attention should be paid to former colonial powers like the United 
Kingdom, where many significant Indian treasures remain. These agreements 

24 
 
could be tied to broader diplomatic and trade relationships, creating incentives 
for cooperation on repatriation issues. 
29.4 To strengthen legal arguments for repatriation, India should invest in 
cutting-edge technological tools for provenance research and authentication. 
Advanced imaging techniques, DNA analysis of organic materials, and AI-
powered databases could help establish the Indian origin of disputed artifacts 
and track the chain of ownership. This scientific evidence could prove invaluable 
in making compelling cases for return, particularly for items with unclear 
provenance records. 
29.5 Additionally, India should explore innovative public-private partnerships 
to support repatriation efforts. The government could establish a “Heritage 
Repatriation Fund” that accepts contributions from corporations, wealthy 
individuals, and the Indian diaspora to support legal challenges, negotiate 
purchases when necessary, and fund transportation and conservation of 
returned artifacts. This approach would expand the resources available for 
recovery efforts while engaging broader segments of society in the mission.

32.2 The Committee recommends establishing a dedicated research program 
for developing advanced conservation technologies. This should include creating 
five specialized Conservation Research Laboratories focused on different 
manuscript materials (palm leaf, birch bark, paper, cloth, and metals) to develop 
non-invasive preservation techniques, research environmentally sustainable 
conservation materials, and establish evidence-based protocols for treatment of 
deteriorating manuscripts. The implementation of a "Preventive Conservation 
Network" with environmental monitoring systems at all major manuscript 
repositories would enable real-time assessment of conservation risks and 
preventive interventions, significantly reducing deterioration rates in vulnerable 
collections.

conservation institutes worldwide would facilitate knowledge exchange, joint

Committee notes that while the NMM employs various methods of preservation 
such as lamination, restoration, and de-acidification, there is a need for more 
systematic research into conservation technologies specific to Indian manuscript

climatic zones across the country and their distinct conservation challenges.

more comprehensive approach to manuscript content utilization that transforms 
static documents into dynamic knowledge resources.

35. As per Paragraph No. 8.1 of Report No. 12 of 2017 of the C&AG Report 
(Annexure), the Ministry of Culture failed to fill up key posts in the National Gallery 
of Modern Art for over a decade resulting in failure to relocate 16,582 works of art to 
a new state of the art storage system, leading to idling of investment of ₹ 3.81 crore 
since March 2014.  Further, as per Para 3.1 of Report No.3 of 2024 of the said Report 
regarding Functioning of IGRMS, there was a shortage of staff in IGRMS as on 2024 
as out of total sanctioned strength of 118 posts in all the cadres, there was a vacancy 
of 36 posts (30.51 per cent) which included five vacancies (100 per cent) in Group A 
cadre. These vacancies will hinder in research and preservation efforts, thereby 
impacting the overall effectiveness of heritage management. 
36. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should prioritize 
the immediate recruitment of qualified personnel to fill the existing vacancies, 
especially at the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA) and Indira Gandhi 
Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya (IGRMS), in critical positions such as those in 
Group A cadres. This will ensure the effective management of cultural heritage, 
facilitate the relocation of artworks, and support research and preservation 
efforts. The Ministry should streamline the recruitment process, establish a 
dedicated task force to monitor progress, and allocate necessary resources to 
ensure timely appointments, thereby strengthening the overall functionality of 
these institutions and preventing any further delays in their operations. 
37. The Committee further observes that the integration of major monuments 
with tourism circuits through modern technological solutions, such as Artificial 
Intelligence and Augmented Reality, is increasing the demand for specialized 
manpower. This includes not only technical roles for preservation but also skilled 
personnel for the management and implementation of these advanced 

30 
 
technologies, which will require a focus on recruiting professionals with expertise 
in both heritage conservation and cutting-edge technological fields. 
38. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that ASI prioritize the 
recruitment of skilled professionals with expertise in both heritage conservation 
and modern technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality, 
to support the integration of major monuments with tourism circuits and ensure 
the effective management and preservation of cultural heritage. 
39. Further, in light of the increasing demand for specialized manpower due to 
the integration of Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality, for the 
digitization and preservation of monuments, the Committee desires to know 
whether the Ministry has made any progress in implementing the 
recommendations from the 2020 Expert Committee regarding the adoption of 
these technologies. The Committee would also like to know the steps taken to 
recruit professionals with expertise in both heritage conservation and cutting-
edge technological fields to manage and execute these initiatives effectively.

10.  The meeting resumed at 02: 40 P.M. to hear the views of the Secretary, Ministry of 
Culture on Demands for Grants (2025 -26) of the Ministry . At the outset, the Chairman opened 
the meeting by welcoming the Members of the Committee, officers and representatives from the 
Ministry of Culture.  
11.  Shri Arunish Chawla, Secretary, Ministry of Culture started his presentation by 
presenting a comprehensive overview of the Ministry’s financial allocations and key policy 
initiatives. He stated that the Ministry has been allocated Rs. 3,360 crore s for the financial year 
2025-26, reflecting a marginal increase over the previous year. The Ministry has consistently 
maintained a high expenditure rate, with 98.47% of the allocated budget utilised in the preceding 
financial year and 89% already expended  in the current fiscal cycle. He outlined the 
implementation of seven Central Sector Schemes, which include Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana, 
Centenaries and Anniversaries, Development of Museums, Development of Libraries and 
Archives, Gyan Bharatam Mission, Gl obal Engagement Scheme, and the National Mission on 
Cultural Mapping. The Secretary also highlighted major accomplishments, such as the successful 
organisation of the World Heritage Committee Meeting in July 2024, the repatriation of 655 
antiquities, and t he recognition of Garba of Gujarat as part of UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural 
Heritage.  
12.   The Secretary emphasised the Ministry’s ambitious vision under Rachanatmak Bharat: 
namely, the National Mission on Creative Economy, which seeks to integrate India’s cultural and 
artistic heritage with modern economic frameworks while initiatives like the Cultural Satellite 
Account, aimed at quantifying the economic contribution of cultural activities, as well as the 
integration of major monuments with tourism circui ts through modern technological solutions, 
including Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality. He reassured the Committee that steps 
were being taken to expedite recruitment processes for vacant positions in ASI, museums, and 
national academies.  

41 
 
 
13.  Thereafter, the Ministry elaborated on its financial strategies, explaining categorization of 
the budget under three verticals: Establishment Expenditure, covering administrative costs and 
institutional overheads; Central Sector Schemes, dedicated to the  implementation of key cultural 
programmes; and Autonomous Bodies and Grantee Institutions, which provide financial support 
to cultural academies, museums, and research institutions.  
14. The Ministry highlighted its efforts to optimize fund utilization an d streamline 
administrative processes. It emphasized the budget for cultural infrastructure and digital 
modernization, with greater investments allocated to digital repositories, archival preservation, 
and museum enhancements. It was informed that internat ional collaborations and public -private 
partnerships were actively being pursued to reduce reliance on domestic financial allocations and 
secure expertise for large -scale cultural preservation projects. The Ministry asserted that its  
approach to prudent f iscal management, strategic planning, and innovative funding mechanisms 
would significantly bolster its ability to preserve the country’s rich cultural legacy and enhance 
global cultural influence. 
15.   The Committee raised the following issues during the course of the Meeting:  
 Members queried on the reasons behind certain funds remaining underutilized  despite an 
increase in budgetary allocations and sought clarity on measures to ensure timely 
expenditure. 
 Concerns were raised regarding vacancies in key i nstitutions such as the ASI, museums, 
and national academies, and their impact on research and preservation efforts. 
 Members raised q ueries regarding the decreasing number of archaeological excavations 
compared to previous years, particularly in historical ly significant sites such as 
Balirajgarh and Harappan settlements. 
 Members sought clarification on whether tribal dances, oral traditions, and other 
indigenous cultural elements were being adequately documented and supported. 
 Members highlighted the need f or financial assistance, pension schemes, and capacity -
building programmes to safeguard the livelihoods of folk artists and craftsmen. 
 Concerns were expressed regarding the perceived inactivity of Zonal Cultural Centres 
and their engagement with local communities. 
 Members sought to know the conditions of artefacts stored in museum basements and the 
Ministry’s plan for their proper preservation and exhibition. 
 Members welcomed efforts to reclaim antiquities from the United States  and urged 
similar bilateral agreements with the United Kingdom and other nations to recover 
significant cultural artefacts.

recommendations:

optimal expenditure of allocated funds;

research and preservation efforts; 
 Adoption of a well -planned approach to increase the number of excavations, particularly 
in historically significant regions; 
 Launching of dedicated initiatives to document and support oral traditions, tribal d ances, 
and indigenous art forms; 
  Integration of c ultural and heritage stu dies into school and university curricula to 
promote awareness and appreciation among students; 
 Creation of p ension schemes and financial assistance programmes to secure the 
livelihoods of folk artists and craftsmen; and 
 Devising of a  detailed inventory an d digitization plan for artefacts stored in museum 
basements to facilitate preservation and exhibition.

INTRODUCTION 
Maritime transport constitutes a fundamental pillar of national infrastructure, 
underpinning the economic growth, trade expansion, and social advancement of the 
country. It plays an instrumental role in shaping the pace, structure, and trajectory of 
development, ensuring India’s connectivity with global markets and reinforcing its 
position in international trade. 
2. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping, and Waterways (MoPSW) bears the paramount 
responsibility for the formulation and execution of policies and programmes aimed at 
fortifying the maritime sector. Its remit encompasses ports, shipping, inland waterways, 
shipbuilding and ship-repair services, with the overarching objective of ensuring a 
modern, efficient, and globally competitive maritime infrastructure. 
3. To address the complexities and evolving demands of the maritime sector, a 
comprehensive, strategic, and future-oriented policy framework is imperative. In 
furtherance of this objective, the Ministry is actively engaged in: 
 Augmenting port capacity by advancing infrastructure, enhancing berths, and 
modernising cargo-handling mechanisms to facilitate seamless trade and efficient 
logistics. 
 Empowering the shipping and waterways industries to assume greater 
responsibility in handling sea-borne trade through indigenous vessels, thereby 
reducing reliance on foreign carriers and reinforcing national maritime 
sovereignty. 
 Encouraging sustainable investment in port infrastructure, recognizing that the 
development of ports demands substantial capital investment, entails prolonged 
gestation periods, and is subject to multifaceted externalities. 

2 
 
4. Historically, port development has been state-driven, necessitated by the 
considerable financial outlay, uncertain returns, and strategic implications inherent in 
such large-scale projects. The Ministry’s proactive approach in navigating these 
challenges is pivotal in fortifying India’s maritime capabilities and ensuring that the 
nation remains at the forefront of global maritime trade. Through infrastructure 
modernization, progressive policy initiatives, and steadfast commitment, the Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping, and Waterways is spearheading the transformation of India’s maritime 
sector, making it a driving force for economic prosperity and global trade leadership.

8. Container Movement Timing Recommendations 
8.1 The Committee recommends immediate attention to the challenges facing 
maritime container movement schedules due to global disruptions and trade 
volatility. The Committee strongly urges the Ministry to implement comprehensive 
digital tracking platforms for real-time monitoring of container movements across 
all major ports. Furthermore, the Committee recommends establishing a dedicated 
Maritime Response Unit to address contingencies arising from geopolitical 
disruptions along key shipping routes. The Committee believes these measures are 
essential to mitigate extended lead times currently affecting Asia-Europe shipments 
and to reduce congestion at strategic port hubs. 
Port Efficiency Recommendations 
8.2 The Committee notes the ambitious targets under Maritime India Vision 2030 
and recommends accelerated implementation of mechanization initiatives at all 
major ports to achieve the sub-20-hour turnaround time goal. The Committee 
strongly advises prioritizing budget allocation for modernizing port infrastructure, 
particularly automated cargo handling systems and digital documentation 
processes. The Committee further recommends quarterly performance reviews of 
port efficiency metrics with standardized benchmarks to ensure measurable 
progress toward capacity enhancement targets. 
Inter-Ministerial Port Connectivity Recommendations 
8.3 The Committee emphasizes that inadequate multi-modal connectivity 
remains a significant bottleneck affecting port efficiency. The Committee 
recommends establishing a dedicated Inter-Ministerial Coordination Cell to 
expedite port connectivity projects under PM Gati Shakti. With reference to 

10 
 
Paradip Port, the Committee recommends immediate completion of pending 
railway linkage projects and upgradation of NH-53A to facilitate smoother cargo 
evacuation. The Committee strongly urges synchronized planning between the 
Ministries of Railways, Road Transport and Highways, and Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways to ensure infrastructure development aligns with projected cargo 
volumes. The Committee recommends that the Paradip Port development model be 
replicated across other major ports to enhance seamless connectivity and reduce 
logistics costs. 
8.4 The Committee notes that the allocation of ₹0.71 crore for Research & 
Development (R&D) in port development is strikingly low, especially considering 
the critical role that technological advancement plays in ensuring the 
competitiveness and efficiency of the country’s maritime infrastructure. The 
Committee strongly recommends a significant augmentation of R&D funding to 
bring out innovation in port infrastructure, automation, and environmental 
sustainability.

Sagarmala Programme 
15. The Sagarmala Programme, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways' 
flagship Central Sector Scheme, promotes port-led development by harnessing 
India’s coastline, waterways, and strategic maritime position. Projects are 
implemented by Central Ministries, State Governments, State Maritime Boards, 
and Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), with the Ministry also supporting high-
impact, low-return projects. For FY 2025-26, ₹ 810 crore has been allocated for 
port infrastructure, coastal berths, road and rail links, fishery harbours, floating 
jetties, skill development, cruise terminals, and Ro-Pax ferry services. Under the 
Sagarmala Scheme, the Ministry is developing the National Maritime Heritage 
Complex (NMHC) at Lothal, Gujarat, as a one-of-a-kind project dedicated to 
India’s maritime heritage. The Ministry is enhancing urban waterways transport 
(Ro-Pax services) to improve cargo movement, reduce travel time, ease road 
congestion, and cut pollution. It is part-funding 26 fishing harbours, with 9 
completed at ₹ 144.5 crore, and upgrading five major harbours—Kochi, Chennai, 
Visakhapatnam, Paradip, and Mallet Bunder. Additionally, 50 floating jetty 
locations have been identified in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, 
Karnataka, and Kerala, while ₹ 56 crore has been allocated for maritime 
infrastructure in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.

expenditure trends under the Sagarmala Programme, notes that while the Budget
