    At the outset, the Chairman, welcomed the Members of the Committee and Secretary 
and other officials from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), National 
Highways Authority of India (NHAI), and National Highways and Infrastructure 
Development Corporation Limited (NHIDCL). 
2.  The Chairman outlined the primary objectives of the meeting , which centred on the scrutiny 
of budget allocations, the efficiency of p roject implementation, the status of road infrastructure 
projects, and the effectiveness of road safety measures . He underscored the urgency of ensuring 
the timely completion of national highways, addressing infrastructural impediments, and 
implementing sustainable transport solutions.  
3.  The Ministry commenced its presentation by outlining the budgetary allocations for the 
financial year 2025 -26, reporting a total allocation of ₹2,87,000 crore . The primary budgetary 
provisions comprised ₹2,76,500 crore for National Highways Development and Maintenance, 
₹10,400 crore for State Roads under the Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF), ₹400 
crore for Road Transport and Road Safety Initiatives, and ₹300 crore for the development of 
Ropeways and Cable Car Projects. The Ministry further reported the expenditure status for FY 
2024-25, noting that ₹2,44,500 crore had already been utilised, amounting to 85% of the total 
allocation, with an expected utilisation of 90% by the financial year’s conclusion. 
4.  On t he investment and funding mechanisms , the Ministry highlighted its reliance on private 
sector participation and asset monetisation . It reiterated its dependence on public-private 
partnerships (PPPs), the Toll Operate Transfer (TOT) model, and Infrastructur e Investment 
Trusts (InvITs) to ensure sustained financial inflows for national highway development. 
5.  Regarding national highway expansion and connectivity improvements, the Ministry affirmed 
its commitment to constructing 10,000 km of new national high ways in FY 2025 -26, with a 
focus on enhancing connectivity in the North-Eastern region (1,100 km) and tribal areas (750 
km). It further detailed its plan to expand high -speed corridors from 4,600 km to 5,800 km, 
develop 10 port -connectivity roads, and cons truct 15 new ropeways to improve accessibility in 
hilly terrains. The Ministry acknowledged that, as of July 2024, 697 projects remained pending , 
with the highest number of delays recorded in Maharashtra (98), Karnataka (40), and Haryana 
(21) with the the  principal causes of project delays being attributed to land acquisition hurdles, 

40 
 
railway clearance bottlenecks, financial constraints affecting contractors, and regulatory delays . 
Land acquisition issues, which accounted for 35% of all project delays , were  attributed to 
protracted disputes over compensation, inaccuracies in land records, and opposition from local 
stakeholders, often resulting in legal cases. Furthermore, 30% of all stalled projects were delayed 
due to railway clearance processes , particular ly in securing approvals for road overbridges 
(ROBs) and underpasses . The Ministry informed the Committee that inter-ministerial 
consultations with Indian Railways have been initiated to streamline approval processes and 
introduce time-bound clearance protocols. 
6.  The Ministry highlighted contractors’ financial distress , noting that several firms were 
struggling with escalating project costs, delays in government disbursements, and increasing 
input costs. It reiterated its commitment to facilitating improved credit access for contractors and 
enforcing a performance -based evaluation framework to enhance financial discipline and 
accountability. Additionally, the Ministry highlighted delays in regulatory and environmental 
clearances, particularly for projects  traversing protected forest areas and ecologically sensitive 
zones. It assured the Committee that efforts were being made to fast-track approvals through a 
single-window clearance mechanism and enhanced coordination with the Ministry of 
Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). 
7.  On the subject of road safety, the Ministry presented its Vision 2028 strategy, which seeks to 
reduce road fatalities by 95% by 2028. The Ministry outlined its efforts to rectify 1,000 accident-
prone black spots during FY  2025-26, with the broader objective of eliminating all hazardous 
locations by FY 2027-28. It further detailed the expansion of Driving Training Centres (DTCs), 
with the aim of establishing at least one centre in each district  to enhance driver competence and 
licensing standards. Updates were also provided on the cashless treatment scheme for accident 
victims, which are presently at the pilot stage in six states , with a commitment to nationwide 
implementation in the ensuing fiscal year . The Ministry stated its intention to introduce 
Intelligent Traffic Management Systems (ITMS), AI -driven automated surveillance, and stricter 
penalties for traffic violations and also integration of  drone-based monitoring of encroachments 
into the enforcement framework, with s cheduled quarterly assessments in urban regions and 
biannual inspections in rural areas. 
8. During the deliberations of the Meeting, Members  raised several concerns and sought 
clarifications on the following issues: 
 Members questioned the Ministry’s assertion that road fatalities could be reduced by 95% 
by 2028 , given the slow pace of black spot rectification and inadequate enforcement 
mechanisms. 
 Concerns were expressed regarding the insufficient number of operational DTCs , with 
only 28 centers established for 650 districts. 
 Members sought explanations for several highway projects that had been inaugurated but 
remained stalled for over two years. 
 Query was made on the Mumbai Coastal Road (₹14,000 crore) , which required repairs 
within a year of completion which may point to serious lapses in quality control. 
 Challenges in awarding contracts and monitoring quality control. 
 Gatishakti Mission and need for breaking departmental silos and fostering integrated 
planning for infrastructure projects. 
 Members widely c riticized the unilateral decision -making by NHAI officials , without 
engaging local MPs and state authorities in highway planning. 

41 
 
9.  To address these concerns effectively, the Committee made the following actionable 
recommendations: 
 Expediting the establishment of Driving Training Centres (DTCs)  in every district within 
two years, using Viability Gap Funding (VGF) or Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
contributions. 
 Implementing a structured six -monthly review mechanism  to assess the progress of 
black-spot rectification efforts. 
 Ensuring mandatory deployment of ambulances  along accident-prone National Highway 
stretches. 
 Introducing third-party quality control audits  for all major National Highway projects to 
ensure contractor accountability. 
 Institutionalising consultations with MPs and state governments  to improve highway 
alignment and infrastructure planning. 
 Enhancing inter -ministerial coordination  between the Ministries of Road Transport, 
Railways, and Ports to eliminate procedural delays. 
10. The Chairman concluded the meeting by stressing the urgency of improving transparency, 
efficiency, and accountability  in the transport sector. While reminding all attendees of the 
confidentiality of the proceedings, the Ministry was directed to submit a written response within 
one week , detailing measures for expediting pending projects, implementing black -spot 
rectifications, and enhancing road safety initiatives.

REPORT 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, is the nodal agency for the 
formulation of national policies and programs and for co-ordination of activities 
with various Central Government Agencies, State Governments/UTs and the 
Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country. It 
plays a crucial role in coordinating and supplementing the efforts of the 
State/Union Territory Governments, catalysing private investment, strengthening 
promotional and marketing efforts and in providing trained manpower resources.  
 
2. The major activities of the Ministry of Tourism can be classified under the 
following heads: - (I) Development of Tourism Infrastructure; (II) Promotion and 
Publicity; (III) Manpower Development; (IV) Regulation of Service Standards for 
Tour Operators & Hotels; (V) Other Initiatives/Programmes. India Tourism 
Development Corporation (ITDC) is the only Public Sector Undertaking under the 
charge of the Ministry of Tourism and the following autonomous institutes under 
its jurisdiction-  
⮚ Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management (IITTM) and 
National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS) 
⮚ National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology 
(NCHMCT) and the Institutes of Hotel Management. 
 
It has an attached office namely the Directorate General of Tourism (DGT). 
 
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES  
3. The Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework marks a shift from tracking 
financial and physical progress to an outcome-based governance model. It defines 

2 
 
measurable indicators to assess scheme objectives, ensuring greater development 
impact and public accountability. By actively monitoring progress against set 
targets, the framework enhances transparency and ensures more effective use of 
public funds in India. 
 
4. The Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) 2025-2026, 
published by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, outlines key financial 
allocations, expected project outputs, and anticipated outcomes for various 
tourism-related schemes. The government has prioritised the enhancement of 
tourism infrastructure, skill development, and promotional activities to boost 
domestic and heritage tourism through the following objectives- 
i. Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage Augmentation Drive 
(PRASHAD) scheme (allocated budget ₹240 crore): The PRASHAD 
scheme aims to rejuvenate religious and heritage sites, with 39 projects to be 
completed and 273 sub-components developed, with the end result being 
creation of  390 direct jobs. 
ii. Domestic Tourism Promotion (allocated budget ₹131.90 crore): A target 
of 35 events and 15 digital campaigns has been set to boost domestic tourism 
by 10%, with 40 additional events to be supported. 
iii. Hospitality and Tourism Education (allocated budget ₹35 crore): Three 
new projects will be initiated for IHMS/FCIs/IITTM institutes, with a 3% 
increase in hospitality job placements. 
iv. Capacity Building for Service Providers initiative (allocated budget ₹25 
crore): It will aim to train 40,000 new service providers and re-skill 30,000 
existing workers, with the goal of a 2% employment rate among trainees, 
while5% are anticipated to become self-employed. 
v. Assistance to Central AgenciesScheme (allocated budget ₹90 crore): 
Four major projects will be launched under central assistance, which in turn 
will see a tourist footfall of 25,000 at ticketed monuments.

FOR GRANTS (2025-26)    
5. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture considered Demand No. 99 containing the details of budget 
allocations of the Ministry ofTourism, for the financial year 2025-26, in its 
meeting held on the 3rdMarch, 2025.For the financial year 2025-26, the Ministry of 
Tourism has identified key focus areas for the development and promotion of 
tourism across India. These include: 
Development of infrastructure-Infrastructure development is a primary 
objective, with efforts directed towards completing projects sanctioned 
under Swadesh Darshan, PRASHAD (Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual 
Heritage Augmentation Drive), Assistance to Central Agencies, and Special 
Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) schemes. Additionally, 
new projects will be approved under Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and Challenge-
Based Destination Development Schemes to enhance tourist destinations 
nationwide. 
Promotion and marketing-To strengthen promotion and marketing, the 
ministry will organise and support various promotional events, trade fairs, 
and exhibitions both within India and overseas. A significant focus will be 
placed on developing promotional films, digital brochures, and media 
campaigns under the Incredible India brand. Furthermore, marketing 
campaigns will be directed at domestic audiences, and Familiarisation 
(FAM) trips will be arranged to highlight India's tourism potential. 
Skill development-In the realm of skills development, the ministry aims to 
provide financial assistance to institutions such as IHMs, FCIs, IITTM, and 
ICI to enhance professional training in the tourism and hospitality sector. It 
will also conduct capacity-building programmes for tourism service 
providers and expand the Incredible India Tourist Facilitators Programme, 
designed to create a pool of well-trained and professional tourist guides. 
Additionally, specialist training programmes will be introduced under the

Paryatan Mitra & Paryatan Didi initiatives to equip local communities with 
tourism-related skills.

19. The Committee notes with serious concern the chronic pattern of fund 
underutilization by the Ministry of Tourism, which represents not merely an 
administrative challenge but a fundamental impediment to the growth of 
India's tourism potential. The alarming statistics of only 33.4% utilization of 
allocated funds in 2023-24 (₹801.81 crore out of ₹2400 crore) and the 
continuation of this trend in 2024-25 (only ₹396.82 crore utilized thus far out 
of ₹2479.62 crore) indicates deep-rooted systemic inefficiencies that require 
comprehensive structural reforms. While the Ministry has attributed this 
underperformance to administrative bottlenecks, procedural delays, and 
coordination challenges with implementing agencies, the Committee finds 
these explanations inadequate and reflective of entrenched operational 
weaknesses that demand immediate redressal. 
 
20. The Committee recommends implementing a comprehensive Integrated 
Digital Project Management System (IDPMS) modeled after successful 
implementations like Tamil Nadu's tourism data collection and analytical 
method for tracking visitor footfalls. This centralized platform would 
facilitate end-to-end project lifecycle management, from proposal submission 
to fund disbursal and utilization certificate processing with embedded 
automatic alerts and escalation protocols for pending actions. The system 
should incorporate real-time dashboards accessible to all stakeholders 
including the Ministry officials, state tourism departments, and implementing 
agencies, providing transparency on project status, fund utilization, and 
procedural bottlenecks requiring immediate intervention. This digital 
infrastructure would enable predictive analytics to identify potential 
implementation challenges before they create delays and would maintain a 
comprehensive digital repository of all project documentation, eliminating 
physical document submission requirements that frequently cause delays.

20.1 The Committee recommends the development of a Tourism 
Implementation Rating System (TIRS) to evaluate and rank states based on 
their efficiency in implementing tourism projects, timely submission of 
required documentation, and overall fund utilization patterns. This 
performance-based framework would create healthy competition among 
states while providing objective metrics for allocating additional resources to 
high-performing regions. States consistently demonstrating superior 
implementation capabilities should receive incentives including priority 
funding for new projects, relaxed procedural requirements, and recognition 
through annual tourism implementation excellence awards. Conversely, states 
with persistently poor implementation records should receive targeted 
capacity-building interventions and simplified pilot projects to build 
implementation expertise before receiving allocations for more complex 
initiatives. This rating system would create accountability while providing 
valuable data on implementation challenges specific to different regions.

Task Force (FUTF) comprising financial experts, project management 
specialists, and representatives from high-performing state tourism 
departments. This dedicated team would conduct monthly reviews of fund

interventions to accelerate fund absorption. The FUTF should develop 
standardized templates for all documentation required throughout the project 
lifecycle—including detailed project reports, utilization certificates, and 
closure documents—thereby eliminating inconsistencies that frequently delay 
approvals. Additionally, the task force would provide hands-on 
implementation support to underperforming states through expert 
deployment, targeted training programs, and developing simplified process

27. Strengthening Implementation of Tourism Infrastructure Schemes 
The Committee has conducted a thorough review of the Ministry of Tourism's 
principal infrastructure development initiatives, specifically the National 
Mission on Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage Augmentation 
Drive (PRASHAD) Scheme, the Special Assistance to States/UTs for Capital 

24 
 
Investment (SACI) Scheme, and the Assistance to Central Agencies for 
Tourism Infrastructure Development Scheme, which collectively represent the 
cornerstone of India's tourism infrastructure development strategy. 
28.  Revitalizing the PRASHAD Scheme Through Technological Integration 
The Committee expresses profound concern regarding the implementation 
inefficiencies plaguing the PRASHAD Scheme, particularly at high-footfall 
pilgrimage sites where infrastructural inadequacies continue to compromise 
visitor experiences despite substantial allocations. To address these persistent 
challenges, the Committee recommends implementing a comprehensive 
Digital Monitoring and Implementation Framework modeled after Tamil 
Nadu's innovative tourism data collection and analytical method for tracking 
visitor footfalls. This system would enable real-time monitoring of project 
progress, fund utilization, and visitor experience metrics through a 
centralized dashboard accessible to all stakeholders. The Ministry should 
establish Implementation Credibility Ratings for all participating states and 
implementing agencies based on past performance metrics, particularly 
focusing on utilization certificate submission timeliness and project 
completion rates. States with consistently high ratings should receive 
implementation incentives including expedited approvals and priority funding 
for new projects. Furthermore, the Committee recommends restructuring the 
brownfield project implementation protocols within PRASHAD, creating 
specialized guidelines with modified timelines and technical assistance 
mechanisms specifically designed to address the unique challenges of 
developing infrastructure at existing pilgrimage sites with operational 
constraints. 
29. Enhancing State Participation Through Reformed SACI 
Implementation 
The Committee acknowledges the potential of the SACI Scheme as a vital 

25 
 
financing mechanism for tourism infrastructure but notes with concern the 
inconsistent participation patterns and persistent delays in DPR submissions 
that threaten to undermine the scheme's effectiveness given its fixed 
termination date of March 31, 2026. To address these implementation 
challenges, the Committee recommends transforming the challenge-based 
selection process into a phased approach with quarterly submission windows 
and corresponding fast-track review mechanisms, enabling continuous 
engagement rather than single-deadline approaches. The Ministry should 
establish a dedicated DPR Technical Support Cell comprised of infrastructure 
planning specialists, tourism experts, and financial analysts to provide hands-
on assistance to states struggling with proposal development, effectively 
reducing preparation time and enhancing submission quality. Additionally, 
the Committee recommends implementing Regional Knowledge Exchange 
Forums where high-performing states can share implementation strategies, 
technical approaches, and administrative innovations with those experiencing 
challenges, creating peer-learning networks that accelerate collective 
capabilities. These structural improvements would significantly enhance state 
participation while maintaining the scheme's competitive elements that drive 
innovation and excellence. 
29.1 Accelerating Completion of Central Agency Projects 
The Committee notes with significant concern that only 60% of projects 
sanctioned under the Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism 
Infrastructure Development Scheme have reached completion, creating 
substantial risk of asset deterioration and visitor dissatisfaction at key tourism 
destinations. To catalyze project execution, the Committee recommends 
implementing a Multi-tier Performance Monitoring System with quarterly 
reviews of all ongoing projects conducted jointly by the Tourism Ministry and 
implementing agency leadership, establishing clear consequences for 
persistent delays including conditional future funding and leadership 

26 
 
accountability mechanisms. The Ministry should develop a specialized Project 
Acceleration Task Force deployable to stalled projects to provide technical 
interventions, administrative solutions, and coordination support to overcome 
implementation barriers. Furthermore, the Committee recommends 
establishing a Tourism Infrastructure Excellence Program wherein Central 
Agencies achieving exceptional implementation efficiency receive recognition, 
performance incentives, and priority consideration for future projects, 
creating positive reinforcement for operational excellence. These innovations 
would transform the accountability framework while providing practical 
mechanisms to accelerate project completion rates across all implementing 
agencies. 
30. Integrating Digital Transformation Across Infrastructure Initiatives 
The Committee recommends leveraging the framework of the emerging 
National Digital Tourism Mission to create an integrated digital ecosystem 
across all tourism infrastructure development schemes. This would involve 
establishing unified digital standards for project proposal submission, 
implementation tracking, and outcome measurement across all schemes, 
eliminating the siloed approach that currently impedes cross-scheme learning 
and coordination. The Ministry should develop a Unified Tourism 
Infrastructure Interface that provides real-time visibility into project status, 
fund utilization, and implementation challenges across all schemes, enabling 
data-driven decision making and timely interventions. Additionally, the 
Committee recommends implementing AI-driven predictive analytics to 
identify potential implementation bottlenecks before they emerge, allowing for 
preemptive resolution of common challenges that typically cause delays. This 
digital transformation would fundamentally enhance the efficiency of all 
tourism infrastructure development initiatives while creating unprecedented 
transparency and accountability throughout the implementation cycle.

36. Analysis of Foreign Tourist Arrivals and India's Global Tourism 
Position 
The Committee has conducted a comprehensive assessment of India's tourism 
performance metrics, including foreign tourist arrivals (FTAs), international 
tourist arrivals (ITAs), foreign exchange earnings (FEEs), and the overall 
contribution of tourism to GDP. While acknowledging the Ministry's various 
promotional initiatives such as participation in international trade fairs, 
roadshows, and the innovative Chalo India Global Diaspora Campaign, the 
Committee observes that despite post-pandemic recovery, significant 
challenges persist in establishing India as a premier global tourism 
destination. Current data indicates that India ranks 39th in the global travel 
and tourism competitiveness index despite possessing extraordinary potential 
through its rich cultural heritage, diverse landscapes, and emerging global 
influence. This positioning represents a substantial gap between India's 
tourism capabilities and its actual market performance, necessitating 
transformative strategies to enhance competitiveness and sustain long-term 
growth in the international tourism sector. 
36.1 Implementing a Multi-Dimensional Competitiveness Enhancement 
Strategy 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a comprehensive 
Tourism Competitiveness Enhancement Framework based on a thorough 
analysis of India's strengths and weaknesses in the global tourism ecosystem. 
This framework should leverage India's significant advantages in natural 
resources (scoring 5.88 out of 7), cultural resources (5.62), and non-leisure 
resources (5.05), while systematically addressing areas of underperformance. 
The Ministry should establish a dedicated Tourism Competitiveness Task 
Force comprising industry leaders, academic experts, and government 
representatives to identify specific barriers to India's advancement in global 
rankings and develop targeted interventions. Furthermore, the framework 

34 
 
should incorporate innovative benchmarking mechanisms that regularly 
compare India's performance against rapidly advancing tourism destinations, 
particularly in emerging markets with similar tourism profiles. Beyond 
conventional tourism metrics, the framework should incorporate 
sustainability parameters, digital readiness indicators, and visitor satisfaction 
indices to ensure a holistic approach to competitiveness enhancement. This 
structured approach would transform India's competitiveness strategy from 
reactive to proactive, positioning the country to advance significantly from its 
current 39th position toward the top 20 global destinations by 2030. 
36.2 Revolutionizing Tourism Marketing Through Advanced Digital 
Strategies 
The Committee recommends a fundamental reimagining of India's tourism 
marketing approach through the implementation of an AI-driven 
Personalized Tourism Marketing Ecosystem. This would leverage the 
revamped Incredible India Digital Platform (IIDP) to create highly targeted, 
personalized marketing campaigns for different international markets based 
on sophisticated data analytics and AI algorithms. The system would analyze 
potential visitors' digital footprints, travel preferences, and cultural interests 
to deliver customized tourism propositions rather than generic promotional 
content. Furthermore, the Ministry should develop market-specific digital 
personas representing key tourist segments from major source countries, 
enabling the creation of tailored content strategies that resonate with specific 
cultural contexts and travel motivations. The Committee also recommends 
establishing a Global Digital Influencer Network dedicated exclusively to 
promoting Indian tourism experiences, systematically engaging with content 
creators who have significant followings in key international markets. This 
revolutionary approach would transform tourism marketing from mass 
communication to precision engagement, substantially improving conversion 
rates and expanding India's share in the global tourism market. 

35 
 
36.3 Transforming the Chalo India Initiative into a Strategic Diaspora 
Engagement Program 
The Committee recommends a significant enhancement of the Chalo India 
Global Diaspora Campaign, transforming it from primarily an incentive 
program into a strategic diaspora engagement framework that systematically 
cultivates the Indian diaspora as tourism ambassadors. The Ministry should 
implement a tiered Diaspora Tourism Ambassador certification program, 
providing specialized training, promotional materials, and digital tools to 
formally recognized diaspora members who actively promote Indian tourism. 
Furthermore, a sophisticated tracking and attribution system should be 
developed to measure the direct impact of diaspora-generated tourism, 
enabling performance-based incentives and recognition for top-performing 
ambassadors. The initiative should incorporate regular virtual forums 
connecting diaspora communities with tourism stakeholders in India, creating 
channels for continuous feedback on international visitor experiences and 
emerging preferences. Additionally, the Committee recommends establishing 
Diaspora Tourism Innovation Grants to support creative diaspora-led 
projects that enhance India's tourism appeal in their respective countries. 
This strategic approach would transform the diaspora from passive 
supporters to active, measurable contributors to India's tourism growth, with 
clearly defined performance indicators ensuring accountability and 
effectiveness. 
37. Implementing Next-Generation Visa Facilitation Programs 
Recognizing visa complexity as a significant barrier to tourism growth, the 
Committee recommends implementing a Progressive Visa Liberalization 
Roadmap that systematically expands visa-free access based on strategic 
tourism priorities rather than conventional diplomatic reciprocity. The 
Ministry, in coordination with the Ministry of External Affairs, should 
develop data-driven criteria for identifying and prioritizing high-potential 

36 
 
source markets for visa liberalization, considering factors beyond current 
arrival numbers to include average spending patterns, length of stay, and 
potential for market growth. Furthermore, the Committee recommends 
implementing a Digital Nomad Visa Program specifically designed to attract 
long-term international visitors who can work remotely while experiencing 
India's diverse destinations, effectively creating a new category of extended-
stay tourism that generates sustained economic impact. For markets where 
visa-free access is not immediately feasible, the Ministry should implement an 
Advanced Traveler Authorization System enabling simplified entry for pre-
approved visitors from key tourism markets. These innovations would 
significantly reduce barriers to entry while maintaining necessary security 
protocols, positioning India as a leader in intelligent border facilitation for 
tourism growth. 
38. Developing Destination-Specific Transformation Initiatives 
The Committee recommends that beyond the general development of 50 
tourist destinations announced in the 2025-26 budget, the Ministry should 
implement a Strategic Destination Transformation Program that selects 10 
high-potential destinations annually for comprehensive development as global 
tourism excellence centers. Each selected destination would receive integrated 
support including infrastructure enhancement, digital transformation, 
capacity building, and targeted international promotion, creating showcase 
models of world-class tourism management. The program should incorporate 
Destination Experience Laboratories where innovative tourism concepts, 
technologies, and service models can be tested and refined before broader 
implementation. Furthermore, the Committee recommends establishing 
Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) with public-private 
governance structures for each selected destination, ensuring professional 
management and sustainable growth through dedicated expert oversight. 
These initiatives would transform India's approach to destination 

37 
 
development from incremental improvement to comprehensive excellence, 
creating globally competitive tourism products that significantly enhance 
India's tourism appeal and international rankings. 
39. Accelerating Medical and Wellness Tourism Through Specialized 
Ecosystems 
Building upon the 'Heal in India' initiative announced in the 2025-26 budget, 
the Committee recommends developing a comprehensive Medical and 
Wellness Tourism Ecosystem that integrates healthcare excellence with 
exceptional tourism experiences. This would involve establishing specialized 
Medical Tourism Corridors in key cities, with integrated services including 
international patient facilitation centers, specialized accommodation, wellness 
tourism packages, and cultural experiences designed specifically for medical 
travelers and their companions. The Ministry should implement a rigorous 
Medical Tourism Certification System for healthcare facilities and associated 
service providers, ensuring consistently high standards specifically tailored to 
international patients' needs and expectations. Furthermore, the Committee 
recommends developing International Insurance Coordination Mechanisms to 
streamline payment processes for international patients, removing a 
significant barrier to medical tourism growth. These specialized interventions 
would position India as the definitive global leader in medical and wellness 
tourism, capturing a substantially larger share of this high-value tourism 
segment.

financial assistance for the expansion and upgradation of Central Institutes of Hotel

48. Strategic Expansion of Hospitality Education Infrastructure 
 
The Committee, while acknowledging the expansion efforts in hospitality 
training institutes, identifies critical geographical disparities that severely 
limit access to quality tourism education in several high-potential tourism 
regions. This education infrastructure gap creates persistent workforce 
challenges and hinders the development of local tourism ecosystems. The 
Committee recommends implementing a Tiered Hospitality Education 
Framework that strategically distributes training facilities based on tourism 
potential and workforce needs rather than conventional administrative 
considerations. This framework would establish three distinct institutional 
models: Comprehensive Institutes of Hotel Management (IHMs) in regional 
hubs, specialized Focused Culinary Institutes (FCIs) aligned with distinct 
culinary heritage zones, and flexible Community Tourism Skill Centers in 
emerging tourism destinations. The Ministry should prioritize establishing at 
least one specialized hospitality training institute in each Northeastern state 
by 2027, with particular focus on developing centers of excellence that align 

43 
 
with each region's unique tourism attributes—adventure tourism in 
Arunachal Pradesh, cultural tourism in Assam, and ecological tourism in 
Meghalaya. Additionally, the Committee recommends introducing the 
Tourism Satellite Campus model, wherein established IHMs develop 
extension facilities in underserved regions, leveraging existing administrative 
infrastructure while expanding geographical reach cost-effectively. This 
transformative approach would systematically address geographical 
disparities while ensuring that educational infrastructure aligns precisely with 
each region's specific tourism development trajectory. 
49. Transforming Hospitality Education Through Industry-Integrated 
Learning 
 
The Committee emphasizes that traditional curriculum development 
processes in hospitality education have become inadequate for preparing 
professionals in the rapidly evolving tourism landscape where technological 
proficiency, sustainability expertise, and experiential delivery capabilities are 
increasingly essential. The Committee recommends establishing a National 
Tourism Education Innovation Council comprising industry leaders, 
academic experts, digital technology specialists, and international hospitality 
education partners to fundamentally reimagine hospitality curriculum beyond 
incremental updates. This collaborative body would develop core curriculum 
frameworks incorporating emerging competencies including digital guest 
experience management, sustainable tourism operations, cultural 
interpretation techniques, and tourism entrepreneurship. Furthermore, the 
Committee recommends implementing a Mandatory Industry Immersion 
Program requiring all hospitality faculty to complete annual industry 
placements of at least four weeks, ensuring instructors maintain current 
practical knowledge alongside theoretical expertise. Additionally, the Ministry 
should establish a Hospitality Education Digital Transformation Initiative 

44 
 
that provides all IHMs and FCIs with integrated learning management 
systems, virtual reality training environments for practical skills development, 
and AI-powered personalized learning pathways that adapt to individual 
student learning patterns. These innovations would transform hospitality 
education from institution-centered to learner-centered while ensuring 
graduates possess the precise competencies required for India's tourism 
growth. 
50. Pioneering Sustainable Funding Models for Tourism Education 
 
The Committee recognizes that the current allocation of ₹35 crore for FY 
2025-26 represents a significant constraint on the necessary expansion and 
modernization of hospitality education infrastructure. Beyond conventional 
funding approaches, the Committee recommends establishing a Tourism 
Education Investment Fund through strategic partnerships with major 
tourism industry stakeholders, international development agencies, and 
corporate CSR initiatives. This dedicated fund would provide sustainable 
financing for infrastructure development, technology acquisition, and faculty 
excellence programs across hospitality education institutions. The Committee 
also recommends developing a Tourism Education Revenue Diversification 
Framework that enables institutes to generate supplementary income through 
establishing commercial training restaurants, student-operated boutique 
hotels, specialized consulting services, and executive education programs for 
industry professionals. Furthermore, the Ministry should implement the 
Destination Adoption Program wherein tourism-intensive destinations 
contribute to hospitality education infrastructure in exchange for dedicated 
workforce development programs tailored to their specific requirements. 
These innovative funding mechanisms would transform hospitality education 
financing from government-dependent to multi-stakeholder supported, 
substantially expanding available resources while creating greater alignment 

45 
 
between educational institutions and industry needs. 
51. Elevating Specialized Tourism Training Through Centers of Excellence 
 
The Committee acknowledges the critical importance of specialized tourism 
training exemplified by the National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS), while 
noting significant limitations in both geographical reach and integration with 
mainstream tourism education. The Committee recommends transforming 
NIWS into the National Center for Adventure Tourism Excellence with 
expanded scope encompassing all adventure tourism segments including 
mountaineering, trekking, wildlife tourism, and desert expeditions, creating a 
comprehensive ecosystem for adventure tourism human resource 
development. The Center should establish Regional Adventure Tourism 
Training Hubs in five strategic locations—Uttarakhand (mountaineering), 
Goa (water sports), Rajasthan (desert tourism), Madhya Pradesh (wildlife 
tourism), and Sikkim (eco-adventure tourism)—ensuring specialized training 
reaches diverse geographical areas with distinct adventure tourism potential. 
Furthermore, the Committee recommends implementing an Integrated 
Adventure Tourism Certification System aligned with international standards 
that creates clearly defined career pathways for professionals across different 
adventure tourism segments. Additionally, the Ministry should develop the 
Adventure Tourism Digital Knowledge Repository, a comprehensive online 
platform providing training resources, safety protocols, and best practices 
accessible to adventure tourism operators nationwide. These transformative 
initiatives would elevate specialized tourism training from isolated programs 
to a comprehensive national framework that develops world-class human 
resources across the adventure tourism ecosystem. 
 
 
 

46 
 
CAPACITY BUILDING FOR SERVICE PROVIDERS: 
Ministry of Tourism under the scheme of “Capacity Building for Service 
Providers” (CBSP) aims to provide education, training and certification to the 
tourism service providers at every level with its main objectives being to train and 
up-grade manpower at every strata of service in order to i) capitalize on the vast 
tourism potential of the country to the fullest, and ii) provide professional expertise 
to the local populace as well as create fresh opportunities for employment 
generation in the tourism sector both in urban as well as rural areas. The Scheme is 
implemented by the Ministry of Tourism through Institutes of Hotel Management 
and Food Craft Institutes including such institutes approved by the All India 
Council for Technical Education (AICTE), Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel 
Management (IITTM), National Council of Hotel Management & Catering 
Technology (NCHMCT).  Training is also given through State/UT/Central 
Training/ Academic Institutions, India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) 
and the specialized academic Training Institutes in the private sector engaged in 
giving training in the hospitality sector.The following programmes are being run 
under the scheme of ‘CBSP’: 
a) Hunar Se Rozgar Tak 
b) Skill Testing & Certification Programme 
c) Entrepreneurship Programme 
d) Tourism Adventure Courses 
e) Linguistic Tourist Facilitators (LTF) 
f) Destination Based Skill Development 
g) Other Programs: Tourism Awareness/Sensitization programs for existing 
service providers are also conducted under this scheme.   
A total of ₹  25 cr has been set aside in this year budget for this head. 
 
52. The Committee acknowledges the importance of skill development in 
improving India’s tourism competitiveness but notes that the CBSP scheme 
has not yet achieved uniform accessibility. Many rural and emerging tourism 

47 
 
hubs lack structured training facilities, limiting opportunities for communities 
that would benefit most from employment in the sector. It therefore urges the 
Ministry to imbibe a more balanced regional approach by increasing training 
coverage in underserved areas. 
 
53. The Committee highlights that the budgetary allocation of ₹25 crore, 
though a step in the right direction, may be insufficient to expand the scheme 
at the scale required. It therefore urges the Ministry to explore additional 
funding sources, including public-private partnerships, corporate 
sponsorships, and collaboration with State Governments, to enhance training 
infrastructure and broaden access to professional development opportunities.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS OF THE COMMITTEE'S 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS 
 
Budget Utilization and Monitoring 
1.   Addressing Underutilization of Funds 
To tackle chronic underutilization, the Committee recommends a three-tier 
monitoring mechanism for Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD schemes, 
involving central oversight, state-level coordination committees, and 
destination-specific implementation teams with quarterly milestones and real-
time digital tracking systems. Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) should be 
leveraged to enhance operational efficiency and attract investments in tourism 
infrastructure. A dedicated Project Management Unit with tourism 
infrastructure specialists should be established to conduct pre-feasibility 
assessments and ensure project viability before fund disbursement. 
2.  Integrated Digital Project Management System (IDPMS) 
The Ministry should implement a centralized digital platform modeled on 
Tamil Nadu’s tourism data system to manage the project lifecycle, track fund 
utilization, and provide real-time dashboards for stakeholders. Predictive 
analytics should be incorporated to identify potential delays, ensuring timely 
interventions. 
3.  Tourism Implementation Rating System (TIRS) 
A performance-based framework to evaluate states on project implementation 
efficiency, fund utilization, and timely documentation is recommended. High-
performing states should receive incentives such as priority funding, while 
underperforming states should receive targeted capacity-building support. 
 

49 
 
4.  Fund Utilization Task Force (FUTF) 
Establish a specialized task force comprising financial experts and project 
managers to address procedural bottlenecks, accelerate fund absorption, and 
provide hands-on support to underperforming states. Standardized templates 
for documentation should also be developed. 
Tourism Infrastructure Development 
5.  Revamping PRASHAD Scheme 
A comprehensive Digital Monitoring Framework should be introduced for 
PRASHAD projects to track progress and visitor metrics in real-time. 
Implementation Credibility Ratings for states/agencies based on past 
performance should guide future funding priorities. Specialized guidelines for 
brownfield projects are recommended to address unique challenges at high-
footfall pilgrimage sites. 
6.  Enhancing SACI Scheme Participation 
Transform the challenge-based selection process into a phased approach with 
quarterly submission windows and fast-track reviews. A DPR Technical 
Support Cell should assist states in proposal development, while Regional 
Knowledge Exchange Forums should foster peer learning . 
7.  Accelerating Central Agency Projects 
Introduce a Multi-tier Performance Monitoring System with quarterly reviews 
and establish a Project Acceleration Task Force to resolve barriers in stalled 
projects. Recognize high-performing agencies through a Tourism 
Infrastructure Excellence Program. 
 
 

50 
 
8.  Digital Transformation Across Schemes 
Develop a Unified Tourism Infrastructure Interface for real-time visibility into 
project status across schemes, supported by AI-driven predictive analytics to 
preempt delays. 
Promotion and Marketing 
9.  Global Tourism Marketing Framework 
Establish an Integrated Global Tourism Marketing Framework leveraging AI-
driven personalization, virtual tourism experiences, and seamless booking 
interfaces under the Incredible India Digital Platform (IIDP). Collaborate with 
Indian Missions abroad for targeted campaigns. 
10.  Balanced Domestic and International Promotion 
Develop a Dual Growth Strategy focusing on emerging domestic destinations 
while promoting unique cultural experiences internationally. Allocate ₹50 
crore for innovative concepts like Caravan Tourism. 
11.   Revival of RSOPPMDA Scheme 
Restructure the Overseas Promotion scheme with market-specific strategies 
and rolling approval mechanisms for global outreach campaigns. Strategic 
partnerships with Indian Missions abroad are essential for effective 
promotion. 
12.   Tourism Hubs Along Highways 
Develop 100 tourism hubs along national highways showcasing regional 
heritage, cuisine, art, and culture as immersive visitor experiences. 
Competitiveness Enhancement 
13.   Tourism Competitiveness Framework 

51 
 
Establish a dedicated task force to systematically address barriers in global 
rankings through benchmarking mechanisms, sustainability metrics, digital 
readiness indicators, and visitor satisfaction indices. 
14.   Advanced Digital Marketing Strategies 
Implement an AI-driven personalized marketing ecosystem targeting 
international markets with tailored content strategies and influencer networks 
to enhance engagement. 
15.   Diaspora Engagement Program 
Transform the Chalo India initiative into a strategic Diaspora Tourism 
Ambassador program with certification training, performance incentives, and 
innovation grants for diaspora-led projects. 
16.   Visa Facilitation Programs 
Introduce Progressive Visa Liberalization based on market potential and 
launch Digital Nomad Visa Programs to attract long-term visitors contributing 
to sustained economic impact. 
17.   Destination-Specific Excellence Centers 
Select 10 high-potential destinations annually for comprehensive development 
as global tourism models with integrated support in infrastructure, capacity 
building, and promotion. 
18.  Medical and Wellness Tourism Ecosystem 
Develop specialized Medical Tourism Corridors with integrated services like 
patient facilitation centers, wellness packages, and cultural experiences 
tailored to international patients’ needs. 
 

52 
 
Domestic Tourism Growth 
19.   Infrastructure for Domestic Tourism 
Collaborate with state governments for capacity assessments at major 
destinations to prevent over-tourism while promoting balanced regional 
development through eco-tourism and rural tourism initiatives . 
20.  Review of Dekho Apna Desh Initiative 
Undertake a formal review of this initiative’s impact to guide future domestic 
tourism strategies effectively . 
Manpower Development 
21.   Hospitality Education Expansion 
Address geographical disparities by establishing tiered hospitality education 
models including IHMs in regional hubs, culinary institutes aligned with 
heritage zones, and community skill centers in emerging destinations. 
22.  Industry-Integrated Learning 
Reimagine hospitality curricula through a National Tourism Education 
Innovation Council incorporating sustainability management, digital 
competencies, and entrepreneurship skills alongside mandatory faculty 
industry immersion programs. 
23.  Sustainable Funding Models 
Create a Tourism Education Investment Fund through partnerships with 
industry stakeholders and CSR initiatives while enabling institutes to generate 
supplementary income through commercial ventures. 
 
 

53 
 
24.  Adventure Tourism Training Excellence 
Expand NIWS into a National Center for Adventure Tourism Excellence with 
regional hubs specializing in activities like mountaineering, water sports, 
desert tourism, wildlife exploration, etc., supported by an integrated 
certification system aligned with global standards. 
Capacity Building 
25.  Balanced Regional Training Coverage 
Expand the CBSP scheme’s reach into underserved rural areas by increasing 
training accessibility through public-private partnerships and state 
collaborations.

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and apprised them 
of the agenda of the meeting i.e. (i) oral evidence of the Secretary, M/o Tourism on Demands for 
Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry ; and (ii) *****i 
 
i. Oral evidence of Secretary, Ministry of Tourism 
2.  The Chairman, extended a warm welcome to all Members of the Committee and senior 
officials of the Ministry of Tourism. 
3. The Chair man underlined the fundamental role of tourism in promoting economic 
growth, employment generation, and cultural preservation. He urged the Ministry to elaborate on 
its expenditure patterns, the obstacles encountered in project implementation, and the strategic 
roadmap envisaged for the upcoming fiscal year. 
4.  The Secretary, Ministry of Tourism commenced her presentation with a detailed account 
of its budgetary allocations and expenditure trends. It was noted that for the 2023 -24 fiscal year, 
an initial allocation of ₹2,400 crore was subsequently revised to ₹1,692 crore, y et actual 
expenditure stood at only ₹801 crore. Similarly, for 2024 -25, the budget initially set at ₹2,479 
crore was later reduced to ₹850 crore, with the Ministry reporting an expenditure of just 51% of 
the revised amount. The Ministry attributed this to delays in project approvals, the restructuring 
of tourism schemes, procedural inefficiencies arising from the transition from Swadesh Darshan 
1.0 to 2.0., and challenges in transitioning to the Treasury Single Account (TSA) system, which 
temporarily disrup ted fund disbursement. Moreover, the Ministry cited COVID -19-induced 
disruptions, which had a lasting impact on infrastructure development and capital expenditure in 
the tourism sector. The Ministry also cited to the long gestation period of infrastructure  projects, 
which naturally led to slower financial outflows. 
5. Alongside financial matters, the Ministry elaborated on the current state of the tourism 
sector, highlighting significant growth in both domestic and international tourism post-pandemic. 
In 20 23, international tourist arrivals reached 0.95 crore, reflecting a 47.9% increase over the 

76 
 
previous year. Domestic tourism also experienced an upward trend a 45% increase over the 
previous year. Despite these encouraging trends, officials acknowledged tha t the country still 
lags behind leading global tourism destinations, necessitating more aggressive international 
marketing efforts, improvements in ease of travel, and substantial infrastructural enhancements. 
The Committee was also briefed on the status o f key tourism infrastructure projects, including 
Swadesh Darshan 2.0, the PRASHAD Scheme, and the Challenge -Based Destination 
Development initiative, which collectively aimed to improve destination -specific tourism 
infrastructure. However, concerns were raised about the overlapping objectives of these schemes, 
prompting a call for greater synergy between them to enhance their effectiveness. 
6.  During the course of the deliberations, Members  raised several concerns and sought 
clarifications on the following issues: 
 Members expressed serious concerns over persistent underutilisation of allocated funds , 
with some projects seeing only 20% of the sanctioned budget spent.  
 Members sought an impact assessment study  on past investments  and questioned the 
reasons be hind the frequent downward revision of budgets  and whether the Treasury 
Single Account (TSA) system was causing financial delays. 
 Members also expressed dissatisfaction over persistent precedural delays  in finalising 
projects under Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and PRASHAD. 
 Members highlighted poor upkeep of government -built tourism infrastructure , with 
abandoned or underutilised tourism facilities  in several states  There were also calls for 
prioritising maintenance of existing sites over developing new destinations. 
 Members sought data on the impact of promotional campaigns , questioning whether they 
translated into higher foreign tourist arrivals.  
 Concerns were also raised over exorbitant hotel prices  discouraging tourists and 
suggested better regulation of accommodation costs.  
 Members also called for a structured feedback mechanism to improve tourist experiences 
and service quality. 
 Members inquired about inter-ministerial coordination with the Ministries of Railways 
and Civil Aviation to improve connectivity to remote destinations.  
 Concerns were also raised over the lack of private sector participation in tourism 
infrastructure and asked the Ministry to identify investment barriers and enhance public -
private partnerships. 
 Members raised concerns over the duplication of efforts between Swadesh Darshan and 
PRASHAD schemes, urging greater synergy and fund optimisation. 
 There were concerns over the slow progress in developing tourism circuits with 
integrated transport linkages, affecting the overall tourist experience. 
 Members also raised queries on eco-tourism policies, questioning what measures were in 
place to ensure sustainability while expanding tourism footprints. 
 
 
 

77 
 
7.  To address these concerns effectively, the Committee made the following actionable 
recommendations: 
 Implementation of  quarterly reviews and a real -time tracking system to ensure timely 
expenditure. 
 Reducing procedural delays and finalization of scheme guidelines promptly. 
 Prioritising existing tourism sites  by allocating more funds for the upkeep and 
maintenance of existing tourism sites instead of launching new destinations. 
 Encouraging public-private partnerships for tourism infrastructure and maintenance. 
 Improveming global marketing efforts and streamline visa policies to attract more foreign 
tourists. 
 Improving the last-mile connectivity by coordinating with the Ministries of Railways and 
Civil Aviation, so as to ensure seamless travel to key destinations. 
 Establishing a struct ured feedback mechanism for tourists, regulate accommodation 
pricing, and strengthen safety measures such as deploying dedicated tourist police in 
high-footfall areas. 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
 
8.   The Chairman expressed appreciation for the Ministry’s efforts in promoting the tourism 
sector which is a real generator of income and employment besides contributing to the nation’s 
GDP growth.  He directed the Ministry that any that any unanswered queries or requests for 
additional information be addressed in writing and submitted to the Secretariat within one week.

1.0 Purpose of the Committee's Report. 
1.1 Examination of the Civil Aviation Safety Environment Amidst Rapid Growth 
1.1.1 India’s civil aviation sector has, over the last two decades, undergone a period of unprecedented expansion and 
transformation, firmly establishing itself as the third -largest domestic aviation market in the world. This remarkable growth 
trajectory, while a testament to the nation's economic dynamism, carries with it a profound and non -negotiable responsibility 
to ensure that safety remains the paramount priority in every facet of aviation operations. The Ministry of Civil Aviation, 
supported by its attache d and autonomous organisations —including the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), the 
Airports Authority of India (AAI), the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), and the Aircraft Accident Investigation 
Bureau (AAIB)—has endeavoured to maintai n a robust safety oversight framework in consonance with the international 
standards and recommended practices prescribed by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). 
1.1.2  However, the very success of the sector has introduced a fresh challen ge that defines the current safety landscape. 
The rapid induction of aircraft into the fleet of airline operators , a surge in passenger traffic, and the proliferation of 
aerodromes under regional connectivity initiatives such as the UDAN scheme have create d new and complex challenges. 
These pressures test the limits of the existing regulatory and operational infrastructure, raising critical questions about t he 
adequacy of technical manpower, the presence of infrastructural constraints at Tier -II and Tier-III airports, the maturity and 
implementation of safety management systems, and the capacity of regulatory surveillance mechanisms to keep pace with 
the industry they oversee. The UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) scheme, a Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS), wa s 
launched by the Government of India in October 2016. Implemented by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, its primary objective 
was to democratize air travel, which was historically perceived as accessible only to a privileged few. The scheme has been 
seminal in transforming India’s regional connectivity landscape by improving flight operations and optimizing the use of 
unserved and underserved airports across the country. The policy's success in activating these smaller regional airports is, 
however, directly linked to the emergence of new safety challenges. These newly operational aerodromes often lack the 
robust infrastructure, experienced technical manpower, and advanced emergency response capabilities characteristic of 
major metropolitan hubs. Consequently,  the laudable policy goal of rapid expansion is creating a significant and growing 
stress test on a safety framework that has not been scaled at a commensurate pace. 
1.1.3 It is against this backdrop of dynamic growth and escalating complexity that the Com mittee considered it both 
timely and imperative to undertake a comprehensive review of the overall safety environment within the civil aviation 
sector. This examination was conceived not merely to scrutinise the current regulatory architecture and its effi cacy, but to 
conduct a holistic assessment of the adequacy of measures being adopted by all stakeholders. The ultimate goal is to ensure 
the safe and secure carriage of passengers and cargo within an aviation ecosystem that continues to expand at a formida ble 
rate, making certain that the foundations of safety are strong enough to support the industry's future growth. 
1.2 Objectives and Scope of the Comprehensive Review 
1.2.1 The Committee’s examination of this critical subject has been guided by a clear an d comprehensive set of 
objectives, designed to probe the systemic health of India’s aviation safety regime. The primary objectives of this review 
were as follows: 
i. To review the overall state of civil aviation safety in India, placing it in the context of r apid growth in fleet, traffic, 
and operational complexity, with particular attention to the nation's compliance with ICAO Standards and 
Recommended Practices (SARPs). 
ii. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) in disc harging its core mandate 
of safety oversight, certification, surveillance, and enforcement, including a thorough review of its financial, 
technical, and human resource capacities. 

11 
iii. To examine the Airports Authority of India’s (AAI) dual mandate of enhancing  air connectivity across the country 
while simultaneously ensuring the safety and efficiency of flight operations within Indian airspace. 
iv. To assess the implementation of Safety Management Systems (SMS) and adherence to the State Safety Programme 
(SSP) by airlines, aerodrome operators, Air Navigation Service Providers, and other key service providers. 
v. To evaluate the operational preparedness of airports nationwide, with a focus on critical areas such as runway 
safety, air traffic management infrastructure, and emergency response mechanisms. 
vi. To analyse the findings of recent safety audits, inspections, and accident investigations to ascertain the extent to 
which their recommendations have been effectively implemented. 
vii. To benchmark India’s regulatory framework and prevailing safety culture against those of leading global aviation 
regulators, such as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) of the United States and the European Union 
Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), to identify global best practices that may be adopted. 
1.2.2 To achieve these objectives, the Committee pursued a rigorous, evidence -based methodology. This involved 
convening a formal sitting on 9 July 2025, where detailed presentations were heard from the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the 
DGCA, the AAI, and a cross-section of industry stakeholders including airlines and airport operators. This oral evidence was 
supplemented by an in-depth review of written submissions, statutory instruments, and international assessments, such as the 
ICAO Universal Safet y Oversight Audit Programme (USOAP) and the FAA’s International Aviation Safety Assessment 
(IASA) findings. A comparative analysis of the structures and practices of leading international regulators further enriched 
the Committee's perspective, informing a  nuanced and comprehensive assessment of India's safety framework is placed at 
Annexure I. 
2.0 Background of Civil Aviation Safety in India. 
2.1 Sector Expansion and Emerging Challenges. 
2.1.1 The growth of India's civil aviation sector has been nothing sh ort of remarkable, with passenger traffic soaring to 
239.4 million in the 2024 –25 period, cementing the nation's status as a global aviation powerhouse. This expansion, 
however, is not merely a story of numbers; it has fundamentally altered the operational  landscape, introducing new and 
multifaceted challenges that demand proactive and sophisticated safety management. The rapid increase in fleet size and the 
extension of air services to smaller Tier -II and Tier -III cities have placed immense strain on the e ntire ecosystem. Key 
challenges that have emerged include ensuring an adequate supply of qualified technical manpower to regulate and operate 
the expanding fleet, addressing significant infrastructural and operational constraints at newly activated regiona l airports, 
and ensuring the consistent and effective implementation of modern Safety Management Systems across a diverse range of 
operators and service providers. 
2.2  Statutory and Regulatory Framework Evolution. 
2.2.1 The legal foundation of India’s civil aviation safety regime has recently undergone a significant and necessary 
modernization. The legacy Aircraft Act of 1934 and its associated rules have been replaced by the Bharatiya Vayuyan 
Adhiniyam, 2024. This landma rk enactment serves to consolidate and update the legal framework governing civil aviation, 
aligning it with contemporary international standards and best practices. Crucially, the new Adhiniyam is designed not only 
to address current realities but also to  be forward-looking, providing enabling powers to accommodate future technological 
developments such as unmanned aerial systems (UAS), remotely piloted aircraft, and emerging navigation technologies. 
This new Act, in conjunction with the comprehensive body  of subordinate legislation and the detailed Civil Aviation 
Requirements (CARs) issued by the DGCA, constitutes the overarching statutory mandate for all aspects of safety oversight, 
including certification, licensing, surveillance, and enforcement.  
2.3  Organisational Structure for Safety Oversight. 
2.3.1 The architecture for aviation safety oversight in India is a multi -tiered structure, with distinct roles and 
responsibilities assigned to several key organisations  to ensure a system of checks and balances. At the apex is the Ministry 
of Civil Aviation, which formulates national policy and exercises overall supervision of the sector. The primary operational 

12 
regulator is the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGC A), which is responsible for the technical aspects of safety, 
including airworthiness standards, flight operations, and the licensing and certification of all personnel, aircraft, and 
operators. The DGCA’s Surveillance and Enforcement Division (SED) overse es safety aspects including air traffic control 
(ATC), communication, navigation, surveillance systems, and pre -flight medical evaluations, monitoring ground activities 
and aircraft movements for regulatory compliance and identifying areas for improvement.  This role is complemented by the 
Airports Authority of India (AAI), which manages the bulk of the nation's airports and provides critical air navigation 
services. Security, an element inextricably linked to safety, is overseen by the Bureau of Civil Aviat ion Security (BCAS). 
Finally, in the event of an accident or serious incident, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) conducts 
independent investigations to determine probable cause and issue systemic safety recommendations to prevent recurrence.  
2.4  International Safety Standing and Audit Performance. 
2.4.1 India's commitment to maintaining a high standard of aviation safety is reflected in its performance in key 
international audits. As a contracting State to the Chicago Convention, India is obligated to establish and maintain safety 
oversight systems that align with the Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) set forth by the International Civil 
Aviation Organisation (ICAO). In the most recent ICAO Universal Safety Oversight Audit Program me (USOAP), India 
achieved an Effective Implementation score of 85.65%, a commendable figure that exceeds the global average and signifies 
a robust regulatory framework on paper. 
2.4.2 Furthermore, India has successfully retained its Category 1 status unde r the International Aviation Safety 
Assessment (IASA) program of the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). This status is a critical enabler for Indian 
air carriers, permitting them to operate and expand their services to the United States without re striction and serving as a 
global benchmark of regulatory credibility. 
2.4.3 However, a central theme emerging from the Committee's review is the paradox that exists between these high -
level international validations and the evidence of significant systemi c weaknesses on the ground. While the high audit 
scores suggest that India's documented regulatory framework is well -aligned with international standards, the subsequent 
sections of this report detail profound challenges in implementation and capacity. Issues such as critical staff shortages, a 
large backlog of unresolved safety findings, and the recurrence of specific operational risks point to a dangerous gap 
between de jure  compliance and de facto safety reality. The high scores, while laudable, may refl ect past efforts and the 
strength of the documented system, but the internal data on deficiencies and resource constraints serves as a more potent 
leading indicator of future risk. This gap suggests that the system's resilience under the immense pressure o f rapid growth 
may be more fragile than the audit scores alone would indicate. 
2.5  Establishment of Safety Management and Reporting Systems. 
2.5.1 To manage safety in a proactive and data -driven manner, India has established a framework rooted in modern 
safety management principles. The cornerstone of this approach is the State Safety Programme (SSP), first instituted in 2010 
and comprehensively revised in 2021 to align with ICAO Annex 19. The SSP provides a structured methodology for the 
systematic identification, analysis, and mitigation of operational safety risks. It requires the establishment and maintenance 
of eight critical elements of a safety oversight system, covering everything from legislative provisions to the resolution of  
safety concerns.Flowing from the SSP is the National Aviation Safety Plan (NASP) for 2024 –2028. The NASP serves as the 
practical and time -bound roadmap for achieving the country's safety objectives. It sets out specific goals, timelines, and 
measurable Safety Performance Indi cators (SPIs) against which the health of the aviation system can be monitored. Key 
risks identified for monitoring under the NASP include mid -air collisions, controlled flight into terrain, runway excursions, 
and wildlife strikes, among others.  
2.5.2 This safety management framework is supported by a two -pronged reporting mechanism designed to capture 
critical safety data. The Mandatory Safety Reporting System (MSRS) requires operators to report any specified occurrence, 
such as a runway incursion or comp onent failure, to the DGCA within a stipulated timeframe. To supplement this, the 
Voluntary Safety Reporting System (VSRS), established as per Rule 29F of Aircraft Rules, 1937, provides a confidential and 
non-punitive channel for individuals to report safe ty concerns without fear of reprisal. All reported occurrences are 
scrutinised by an Occurrence Review Board (ORB), which convenes within 72 hours of a major incident to determine the 
appropriate investigative and follow-up actions, ensuring that safety data is translated into preventive measures. 
3.0  Key Areas for Systemic Improvement. 

13 
3.1  Enhancing Regulatory Autonomy and Capacity. 
3.1.1  Background: Critical technical staff shortages in the DGCA. 
3.1.1.1 The Directorate General of Civil Aviation, the nation's primary aviation safety regulator, is currently grappling 
with a profound and persistent shortage of technical and regulatory personnel. The data presented to the Committee reveals a 
stark reality: out of a total sanctioned strength of 1,063 posts , only 553 are currently filled. This represents a staggering 
shortfall of nearly 50% of the required manpower. This deficit is not a mere administrative statistic; it is a critical 
vulnerability that exists at the very heart of India's safety oversight sy stem, occurring precisely at a time when the sector's 
unprecedented growth demands more, not less, regulatory vigilance and capacity. While the Ministry has expressed an 
intention to increase the staffing level to approximately 850 within the next six mont hs, the current gap remains a matter of 
grave concern. 
3.1.2  History: Unimplemented recommendations from past expert committees. 
3.1.2.1 The critical need to empower the DGCA with greater autonomy is not a new discovery. For nearly two decades, 
this issue has been studied and highlighted by a series of high -level expert bodies. The Naresh Chandra Committee (2003), 
the Kaur Committee (2006), and, this  Committee in its 204th Report on the Creation of Civil Aviation of Authority of India 
Bill in the year 201 4 arrived at the same unanimous and unequivocal conclusion: to ensure the safety and efficiency of 
India’s aviation oversight, the DGCA must be granted statutory and administrative autonomy, with full control over its 
recruitment and administrative functio ns. The fact that these well -reasoned recommendations, repeatedly acknowledged by 
the Ministry, remain largely unimplemented points to a long -standing and systemic inertia in undertaking fundamental 
regulatory reform. 
3.1.3  Analysis: Ineffective recruitment via UPSC and deputation. 
3.1.3.1 The root of the DGCA's staffing crisis lies in a recruitment model that is not matching for a modern, specialized 
technical regulator. A significant number of vacant posts are pending recruitment through the Union Public  Service 
Commission (UPSC). The Ministry itself described this process as "slow and inflexible," resulting in unacceptable delays in 
filling critical regulatory positions that require niche expertise.  
3.1.3.2 The alternative channel, recruiting personnel on deputation, has proven equally ineffective, particularly for 
sourcing talent from the Indian Air Force. Experienced Air Force officers are unwilling to join the DGCA on deputation 
because doing so entails a significant loss of service benefits and allow ances, rendering the proposition financially 
unattractive. Consequently, posts reserved for this vital stream of expertise remain chronically unfilled. 
3.1.3.3 This leaves the DGCA in an unsustainable position. It currently lacks the independent authority to recruit its own 
personnel, to determine service conditions tailored to the specialized nature of the aviation sector, or to offer competitive , 
market-based remuneration. Unlike its international counterparts, the DGCA remains entirely dependent on  gove rnment 
allocations and procedural controls, making it impossible to attract and retain the highly skilled professionals —experienced 
pilots, airworthiness inspectors, and flight operations specialists —who are essential for conducting credible surveillance o f 
the private aviation industry. The Ministry on a specific query on the issue has submitted that there is no proposal under 
consideration for undertaking direct recruitment by DGCA. 
3.1.4  Interpretation: Lack of autonomy hinders the regulator's ability to attract talent and enforce compliance. 
3.1.4.1 The evidence leads to a conclusion that the DGCA, in its current form, is not in a position to discharge its duties 
for which it was established. It is tasked with overseeing a hyper -dynamic, technologically advanced, and rapidly expanding 
private industry, yet it is shackled by a slow -moving service recruitment structure followed by DGCA. Effective regulation 
demands that the regulator possesses expertise that is, at a minimum, on par with the industry it ov ersees. The private 
aviation sector offers highly competitive salaries and career paths for experienced professionals. The DGCA's current 
framework simply cannot compete with these market realities. 
3.1.4.2 This disparity creates a critical "competency gap ," where the regulator lacks both the quantity and, potentially, the 
requisite experience level of personnel needed to conduct rigorous and effective oversight. The staffing crisis is therefore not 
merely an administrative problem; it is an existential thr eat to the integrity of India's aviation safety system. This 
foundational weakness is a direct root cause of many of the other systemic issues detailed later in this report, including th e 

14 
alarming backlog in closing surveillance findings and a potential in ability to rigorously audit the influx of new aircraft, the 
commissioning of new airports, and the operations of new airlines. The lack of administrative and financial autonomy is the 
single greatest impediment to the DGCA's ability to fulfill its statutory mandate effectively. 
3.1.4.3 This critical deficit necessitates not only the ability to attract talent through competitive remuneration, but also a 
strategic national effort to cultivate a dedicated pipeline of regulatory professionals. Emphasizing domes tic manpower skill 
development within the safety network means proactively training and nurturing specialists in aviation law, airworthiness, 
flight operations, and surveillance methodologies from within the country to serve in critical public sector roles , ensuring 
that the regulator's expertise remains on par with the rapidly evolving industry it oversees 
3.1.5  Recommendations: A time-bound plan to grant the DGCA full administrative and financial autonomy. 
3.1.5.1 The Committee expresses its deep concern  over this persistent and critical issue. It is the considered view of the 
Committee that incremental solutions are no longer sufficient. A fundamental structural reform is urgently required. 
3.1.5.2 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry o f Civil Aviation develop a clear and time -bound plan to 
strengthen the human resource capacity of the DGCA. This plan must include the following key actions: 
i. Grant Full Autonomy: Immediately act upon the long -pending and unanimous recommendations of the Na resh 
Chandra and this Committee’s earlier recommendations contained in its 204 report on the Civil Aviation Authority 
of India Bill   to grant the DGCA full statutory, administrative, and financial autonomy.  The committee 
recommends that matters on which the government could override the authority of the proposed regulator/ 
regulatory body be clearly delineated in the rules and regulations framed subsequently 
ii. Establish a Specialized Recruitment Mechanism: Decouple DGCA recruitment from the framework of the  UPSC. 
A new, specialized recruitment body or mechanism must be established, with the flexibility to respond swiftly to 
the dynamic needs of the aviation sector. This mechanism should also explore dedicated training programmes and 
academies for regulatory professionals within India, potentially offering scholarships or assured placements to 
attract promising engineering, legal, and operational graduates directly into the DGCA's workforce, thereby 
building a sustainable domestic talent pool for the safety oversight function. 
iii. The Committee observed that the present system of recruitment to the Directorate General of Civil Aviation has 
scope for refinement in order to strengthen the organisation with enhanced professional and technical expertise. It 
is of the c onsidered view that the Ministry of Civil Aviation may explore the creation of a dedicated specialist 
cadre, drawing upon a Group ‘A’ service exclusively for the civil aviation sector. Such an initiative would, in the 
Committee’s assessment, help ensure th e sustained availability of officers with domain knowledge and long -term 
commitment to the sector, thereby augmenting the regulator’s capacity to effectively meet the evolving challenges 
of civil aviation oversight. Further, the Committee suggests a review  of existing remuneration structures and the 
introduction of a Civil Aviation Technical Allowance (CATA), in line with the National Civil Aviation Policy,
