6.8.1 Observation 41 — ATF Inclusion under GST: Quantified Advocacy 
The Committee observed that the Ministry's advocacy for inclusion of ATF under GST has been 
insufficient. ATF constitutes 30 -40 per cent of airline operating costs in India, compared to 
significantly lower proportions in competing jurisd ictions, directly inflating airfares and constraining 
route viability on short-haul and regional routes. 
6.8.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare and present to the 
GST Council a comprehensive quantified impact analysis demo nstrating the effect of ATF inclusion 
under GST on airline operating costs, ticket prices, route viability, and traffic growth, drawing on the 
experience of the 21 States that have already reduced VAT. 
6.8.2.1 The Committee further recommends that the Mini stry consider instituting a structured and 
transparent ATF pricing framework, including publishing a comparative Fuel Price Index and a 
regular comparison of fuel prices across States, along with incentives for States to support lower ATF 
costs. 
6.8.3 Observation 42 — International Hub Strategy 
The Committee observed that despite India's strategic geographic location and population of 1.4 
billion, the country lacks a major international aviation hub. During oral evidence, the Committee 
drew comparisons with Dubai and Sharjah, which handle 30 -40 million international passengers with 
minimal local populations. 

24 
 
6.8.4 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a formal 
International Hub Development Strategy, requiring coordinated action o n airport infrastructure, slot 
allocation, bilateral air service agreements, transit visa policy, ground handling standards, and airline 
scheduling. The Ministry should identify two to three candidate airports and prepare an integrated 
action plan. 
6.8.4.1 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry explore building partnerships with 
established international hubs through coordinated flight schedules and smoother transit facilities to 
ensure seamless coordination between Indian carriers and global ne tworks, while Indian airports 
gradually develop as transit hubs. Further, identification of select airports as national hubs with 
focused policy support, including tax measures and multiple bilateral alignments, would strengthen 
India’s position in international aviation. 
6.8.5 Observation 43 — General Aviation Development Policy 
The Committee observed that general aviation has never developed in India despite 80 years of 
independence. This concern was raised during oral evidence, comparing India with the U nited States, 
which has approximately 40,000 airports including 20,000 private airports. 
6.8.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry formulate a comprehensive 
General Aviation Development Policy addressing regulatory simplification, sm all airport 
development, airspace access, and creation of an enabling environment for private aviation. The 
absence of general aviation infrastructure constrains not only recreational and business flying but also 
pilot training capacity and the aviation ecosystem more broadly. 
6.8.6.1 The Committee further recommends the introduction of a National Open Skies  for General 
Aviation framework to provide a single -window, pan -India clearance across airstrips, along with 
mandatory baseline safety standards, periodic audits, and pilot training norms to complement ease of 
operations with robust safety oversight. 
6.9 Cybersecurity, Data Governance and Pilot Training Access 
6.9.1 Observation 44 — Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment 
The Committee observed that the expanding digital attack surface created by eGCA, DigiYatra, 
Digital Sky, EPL, ATM infrastructure, and airline systems has not been subjected to a systematic 
maturity assessment. 
6.9.2 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry direct DGCA to commission 
a comprehensive Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment of all constituent organisations and major 
regulated entities. The assessment should establish baseline maturity scores with improvement targets 
and be completed within one year. 
6.9.2.1 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry consider instituting a dedicated Aviation 
Cyber Security Operatio ns Centre (A -CSOC) with sector -wide coverage, integrating threat 
intelligence sharing, real-time network monitoring, supported by periodic red-teaming exercises. 
6.9.3 Observation 45 — FTO Geographic Distribution and Affordability 
The Committee observed severe geographic concentration in pilot training infrastructure: Bihar (130 
million population) has only one flying club, Uttar Pradesh (240 million population) has five, and 
entire states in the North East have zero FTOs. The cost of pilot training at Rs. 35 -50 lakh makes the 
profession inaccessible to the vast majority. 

25 
 
6.9.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a plan for equitable 
geographic distribution of FTOs, explore interest subvention schemes, scholarship programmes 
funded through a civil aviation development cess, expansion of public -sector FTO capacity through 
IGRUA, and partnerships with international training providers to bring down costs and improve 
access. 
6.9.4.1 The Committee further rec ommends that the Ministry explore the feasibility of establishing 
Flight Training Organisations in underserved regions, drawing on the United States’ widely 
distributed and airport-linked pilot training ecosystem, to further democratise access to pilot tra ining. 
Additionally, the Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a periodic audit of pilot training 
programmes across countrywide FTOs covering parameters such as training quality, cost of training, 
and instructor quality, among other critical parameters. 
6.10 Infrastructure Quality, Privacy and Safety Accountability 
6.10.1 Observation 46 — Noida International Airport: Timeline Accountability 
The Committee observed that security clearance issues including BCAS compliance requirements and 
an incompl ete perimeter wall (7 of 14.5 km) have delayed the Noida International Airport. The 
opacity of communication on the status of this nationally significant project was a specific concern 
during oral evidence. 
6.10.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends t hat the Ministry provide a detailed status 
report on the Noida International Airport to the Committee within 90 days, including current BCAS 
compliance status, perimeter wall completion, revised timeline, and measures to prevent recurrence of 
such delays. 
6.10.3 Observation 47 — Airport Quality Assurance and Defect Liability 
The Committee observed with concern the reports of damaged fixtures within three months of the 
inauguration of the Patna airport terminal despite an investment of Rs. 1,400 crore over e ight years. 
The degradation of publicly funded infrastructure within weeks of commissioning is unacceptable. 
6.10.4 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a formal defect 
liability and quality assurance framework for newly con structed airport terminals, review the defect 
liability period, retention money provisions, and third -party quality audit mechanisms in AAI's 
standard contract conditions. 
6.10.5 Observation 48 — DigiYatra Data Privacy and Biometric Governance 
The Committee observed that over 2 crore citizens have enrolled in DigiYatra and that the system 
processes sensitive biometric data at 30 airports. No independent audit report on data privacy and 
security has been placed before the Committee. 
6.10.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission an independent 
data privacy and security assessment of the DigiYatra system, covering consent architecture, 
biometric data storage and retention policies, data breach vulnerability, compliance with applic able 
data protection legislation, and governance of the DigiYatra Foundation. 
6.10.7 Observation 49 — Consolidated Annual Aviation Safety Report 

26 
 
The Committee observed that the current fragmented reporting across DGCA, AAIB, and BCAS does 
not provide Parli ament or the public with a single authoritative assessment of the state of aviation 
safety in India. 
6.10.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry direct DGCA to publish an 
annual Consolidated Aviation Safety Report, on the lines of the EASA Annual Safety Review, 
providing a comprehensive picture including accident and incident statistics, enforcement actio ns, 
surveillance outcomes, fleet airworthiness data, pilot licensing statistics, and safety improvement 
recommendations. 
6.10.9 Observation 50 — Performance Audit of Air India Post-Privatisation Safety Compliance 
The Committee observe that Air India received nine show-cause notices in six months preceding July 
2025, approximately 100 safety lapses were flagged in a single DGCA audit, 137 of 166 inspected 
aircraft showed recurring technical defects, and a penalty was imposed for operating flights without a 
valid Airworthiness Review Certificate. These findings occurred in the context of India's deadliest 
aviation disaster in recent decades. 
6.10.10 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry request the Comptroller 
and Auditor General to conduc t a performance audit of Air India's post -privatisation safety 
compliance and regulatory adherence, covering the period from the Tata Group's acquisition in 
January 2022 to the present. The severity and recurrence of safety findings warrant independent 
examination by the supreme audit institution. 
6.11 Geopolitical Resilience and Inter-ministerial Coordination 
6.11.1 Observation 51 — Impact of War in Gulf on India’s Civil Aviation 
The Committee noted with concern the closure and restriction of airspace across several countries in 
West Asia, beginning 28 February 2026, arising from the escalating Iran –Israel–United States 
conflict, which has posed significant and multi-dimensional challenges to India’s civil aviation sector. 
As roughly half of India’s int ernational passenger traffic transits through Gulf hubs such as Dubai, 
Doha and Abu Dhabi, the disruption led to cancellation of over 2,600 flights by Indian carriers within 
the first week, with 410 flights cancelled on 28 February and 444 on 1 March alone , stranding an 
estimated 60,000 passengers on the first day. Airspace closures by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, 
the UAE and Israel effectively shut down the primary air corridor linking Asia, Europe and Africa. 
Airlines were forced to reroute westbou nd flights via the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean airspace, 
adding 2 to 4 hours of flight time and substantially increasing fuel consumption. Block times on the 
Dubai–Delhi sector rose from 3 hours 30 minutes to nearly 6 hours. The Committee appreciated th e 
Government’s swift and decisive evacuation response: over 2,20,000 Indian nationals were facilitated 
to return from Gulf countries between 1 and 16 March 2026, including 32,107 on Indian carriers in 
the first week alone, with the Ministry of External Aff airs establishing a dedicated Special Control 
Room, 24/7 Embassy helplines, and coordinating land border crossings from Iran into Armenia and 
Azerbaijan. The Committee further observed that the disruption has had cascading consequences 
across three critical dimensions. First, on international route viability: carriers have been compelled to 
suspend, curtail or reroute services, with Air India alone suspending 50 westbound flights on 1 March, 
and Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad temporarily halting all ope rations. Second, on Air Turbine 
Fuel supply and pricing: global jet fuel prices surged by 58.4 per cent to USD 157.41 per barrel in the 
week ending 6 March 2026 (IATA/S&P Global Platts), crude oil briefly touched USD 119.50 per 
barrel on 9 March, and ATF i n India was revised upward by Rs. 5,215 per kilolitre effective 1 March 
2026 to Rs. 96,638 per kilolitre, prompting Air India, IndiGo and Akasa Air to impose fuel surcharges 
ranging from Rs. 199 to Rs. 2,300 per sector. Third, on domestic flight frequency:  the redeployment 

27 
 
of aircraft and crew for longer international routings, combined with elevated fuel costs, has reduced 
the fleet and crew available for domestic operations, with the Civil Aviation Minister acknowledging 
that the ATF price impact would be  felt from April 2026 and that the matter requires a multi -
departmental exercise involving the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Ministry of External Affairs, and 
the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. 
6.11.2 The Committee observed with particular concer n that the rapid escalation in international 
crude oil prices arising from the West Asia crisis has placed the Indian airline industry under acute 
financial stress. With ATF priced on the basis of international crude benchmarks and constituting 35 
to 40 per cent of airline operating costs, the burden on domestic carriers has become severe. Airlines 
face a stark choice between incurring unsustainable losses or grounding capacity, both of which 
outcomes are against the larger public interest of maintaining ai r connectivity across the country. The 
Committee noted that between 2022 and 2024, the Government had instituted a mechanism capping 
the floor and ceiling of ATF pricing for domestic airlines, which provided a measure of stability 
during a period of global  price volatility. The Committee is of the considered view that the present 
crisis, which is more severe in its scale and duration than earlier episodes, warrants the revival of a 
similar ATF pricing stabilisation arrangement in the public interest. The Co mmittee accordingly 
recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas jointly 
and urgently examine the feasibility of reinstating a structured ATF pricing band for domestic airline 
operations for the duration of t he crisis, calibrated to protect both airline viability and passenger 
affordability, while ensuring that Oil Marketing Companies are not subjected to uncompensated 
under-recoveries. 
6.11.3 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation, building on 
the Government’s demonstrated and commendable crisis response capability including the evacuation 
of over 2,20,000 nationals, develop a comprehensive inter -ministerial Aviation Resilience and 
Diversification Framework (ARDF) in coord ination with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, 
the Ministry of External Affairs, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Airports Authority of India, and 
the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, structured on three time-bound pillars: 
(a) Accelerate p oint-to-point long -haul services: Incentivise Indian carriers to launch and expand 
direct wide -body services from emerging and secondary hubs (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, 
Kolkata, Pune) to Europe and North America within 12 months, progressively reducin g dependence 
on Gulf transit. Fast-track slot allocation, wet-lease approvals, and bilateral air service agreements on 
under-used routes, in close coordination with the Ministry of External Affairs. The Committee notes 
that Turkish Airlines continued operations via Istanbul and European carriers (Air France, Lufthansa, 
British Airways) maintained US–India connectivity by avoiding Gulf airspace entirely, demonstrating 
the viability of non-Gulf routing. 
(b) Identify and secure alternative transit hubs: Conclu de overflight and traffic -right arrangements 
with non -Gulf nodes (Istanbul, Athens, Frankfurt in Europe; Nairobi in Africa; and Singapore in 
South-East Asia) to provide contingency connectivity when Gulf hubs are compromised. Leverage 
existing air -service agreements and, where needed, negotiate temporary contingency clauses under 
ICAO Annex 9. The Committee notes that the Government has already identified ‘safe airports’ 
including Muscat, Fujairah, Ras al Khaimah, Jeddah, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi for consolidat ion and 
evacuation, a model that should be institutionalised. 
(c) Deploy pre-defined contingency routing protocols and inter-ministerial coordination: Mandate that 
every scheduled international operator file three alternate routings (northern corridor via Central Asia, 
southern corridor via the Indian Ocean, and Pacific-side corridor via South-East Asia) with associated 
fuel-stop plans. Establish a permanent 24/7 Aviation Crisis Cell under DGCA, modelled on the 
successful coordination demonstrated during th e current crisis, to issue real -time NOTAM synthesis, 
coordinate evacuations, and activate pre -approved reroutes within two hours of airspace closure. In 

28 
 
parallel, the Ministry should coordinate with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to ensure 
contingency ATF supply arrangements at alternate refuelling points, institute a crisis -period ATF 
pricing stabilisation mechanism, drawing on the floor -ceiling pricing band that operated successfully 
between 2022 and 2024, to moderate the impact of global crud e price surges on domestic airline 
operations (noting that ATF prices surged 58.4 per cent in a single week in March 2026 and carriers 
were compelled to impose fuel surcharges), monitor the cascading effect on domestic flight frequency 
arising from fleet a nd crew redeployment on longer international routings, and engage with the 
Ministry of Finance to explore temporary tax relief on ATF during periods of sustained geopolitical 
disruption. 
6.11.4 Expected outcome: Building on the Government’s decisive and co mmendable evacuation 
response and the demonstrated inter -ministerial coordination between the Ministry of Civil Aviation, 
the Ministry of External Affairs, and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the ARDF would 
ensure improved continuity of essentia l air connectivity during geopolitical disruptions, a calibrated 
and progressive reduction in excessive dependence on Gulf transit hubs over the medium term, stable 
ATF supply and pricing during disruption periods through institutional coordination with th e 
petroleum sector, minimised impact on domestic flight availability and airfares, and progressive 
strengthening of Indian carriers as independent long -haul operators capable of connecting India 
directly to major global destinations. 
6.12 Helicopter Safety Policy  
6.12.1 Observations 52 - Institutionalizing Helicopter Safety 
The Committee observes a systemic gap in safety oversight within the charter sector of the aviation 
industry, transitioning from a "lightly regulated adjunct" to a high -risk sector. Fat al incidents —
specifically the June 15, 2025, Aryan Aviation crash (Bell 407) and the non -fatal February 24, 2026, 
Pawan Hans sea crash -landing—expose a "pressure culture" where the consideration for commercial 
revenue and VIP schedules tends to override "N o-Go" weather decisions during the high -density 
pilgrim rush. Technical evidence points to recurring mechanical instability, including stuck collective 
controls and tail rotor malfunctions, which are lethal in high -altitude or maritime corridors when 
flying single-engine helicopters that lack power redundancy. Furthermore, the absence of localized 
Air Traffic Control (ATC) and 24 -hour weather stations, coupled with chronic Flight Duty Time 
Limitation (FDTL) violations, indicates that the current regulatory framework is inadequate in 
protecting the lives of the crews and passengers operating the 250+ registered units. 
6.12.2 Recommendation: The Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) may consider incorporating a 
dedicated Helicopter Wing within the DGCA, led by tec hnical aviation professionals, to 
institutionalize specialized maintenance audits and ex -military pilot "familiarization" training, since 
the drive to reach a destination or complete a task overrides prudent safety decisions, such as delaying 
or cancelling a flight due to adverse weather, when ex -military pilots fly civilian aircraft. A statutory 
mandate could be considered under the aegis of a high -powered committee to transition all high -risk 
pilgrimage and inter -island routes to twin -engine helicopters o nly, providing a vital safety buffer 
against mid -air technical snags. To manage operational saturation, the DGCA must fast -track the 
deployment of localized ATC systems and automated weather interlocks that prohibit takeoffs during 
"poor visibility" windows. Finally, the regulator must enforce transparency by ranking the 133 Non -
Scheduled Operators (NSOs) on safety performance, auditing ADS -B (Automatic Dependent 
Surveillance Broadcast) and CVR (Cockpit Voice Recorder) data to ensure the 12 -hour rest mandate 
is met, and fixing accountability for any flight launched with known mechanical deficiencies or under 
commercial duress. 
6.13 Aviation Safety Pertaining to VIP and Charter Flights 

29 
 
6.13.1 Observation 53 
The Committee notes with concern that incidents invo lving chartered jets ferrying VIPs point to a 
recurring pattern of operational vulnerabilities. Evidence suggests that adverse weather conditions, 
including poor visibility, have frequently been a contributing factor. The Committee is particularly 
concerned that pilots may, at times, face implicit or explicit pressure to adhere to demanding 
schedules, even when prevailing conditions fall below safe operational thresholds. 
6.13.2 The Committee further observes that the sterile cockpit rule, which prohibits non-essential 
communication during critical phases of flight, is not consistently respected during VIP charter 
operations. This introduces avoidable distraction at moments demanding absolute crew attention. 
6.13.3 The Committee also notes that frequent las t-minute schedule changes impose considerable 
strain on flight crew, compelling already fatigued personnel to extend duty hours beyond safe limits. 
This raises concerns regarding crew alertness and sound decision-making. 
6.13.4 The Committee places on reco rd its appreciation for the DGCA's firm position that no 
commercial or logistical consideration may override any safety parameter. 
6.14 Recommendations 
(a) When visibility falls below prescribed safety minima, diversion to a better -equipped airport 
must be the only acceptable course of action. The sterile cockpit rule must be strictly enforced across 
all charter and VIP operations. 
(b) Flight Duty Time Limitations must be enforced uniformly, without exception, across all 
categories of flights. Pilot trainin g must mandatorily cover weather awareness and sound decision -
making in uncontrolled environments. 
(c) The Committee further emphasises that ex -military pilots transitioning to civilian aviation 
must undergo structured familiarisation training. In civil av iation, delaying or cancelling a flight on 
safety grounds is not a failure of resolve. It is an affirmation of professional responsibility.

Introduction 
1. I, the Chairman, Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture, 
having been authorised by the Committee, have the honour  to present on its behalf this Report on the Demands 
for Grants (2026 -27) of the Ministry of Culture (Demand No. 18). The Committee was constituted in 
accordance with the Rules and Procedures governing Parliamentary Standing Committees and authorised by th e 
Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, to examine the said Demands for Grants and to present its Report to the 
House. 
2. The Committee has examined the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in view of the central importance that 
the preservation, promotion, and dis semination of India’s tangible and intangible cultural heritage occupies in 
the nation’s civilizational identity and global standing. With a Budget Estimate of Rs. 3,416.63 crore for 2026 -
27 and a Ministry -projected requirement of Rs. 5,219.97 crore, the M inistry of Culture administers a wide -
ranging portfolio encompassing the Archaeological Survey of India, national museums, libraries, akademies, 
zonal cultural centres, Buddhist and Tibetan institutions, and flagship missions including the Gyan Bharatam 
Mission and the National Mission on Cultural Mapping. 
3. The Committee undertook a structured examination of the Demands in accordance with established 
parliamentary practice. The Ministry furnished its Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No. 18, 2026 -27), and 
budgetary documentations comprising covering the Expenditure Statement, the Output Outcome Monitoring 
Framework (OOMF) for 2026 -27, head -wise financial summaries, and scheme -wise physical and financial 
targets. In addition, the Ministry submitted Writte n Replies to questions put by the Committee. The 
representatives of the Ministry were also heard in oral evidence on 24 February 2026. The Annual Report of the 
Ministry of Culture for the year 2025 -26 was also placed before the Committee and served as an i mportant 
corroborating source of performance information. 
4. The Committee’s examination encompassed five principal thematic areas: the Financial Architecture and 
Budgetary Discipline; Scheme -Wise Performance and Physical Outcomes covering the ASI, Centena ries and 
Anniversaries, Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana, Development of Museums, Development of Libraries, Gyan 
Bharatam Mission, Global Engagement, and the National Mission on Cultural Mapping; Historical Expenditure 
Trends and Savings Analysis; Cross -Cutting Governance and Equity; and Audit Compliance and 
Accountability.  
5. This Report synthesises evidence received from the Ministry, the detailed budgetary documentation, oral 
evidence tendered on 24 February 2026, and the Committee’s own analysis of multi -year financial trends. It 
places fiscal prudence, outcome accountability, and equitable regional development at the centre of its 
assessment. The Committee’s recommendations are framed in a spirit of constructive engagement and are 
intended to support the Mi nistry in strengthening the planning, execution, and monitoring of its programmes. 
The Committee expects that the Ministry will give careful and sympathetic consideration to these 
recommendations and that appropriate action taken notes will be communicated  to the Committee in a timely 
manner. 
6. The Committee places on record its sincere appreciation of the assistance rendered by the officers of the 
Rajya Sabha Secretariat in facilitating the examination of the Demands for Grants, and of the cooperation 
extended by the Ministry of Culture in providing detailed documentation, responses to the Committee’s 
questionnaire, and written submissions.

Executive Summary 
(i) The Ministry of Culture presented a Budget Estimate of Rs. 3,416.63 crore for 2026 -27 under Demand No. 
18, comprising Revenue expenditure of Rs. 3,216.63 crore and Capital expenditure of Rs. 200 crore. The 
Ministry's own projected requirement stood at Rs.  5,219.97 crore, resulting in a gap of Rs. 1,803.34 crore 
(approximately 34.55 per cent). The approved allocation represents an increase of only Rs. 55.67 crore (1.66 per 
cent) over the Budget Estimate of 2025-26.

CHAPTER I: BUDGETARY ANALYSIS 
A. Overview of Demands for Grants (2026-27) 
1.1 The Ministry of Culture is the nodal agency for formulation of national policies and programmes for 
the preservation and promotion of India’s cultural heritage. The Ministry oversees the Archaeological 
Survey of India (ASI), National Archives of India, national museums, national academies (Sahitya 
Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi), the National School of Drama, Zonal Cultural 
Centres, and 34 Autonomous Bodies, among other institutions and organisations. 
1.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that for the financial year 2026 -27, it has been allocated Rs. 
3,416.63 crore (Demand No.  18) against its projected demand of Rs. 5,219.97 crore, a shortfall of Rs. 
1,803.34 crore (approximately 34.55 per cent). The approved allocation represents an increase of only Rs. 
55.67 crore (1.66 per cent) over the Budget Estimate of 2025 -26. The allocation comprises Revenue 
expenditure of Rs. 3,216.63 crore and Capital expenditure of Rs. 200 crore. 
1.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry’s budgetary structure is institution-centric, with approximately 
87 per cent of the allocation directed towards institutions and only 13 per cent available for central sector 
schemes. The ASI accounts for Rs. 1,235.78 crore (36.17 per cent of the total allocation). 
1.4 The Committee observes that the gap of Rs. 1,803.34 crore between the Ministry’s projected 
demand and the allocation constitutes a constraint on the Ministry’s capacity to fulfil its mandate. 
Given that the Ministry has reported near 100 per  cent expenditure rates and has received 
additional funds in Revised Estimates in the current year, the Committee is of the view that the 
budgetary allocation is not commensurate with the projected demand and the expenditure 
performance demonstrated by the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministry engage 
with the Ministry of Finance to secure enhanced allocations, including through Supplementary 
Demands, and present a detailed justification note linking the additional demand to specific 
programme outcomes and deliverables. 
B. Budgetary Trends and Fund Utilisation 
1.5 The Committee notes that the Ministry has reported near 100 per cent expenditure rates in the current 
financial year and has received additional funds at the Revised Estimate stage. 
1.6 The Committee notes from the Detailed Demands for Grants that the Capital expenditure head has a 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 200 crore for 2026 -27. The actual Capital expenditure in 2025 -26 stood at Rs. 
66.84 crore (up to 19 January 2026), representing a ut ilisation rate of approximately 33.4 per cent. The 
Committee observes that this level of Capital expenditure is a matter of concern. 
1.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a detailed Capital expenditure plan for 
2026-27 with quarterly milestones and furnish quarterly progress reports to the Committee. 

2 
 
C. Ticketing Revenue 
1.8 The Committee further notes that the Ministry stated that ticketing revenue from centrally protected 
monuments amounts to approximately Rs. 365 crore annually. This rev enue goes to the Government 
exchequer and is not available to the Ministry or the ASI as departmental revenue for reinvestment in 
conservation and maintenance activities. 
1.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with the Ministry of Finance, 
earmark a portion of the ticketing revenue of Rs. 365 crore annually for reinvestment in the 
conservation, maintenance, and visitor infrastructure of centrally protected monuments. The 
Ministry may present a detailed proposal for such a ring -fenced revenue mechanism to the 
Committee within six months. 
D. Shortfall in Projected Demand 
1.10 The Committee repeatedly emphasised during the evidence that the budget is insufficient given the 
scope of the Ministry’s work. The Museums Development scheme and  the proposed new infrastructure 
scheme under the 16th Finance Commission cycle require substantially higher allocations. NITI Aayog 
has set annual targets of 8 new museums and 15 new public libraries. The Committee observed that these 
targets cannot be achieved with current funding levels. 
1.11 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a demand note for the 16th Finance 
Commission cycle, clearly linking budgetary requirements to the NITI Aayog targets for museums 
and libraries (as noted in Para 1. 10), the proposed infrastructure scheme, and the institutional 
capacity requirements of autonomous bodies and subordinate organisations. The demand note 
should include a phased expenditure plan, institutional capacity assessments, and a strategy for 
leveraging additional resources including CSR funds, the National Culture Fund, and PPP models. 
E. Alternative Revenue and Funding Sources 
1.12 The Committee observed during the evidence that Rs. 35,000 crore in CSR funds are available 
nationally, while the Mini stry’s budget is approximately Rs. 3,416.63 crore. The Committee suggested 
that the Ministry should actively tap CSR funds for museums and libraries in each district. The 
Committee notes that under Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013, protection of national heritage, art 
and culture, including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance, is already an eligible 
category for CSR expenditure. In FY 2022 -23, corporate spending on heritage, art and culture stood at 
approximately Rs. 441 crore  nationally, indicating significant headroom for enhanced engagement 
between the Ministry and the corporate sector. 
1.13 The Committee further suggested that cultural heritage should be included as an eligible category for 
Members of Parliament Local Area Development (MPLAD) fund expenditure. The Committee cited the 
example of earning Rs. 18 crore from a planetarium developed under the Smart City project. 
1.14 The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a strategy for leveraging alternative 
funding s ources, including: (a) a dedicated CSR engagement plan for museums, libraries, and 
heritage conservation, with clear guidelines for corporate participation and model project 
frameworks to facilitate adoption by eligible companies; (b) a proposal to the Min istry of Finance 

3 
 
and Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation for inclusion of cultural heritage as an 
eligible expenditure category under the MPLAD scheme; and (c) expansion of the restructured 
National Culture Fund model to attract private don ations for conservation. The Ministry may 
furnish this strategy to the Committee within six months. 
F. Grant-in-Aid Salary Reduction 
1.15 The Committee notes that the GIA Salary head has been reduced from Rs. 429 crore (BE 2025-26) to 
Rs. 352 crore (BE 202 6-27), a reduction of Rs. 77 crore (17.95 per cent). All 34 Autonomous Bodies 
under the Ministry remain entirely dependent on Government grants-in-aid for salary expenditure. 
1.16 The Committee is concerned at the reduction of Rs. 77 crore in the GIA Salar y head for 
Autonomous Bodies at a time when these bodies already face significant vacancy levels. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish to the Committee: (a) a body -wise break-up of 
the GIA Salary allocation for 2026-27, with the rationale for the reduction; (b) the current vacancy 
position in each Autonomous Body; and (c) an assessment of the impact of the reduction on the 
functioning of these bodies. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken in this 
regard. 
G. Mandatory Sub-Allocations: SCSP, TSP, and NER 
1.17 The Committee notes that the mandatory sub -allocations for 2026-27 include Rs. 49.50 crore under 
the Scheduled Caste Sub-Plan (8.3 per cent of schemeable BE), Rs. 25.65 crore under the Tribal Sub-Plan 
(4.3 per cent), an d Rs. 59.64 crore for the North -East Region (10.0 per cent), totalling Rs. 134.79 crore 
(22.6 per cent of schemeable BE). 
1.18 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a scheme -wise and State-wise break-up 
of expenditure incurred under the SCSP, TSP, and NER mandatory sub -allocations for 2024 -25 
and 2025 -26 (up to date), along with the physical outcomes achieved under each allocation. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry ensure that these earmarked funds are utilised 
for the intended beneficiary categories and not diverted to general expenditure. The Ministry may 
furnish utilisation reports within three months.

CHAPTER II: SCHEME-WISE ANALYSIS 
A. Restructured Schemes for the 16th Finance Commission Cycle 
2.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that it is restructuring from 7 existing programmes to 6 new 
schemes for the 16th Finance Commission period (2026-31): 
(a) Centenaries and Anniversaries (with infrastructure component removed). 
(b) Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana (expanded scope). 
(c) Gyan Bharatam Mission (continuation with existing 5-year allocation). 
(d) Expanded Global Engagement Scheme, now incorporating Project Mausam (for multinational 
UNESCO nominations) and Project Bharat Bharat (focus on multinational heritage inscriptions). 
(e) New Infrastructure Scheme: Development and Enhancement of Sanskrit Sampada and Heritage, 
comprising seven elements: (i) 15 excavation and heritage site development; (ii) new science 
cities and centres; (iii) new public libraries; (iv) new museu ms and enhancement of existing 
facilities; (v) protection of architectural heritage (100 -200 year old facades); (vi) creative 
economy component for artisan and artist market opportunities; and (vii) YugeYugeen Bharat 
Museum. 
(f) YugeYugeen Bharat Museum as a standalone project. 
2.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that the proposed infrastructure scheme involves a proposed 
investment of Rs. 12,000 crore and above over five years. The Centre -State cost-sharing formula was not 
specified in the documents examin ed by the Committee. If Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) 
approvals are obtained, scheme funding would increase from the current Rs. 569 crore to approximately 
Rs. 2,000 crore. 
2.3 The Committee notes that the proposed infrastructure scheme uses a centra lly-sponsored format 
requiring State participation and ownership for sustainability. The Ministry stated that it has written to all 
State Governments seeking support. 
2.4 The Committee recommends that all EFC notes for new schemes under the 16th Finance 
Commission cycle be accompanied by: (a) detailed implementation roadmaps with year -wise 
milestones; (b) institutional capacity assessments, given the current staffing shortages across the 
Ministry and its subordinate organisations; (c) State -wise absorption plans; (d) a phased scaling 
mechanism linked to demonstrated expenditure performance; and (e) a clear framework for 
recurring operational costs, specifying the Centre -State cost -sharing formula and sustainability 
provisions beyond the scheme period. The Co mmittee further recommends that the Ministry 
present the draft EFC notes to the Committee before final submission. 
2.5 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry notify a performance -linked Centre -
State cost-sharing framework for the proposed herit age infrastructure scheme at the outset, with 
funding tranches to States tied to measurable outcomes such as conservation quality indices, visitor 
footfall growth, local artisan and craftsperson employment generation, and annual site 
maintenance compliance . The experience of outcome -based funding models in comparable 
centrally-sponsored schemes suggests that tying financial flows to demonstrated results promotes 

5 
 
both accountability and long -term sustainability. The Ministry may apprise the Committee of the 
framework so devised.

CHAPTER III: ARCHAEOLOGICAL HERITAGE AND MONUMENT 
CONSERVATION 
A. Archaeological Survey of India: Overview 
3.1 The Committee notes that the ASI maintains 3,685 centrally protected monuments through 38 Circles. 
The ASI has been allocated Rs. 1,235.78 crore for 2026 -27, constituting 36.17 per cent of the Ministry’s 
total allocation. During 2025 -26, ‘Maratha Military  Landscapes of India’ was inscribed as a World 
Heritage Site, and 14 sites were added to India’s UNESCO Tentative List, bringing the total to 69. India 
now ranks 6th globally for World Heritage Sites. 
3.2 The Committee notes from the financial data that AS I conservation expenditure has maintained 
utilisation rates above 99 per cent over the period 2021 -22 to 2024 -25. In 2025 -26, the utilisation rate 
stood at 67.17 per cent (Rs. 232.52 crore against Rs. 346.15 crore, up to 21 November 2025). 
3.3 The Committee notes the sustained high utilisation rates in ASI conservation expenditure over 
2021-22 to 2024-25 and recommends that the Ministry ensure that the utilisation rate for 2025 -26 is 
brought to the level of previous years by the close of the financial year.  The Ministry may furnish 
the final utilisation figures for 2025-26 within 90 days of the close of the financial year. 
3.4 The Committee further notes that India’s growing portfolio of World Heritage Sites, now 
ranking sixth globally with 44 inscribed properties, carries with it a corresponding obligation under 
the UNESCO Operational Guidelines to maintain standards of conservation, interpretation, and 
visitor management commensurate with the Outstanding Universal Value of these sites. With the 
inscription of the Maratha Military Landscapes in 2025, India’s international visibility in the 
heritage domain has been further enhanced. The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in 
coordination with the ASI, undertake a comprehensive review of maintenance standards and visitor 
facilities at all World Heritage Sites and prepare a time -bound upgradation plan to ensure that the 
condition, interpretation infrastructure, and management of these sites are aligned with their 
global recognition. The Committee expects to be apprised of the action taken in this regard. 
B. Sites and Excavations 
3.5 The Ministry informed the Committee that the development of 15 significant archaeological sites has 
been announced, including Rakhigarhi, Dholavira, Hastinapura, Adichanallur, and Shivsagar, with visitor 
infrastructure and interpretation centres. 
3.6 The Ministry stated that the excavation process is archaeologist-driven. Under the new initiative, sites 
will be developed for visitor access, a departure from the traditional practice of closing excavated sites. 
3.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a detailed project -wise status report for 
all 15 archaeological site development projects, including physical and financial progress, timelines 
for completion, and provisions for ongoing conservation and visitor management, within 90 days. 
C. Underwater Archaeology 
3.8 The Ministry stated that underwater archaeology offers significant scope for expansion. The Ministry 
informed the Committee that it has planned 8 -10 expedition s in the coming financial year through 

9 
 
collaborations with the National Institute of Oceanography, the Indian Navy, the Indian Coast Guard, and 
international groups, including a Danish collaboration for a 17th century shipwreck off the Tamil Nadu 
coast. The Ministry stated that the division is being strengthened. 
3.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry present an action plan for underwater 
archaeology to the Committee within 90 days, including: (a) the proposed expeditions with 
timelines and budgetar y provisions; (b) the institutional strengthening plan for the underwater 
archaeology division; (c) international collaboration agreements; and (d) a strategy for display of 
findings. The Committee further recommends that all findings from underwater archa eological 
expeditions be systematically documented and made accessible through a dedicated digital 
repository, thereby preserving and disseminating the knowledge generated from these explorations 
for research and public awareness. The Committee also recomm ends that the Ministry explore 
structured collaboration with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways for logistical and 
maritime support in underwater heritage survey and recovery operations. 
D. Monument Protection and Maintenance 
3.10 The Committee raised concerns during the evidence about ASI -protected sites lacking protectors. 
The Committee noted that monuments are being used as relieving spots due to the absence of staff 
presence. The staffing implications are discussed in detail in Chapter VII. 
3.11 The Ministry informed the Committee that it denotified 18 sites during the current year after careful 
survey, while notifying 15 -16 new sites. The Ministry stated that the denotification  process is conducted 
carefully to prevent manipulation by real estate developers. 
3.12 The Committee raised the specific issue of British -era horse monuments in various parts of the 
country where the ASI’s restrictions prevent repair of a school located w ithin 100 metres of the protected 
site. 
3.13 The Ministry informed the Committee that the AMASR Act amendment has been prepared for 
Parliament. The Ministry stated that the new rules will make the 100 -metre and 200 -metre buffer zone

3.14 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry ensure expeditious passage of the AMASR

timeline not exceeding 90 days from receipt of application to final decision; (c) the Ministry

measures recommended in Chapter VII be implemented on priority for ticketed monuments. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry actively explore models of structured community

guidelines for engaging local communities, heritage volunteers, and self-help groups in the custodial 
care and routine maintenance of monuments, with appropriate training and supervision 
frameworks. The Ministry may report on each of these measures within 90 days.

culture centre. 
4.3 The Ministry informed the Committee that science museums and planetariums are largely self -
sufficient in generating revenue, but pure cultural museums require Government grants for sustenance. 
4.4 The Committee is concerned at the inadequacy of the Museums Development allocation against 
the NITI Aayog target of 8 new museums annually, as noted in Para 1.10. The Committe e 
recommends that the Ministry: (a) clarify the discrepancy between the Rs. 210 crore and Rs. 37 
crore figures stated during oral evidence and the Rs. 150 crore figure in the Detailed Demands for 
Grants; (b) secure restoration of adequate allocation throug h a Supplementary Demand if 
warranted; and (c) prepare a district -wise museum development plan, prioritising districts that 
currently lack any museum facility. 
B. YugeYugeen Bharat Museum 
4.5 The Ministry informed the Committee of the proposal to convert t he North and South Blocks into the 
YugeYugeen Bharat Museum. 
4.6 The Ministry stated that the Light and Lotus exhibition at Qila Rai Pithora, showcasing the recovered 
Pipurva relics, serves as a precursor for the quality standards to be maintained at the Y ugeYugeen Bharat 
Museum. 
4.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a detailed project plan for the 
YugeYugeen Bharat Museum, including timelines, budgetary requirements, institutional 
arrangements for curatorial and administrative management, and the strategy for sourcing 
collections. 
C. Libraries and Archives 
4.8 The Ministry informed the Committee of a major National Archives digitisation project targeting 30 
crore pages. The Ministry stated that 11 crore pages (approximately one -third) have been digitised and 
uploaded on the Abhilek portal. The Ministry stated that it plans to complete the remaining two -thirds in 
the next year. 

13 
 
4.9 The Ministry informed the Committee that it is taking the digitisation initiative to States through a 
new project with funding support. 
4.10 During the evidence, the Committee raised concerns regarding the Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Library, 
Patna, where the Director’s post has been vacant since August 2023 despite the submission of panels for 
appointment. 
4.11 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry set a defined timeline for the completion of 
the National Archives digitisation project and furnish quarterly progress reports to the Committee; 
(b) the Ministry develop Standard Operating Procedures for State archive  coordination, including 
quality standards for digitisation and conservation, to be issued as formal guidelines to all State 
Governments; (c) the Ministry fill the vacancy of Director, Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Library, within 
90 days and furnish a report on t he reasons for the delay; and (d) the underutilisation of the 
Development of Libraries scheme, as noted in Para 2.17, be addressed with urgency. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry develop a strategy for the meaningful utilisation 
of digitised archival content, ensuring that the digitisation effort translates into enhanced access for 
researchers, students, and the general public. The Ministry may explore integration of digitised 
collections with educational platforms and the National Digital Library ecosystem, in coordination 
with the Ministry of Education, to maximise the scholarly and public value of the National 
Archives’ digital holdings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

14 
 
CHAPTER V:  
REPATRIATION OF ANTIQUITIES AND INTERNATIONAL CULTURAL 
ENGAGEMENT 
A. Repatriation of Antiquities 
5.1 The Ministry informed the Committee of the recovery of the Piprahwa relics from Hong Kong after 
127 years. The Ministry stated that the relics, originally excavated in 1898, were brought to India on 30 
July, 2025 and the exhibition was inaugurated on 3 January, 2026. 
5.2 The Ministry further informed the Committee during the oral evidence that the United States has 
repatriated many objects in recent years, and the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Germany are 
expected to repatriate 8-10 more objects in the next two months. 
5.3 The Committee recommends that the Ministry: (a) prepare and publish a repatriation 
roadmap, including a prioritised international inventory of Indian antiquities in foreign collections, 
legal strategies, and bilateral engagement plans; (b) develop a self -surrender portal for voluntary 
return of heritage items; and (c) furnish to the Committee a status report on all ongoing 
repatriation cases within 90 days. The Committee notes with appreciation the rec overy of the 
Piprahwa relics. 
B. UNESCO Inscriptions and Nominations 
5.4 The Ministry informed the Committee of the following UNESCO inscriptions achieved in 2024: (a) 
Diwali inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage representative list; (b) 12 forts listed as 
World Heritage Sites under “17th to 19th century forts of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj”; (c) Lucknow 
listed under the Creative Cities Network; and (d) the Natya Shastra and Bhagavad Gita manuscripts 
inscribed in the Memory of the World register. 
5.5 The Ministry informed the Committee that nominations in progress include: (a) Chhath Mahaparv as a 
multinational nomination; (b) shadow puppetry; and (c) Valmiki Ramayana manuscript. 
5.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a five -year UNESCO nomination 
strategy, including: (a) a pipeline of at least 10 potential nominations; (b) a structured engagement 
plan with partner countries for multinational nominations; and (c) dedicated staff and budgetary 
provision for preparing nomination d ossiers. The Ministry may present this strategy within one 
year. 
C. International Conservation and Cultural Diplomacy 
5.7 The Ministry informed the Committee that the ASI undertakes international conservation work with 
Ministry of External Affairs funding in Cambodia, Myanmar, Maldives, and Mongolia. 
5.8 The Ministry informed the Committee of India’s participation in the Venice Biennale after years of 
absence, under a public-private partnership, with five emerging artists representing regional diversity. 

15 
 
5.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry in coordination with the Ministry of External 
Affairs develop a structured international cultural diplomacy framework, formalising partnerships 
with major international museums and institutions. 
D. Buddhist Heritage Initiatives 
5.10 The Ministry informed the Committee that the Government has been taking Lord Buddha’s relics to 
other countries. The Ministry stated that recent tours include Vietnam, Russia (Kalmykia province), 
Bhutan, and Sri Lanka. 
5.11 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a Buddhist Heritage Action Plan, 
integrating relic tours, monastery preservation, and Buddhist circuit development (in coordination 
with the Ministry of Tourism), with measurable targets. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

16 
 
CHAPTER VI:  
DIGITAL INITIATIVES AND AI INTEGRATION 
A. AI-Enabled Unified Search Tool 
6.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that it has approximately 60 portals with no unified search 
capability. The Ministry stated that it is engaging an agency to build an AI tool connecting all portals for 
searchability, expected to launch in the first quarter of 2026-27. 
6.2 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry ensure the AI -enabled unified search tool is 
launched within the first quarter of 2026 -27 as committed and furnish a progress report; (b) the 
tool incorporate multilingual capability in a t least 10 Indian languages and English; and (c) the 
Ministry integrate the AI tool with social media platforms for wider public engagement. 
B. Mera Gaon Mera Dharohar (National Cultural Mapping) 
6.3 The Ministry informed the Committee that the MGMD portal has received inputs from villages across 
the country, with 50-60 per cent response from some States and 4 lakh and above inputs being updated. 
6.4 The Committee noted that data is not up to date and many villages only show a name without details. 
The Committee observed that mapping 6 lakh villages requires nodal districts and States for coordination. 
6.5 The Ministry informed the Committee that the portal will be opened for crowdsourcing. 
6.6 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry establish a nodal officer or agency at the 
district level for MGMD data collection and quality assurance; (b) a minimum data standard be 
defined for each village entry; (c) the crowdsourcing module include a verification mechanism; and 
(d) the Ministry set annual targets for MGMD coverage and quality, with a progress report 
furnished every six months. The Committee further recommends that both the AI -enabled unified 
search tool and the MGMD cultural mappin g portal incorporate user feedback mechanisms and a 
structured data correction feature, enabling citizens, local researchers, and cultural practitioners to 
flag errors, suggest corrections, and contribute verified local knowledge. Such participatory quality 
assurance would enhance the reliability and comprehensiveness of the cultural databases. The 
Committee further notes the near -zero expenditure under the National Mission on Cultural 
Mapping in 2025 -26 as discussed in Para 2.19 and expects the Ministry to  ensure that the 
institutional machinery for this Mission is fully operational in 2026-27. 
 
 
 
 

17 
 
CHAPTER VII:  
MANPOWER AND STAFFING 
7.1 The Committee notes with concern that all departments within the Ministry of Culture are 
experiencing severe staffing sho rtages. The Committee noted during the evidence that ASI sites 
designated as “protected areas” have no protectors present. Inadequate staffing directly impacts 
conservation, maintenance, visitor experience, and revenue collection. 
7.2 The Committee notes f rom the CAG Report No.  3 of 2024 that the Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav 
Sangrahalaya (IGRMS), Bhopal, has a vacancy level of 30.51 per cent and that only 26 per cent of its 
objects are displayed. The Committee views this as indicative of a wider institutio nal capacity deficit 
across the Ministry’s organisations. 
7.3 During the evidence, the Committee raised the concern that they had been unable to get an 
appointment with the Ministry since April. The Ministry apologised during the evidence and committed 
to ensuring it does not recur. 
7.4 The Committee recommends that the Ministry: (a) prepare a time -bound recruitment plan for 
all vacant posts across the ASI, national academies, Zonal Cultural Centres, museums, and all 
subordinate organisations; (b) ensure th at every centrally protected monument has minimum 
designated staff for protection, maintenance, and visitor management; (c) institute a standard 
protocol for ensuring accessibility of senior Ministry officials to Members of Parliament; and (d) 
furnish a specific action plan for addressing the 30.51 per cent vacancy at the IGRMS, Bhopal, and 
for increasing the proportion of objects on display from the current 26 per cent. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

18 
 
CHAPTER VIII:  
NORTH-EASTERN REGION 
 
8.1 The Committee emphasised during the evidence that the North East Zonal Cultural Centre (NEZCC) 
should undertake tangible documentation work, rather than confining itself to event participation. The 
Committee noted that the current programme showed 6 of 9 activities as merely “par ticipating” in 
festivals elsewhere. 
8.2 The Committee notes that the North -Eastern region has oral traditions rather than manuscripts, 
requiring specialised documentation methods. 
8.3 The Ministry informed the Committee that it would provide technical supp ort for developing unique 
scripts for 26 tribes in Arunachal Pradesh, rather than using Roman letters. The Santhal community’s 
Olchiki script was cited as a model. 
8.4 The Committee notes that not a single NEZCC direction meeting has been held recently and  that 
State-level meetings have not been held for two years. 
8.5 The Committee recommends that: (a) the NEZCC be directed to shift its focus from event 
participation to substantive documentation of oral traditions, folk arts, and tribal heritage, with 
measurable annual documentation targets; (b) the Ministry pursue the development of unique 
scripts for Arunachal Pradesh tribes as a priority initiative, with a status report within one year; (c) 
the Ministry coordinate with North -Eastern State Governments to resolve the recurring cost 
impasse for non -functional cultural centres; (d) NEZCC direction meetings be resumed 
immediately, with at least two meetings per year; and (e) the Ministry develop a dedicated 
Northeast cultural heritage documentation programme w ithin the new infrastructure scheme 
under the 16th Finance Commission cycle. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

19 
 
CHAPTER IX:  
INSTITUTIONAL AND GOVERNANCE ISSUES 
 
A. State Coordination 
9.1 The Committee noted that State archaeological sites are often poorly maintained, with contractor -
driven repairs that alter the original character of structures. The Committee called for SOPs for 
intervention. The need for a formal Centre -State coordination mechanism for archives and heritage was 
also emphasised. The Committee noted that Zonal Cultural Centres typically cover 8 States but 
coordination is weak. 
9.2 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry develop and issue Standard Operating 
Procedures for conservation intervention at State -level archaeological sites; (b) a formal 
mechanism for Centre-State coordination on archives and heritage preservation be established; and 
(c) the functioning and coordination of Zonal Cultural Centres be reviewed, with findings 
presented to the Committee within 90 days. 
B. Heritage Preservation Beyond ASI Jurisdiction 
9.3 The Committee raised the issue of British -era heritage sites requiring preservation. Specific examples 
cited included: (a) 74 district Collectorat e buildings being demolished; (b) the DG post building in 
Darbhanga (150 years old); and (c) the Patna clock tower. The Committee also noted the need for 
preservation of churches and chapels in Goa and nationwide. 
9.4 The Committee raised concerns about un manned forts, including Sasaram Fort (Sher Shah Suri) in 
Bihar. 
9.5 The Committee further suggested coordination with Railways, Shipping, and Aviation ministries for 
heritage preservation of rail engines, ships, and aircraft. The Committee also raised the need for penal 
provisions for defacing cultural items. 
9.6 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry prepare an inventory of non -ASI heritage 
structures at risk, in coordination with State Governments; (b) the protection of architectural 
heritage com ponent under the proposed new infrastructure scheme specifically address 100 -200 
year-old facades and structures; (c) the Ministry coordinate with the Ministries of Defence, 
Railways, Ports, Shipping and Waterways, and Civil Aviation for preservation of he ritage assets; 
and (d) the need for penal provisions for defacing or destroying cultural property be examined and 
a legal note submitted to the Committee within one year. 
C. Audit Compliance 
9.7 The Committee notes that as of February 2026, two CAG audit p aragraphs remain outstanding: (a) 
Report No.  10 of 2022, concerning ASI monument preservation, with a revised Action Taken Note in 
process; and (b) Report No.  3 of 2024, concerning IGRMS Bhopal (30.51 per cent vacancy; 26 per cent 
objects displayed), with a final Action Taken Note in process. 

20 
 
9.8 The Committee views the non -finalisation of Action Taken Notes on outstanding CAG audit 
paragraphs as a serious matter. The Committee recommends that the Ministry finalise and submit 
the Action Taken Notes on both outstanding CAG audit paragraphs within 90 days and furnish 
copies to the Committee. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry institute a standing 
mechanism for time-bound disposal of CAG audit paragraphs. 
D. Branding and Public Engagement 
9.9 The Committee suggested developing “Incredible Culture” as a keyword branding initiative and that 
all Ministry presentations should be drafted as educational courses for curricula. The Committee also 
noted the formation of 60 international Parliamentary frie ndship groups and recommended formal 
Ministry engagement. 
9.10 The Committee recommends that the Ministry: (a) develop a cultural branding strategy, 
including the feasibility of an “Incredible Culture” initiative, and present it to the Committee 
within 90 days; (b) coordinate with the Ministry of Education for integration of cultural heritage 
content into school curricula; and (c) engage with the parliamentary friendship groups to provide 
structured cultural content for international engagement. 
E. Members’ Accessibility to Sites and Information 
9.11 The Committee raised the issue of Vedic heritage centres in villages named Riga, Athari, Yajur, and 
Samar in Bihar. 
9.12 The Committee also highlighted the existing state of infrastructural facilities, its poor conditions and 
expensive costumes at the National School of Drama. 
9.13 In view of the observations regarding the villages of Riga, Athari, Yajur and Samar in Bihar,  
which are believed to have possible associations with the Vedic tradition, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry examine the matter and explore the feasibility of undertaking 
appropriate studies, in consultation with the Archaeological Survey of Indi a and other concerned 
institutions, to ascertain the historical and cultural significance of these sites. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry take appropriate steps to address issues relating to infrastructural 
facilities and the cost of costumes at the National School of Drama. The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the action taken in this regard. 
 
 
 
 

21 
 
CHAPTER X:  
SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS 
The following is a consolidated summary of the thirty two recommendations made by the Committee. For 
full context, the relevant paragraph references are indicated. 
I. Financial Management and Budgetary Discipline 
Recommendation 1 (Para 1.4): The Committee recommends that the Ministry engage with the Ministry 
of Finance to secure enhanced allocations, inc luding through Supplementary Demands, and present a 
detailed justification note linking the additional demand to specific programme outcomes. 
Recommendation 2  (Para 1.7): The Committee recommends a detailed Capital expenditure plan for 
2026-27 with quarterly milestones and an explanation for the low Capital expenditure rate in 2025-26. 
Recommendation 3 (Para 1.9): The Committee recommends that the Ministry earmark a portion of the 
ticketing revenue of Rs. 365 crore annually for reinvestment in centrally pro tected monuments, with a 
detailed proposal. 
Recommendation 4  (Para 1.11): The Committee recommends a demand note for the 16th Finance 
Commission cycle linking budgetary requirements to NITI Aayog targets and a strategy for leveraging 
CSR, NCF, and PPP resources. 
Recommendation 5 (Para 1.14): The Committee recommends a strategy for alternative funding sources, 
including CSR engagement plans with model project frameworks, MPLAD eligibility for cultural 
heritage, and expansion of the NCF model. 
Recommendation 6 (Para 1.16): The Committee recommends a body -wise break-up of the GIA Salary 
allocation, current vacancy position in each Autonomous Body, and an impact assessment of the Rs. 77 
crore reduction. 
Recommendation 7  (Para 1.18): The Committee recommends scheme -wise and State -wise utilisation 
reports for SCSP, TSP, and NER mandatory sub-allocations, with physical outcomes. 
II. Project Implementation and Scheme Delivery 
Recommendation 8  (Para 2.4): The Committee recomm ends that all EFC notes for 16th FC schemes 
include implementation roadmaps, capacity assessments, State-wise absorption plans, phased scaling, and 
Centre-State cost-sharing frameworks. 
Recommendation 9  (Para 2.5): The Committee recommends that the Ministr y notify a performance -
linked Centre-State cost-sharing framework for the heritage infrastructure scheme, with funding tranches 
tied to measurable outcomes such as conservation quality indices, visitor footfall, and local artisan 
employment generation. 
Recommendation 10 (Para 2.8): The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a standardised 
impact assessment framework for all national commemoration programmes, quantifying outcomes in 
terms of public participation, geographical spread, educational outreach, and citizen awareness. 

22 
 
Recommendation 11  (Para 2.11): The Committee recommends replication of the Lalit Kala Akademi 
market-access model across academies and ZCCs, examination of a Heritage Conservation Corpus from 
art exhibition proceeds, and a note on KSVY pending liabilities. 
Recommendation 12  (Para 2.13): The Committee recommends an explanation for Gyan Bharatam 
Mission underutilisation, an institutional readiness assessment, a quarterly expenditure plan, and a 
milestone-linked fund release mechanism. 
Recommendation 13 (Para 2.15): The Committee recommends justification for the six -fold increase in 
Global Engagement allocation, an absorptive capacity assessment, and that future funding be linked to 
measurable international outcomes. 
Recommendation 14  (Para 2.17): The Committee recommends an explanation for chronic 
underutilisation under the Development of Libraries scheme and a corrective action plan. 
Recommendation 15 (Para 2.19): The Committee recommends reasons for near -zero expenditure under 
Cultural Mapping in 2025 -26, constitution of a dedicated Mission Implementation Unit, a quarter -wise 
plan for 2026-27, and a mid-year review. 
III. Heritage Conservation and Cultural Outcomes 
Recommendation 16 (Para 3.3): The Committee recommends that the A SI conservation utilisation rate 
for 2025-26 be brought to the level of previous years and that final figures be furnished within 90 days of 
the close of the financial year. 
Recommendation 17 (Para 3.4): The Committee recommends a comprehensive review and upgradation 
plan for maintenance standards and visitor facilities at all World Heritage Sites, commensurate with their 
global recognition. 
Recommendation 18  (Para 3.7): The Committee recommends a project -wise status report for all 15 
archaeological site development projects. 
Recommendation 19 (Para 3.9): The Committee recommends an action plan for underwater archaeology, 
including a digital repository for findings and collaboration with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways. 
Recommendation 20 (Para 3.14): The Committee recommends expeditious passage of the AMASR Act 
amendment, SOPs for denotification with a 90 -day timeline, a staffing plan for centrally protected 
monuments, and structured community participation models for monument conservation. 
Recommendation 21  (Para 3.16): The Committee recommends progress reports on the souvenir shop 
programme. 
Recommendation 22  (Para 3.18): The Committee recommends measurable annual targets for the 
restructured National Culture Fund. 
Recommendation 23 (Para 3.20): The Committee recommends documentation and replication of the Red 
Fort curation model. 

23 
 
Recommendation 24  (Para 3.22): The Committee recommends resolution of Bodh Gaya restoration, 
conservation plans for Kumhrar and Vaishali, and measures at Charminar. 
Recommendation 25  (Para 4.4): The Committee recommends clarification of the Museums scheme 
figure discrepancy, restoration of adequate allocation, and a district-wise museum development plan. 
Recommendation 26  (Para 4.7): The Committee recommends a detailed project plan for the 
YugeYugeen Bharat Museum. 
Recommendation 27 (Para 4.11): The Committee recommends a defined timeline for National Archives 
digitisation, SOPs for State archives, filling of the Khuda Bakhsh Library Director vacancy, meaningful 
utilisation of digitised content through integration with educational platforms, and attention to Libraries 
underutilisation. 
IV. Sector Reforms and Regulatory Matters 
Recommendation 28  (Para 5.3): The Committee recommends a repatriation roadmap, a self -surrender 
portal, and a status report on ongoing cases. 
Recommendation 29 (Para 5.6): The Committee recommends a five -year UNESCO nomination strategy 
with a pipeline of at least 10 nominations, within one year. 
Recommendation 30  (Para 7.4): The Committee recommends a time -bound recruitment plan for all 
vacant posts, minimum staff for all centrally protected monuments, and a specific action plan for IGRMS 
Bhopal. 
Recommendation 31 (Para 8.5): The Committee recommends that NEZCC shift focus to documentation, 
unique scripts for Arunachal Pradesh tribes be developed, non -functional cultural centres be made 
operational, NEZCC meetings be resumed, and a dedicated Northeast heritage programme be created. 
V. Technology, Digital Governance, and Transparency 
Recommendation 32  (Para 9.8): The Committee recommends finalisation and submission of Action 
Taken Notes on both outstanding CAG audit paragraphs within 90 days and a standing mechanism for 
time-bound disposal of CAG observations.

INTRODUCTION 
1. I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, present this Report on the 
Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (Demand 
No. 78). 
2. The Committee examined the Demands for Grants in the context of the strategic centrality 
of the maritime sector to India’s economic architecture, trade competitiveness, and logistical 
efficiency. India possesses a coastline of 11,098 km, 12 Major Ports, approximately 217 
other-than-major ports, and 111 declared National Waterways. The maritime sector transports 
approximately 95 per cent of India’s trade by volume and 68 per cent by value. The Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways exercises policy and regulatory oversight across this 
sector, encompassing port development, shipping regulation, shipbuilding promotion, ship 
repair and recycling, dredging, lighthouse administration, and inland water transport. The 
pace and quality of infrastructure modernisation, regulatory reform, and capacity creation 
within this sector have a direct bearing on the nation’s logistics costs, trade facilitation, and 
the objective of establishing India as a global maritime leader under the Maritime Amrit Kaal 
Vision 2047. 
3. The Committee’s scrutiny was directed not merely at the adequacy of financial allocations 
but at the structural coherence between budgetary intent and ground-level outcomes. 
Particular attention was devoted to: the absorptive capacity of the Ministry for an 
unprecedented 78 per cent increase in net GBS; the operationalisation of three new schemes 
(SBFAS, SbDS, and MDF) approved barely three months before the commencement of the 
financial year; the persistent concentration of IWT cargo on five waterways out of thirty-two 
operational; the disparity between created port capacity and actual throughput; the rate of 
Sagarmala project completion after a decade of implementation; the adequacy of last-mile rail 
and road connectivity to ports; the implementation architecture for five landmark maritime 
Acts enacted in 2025; and the readiness of the maritime workforce for a projected forty-five-
fold expansion in shipbuilding capacity by 2047. 
4. In the course of its examination, the Committee issued a detailed questionnaire to the 
Ministry and scrutinized the following documents: 
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No. 78), financial year 2026-27; 
(ii) Ministry’s Written Submission to the Committee’s Questionnaire; 
(iii) Ministry’s Depositional Notes (scheme-wise Reply/Status); 
(iv) Annual Report of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (2025-26); 
(v) Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF), financial year 2026-27; 
(vi) Annual Action Plan 2026-27 and Sector-wise Budgetary Outlays; 

 
iii 
(vii) Statement indicating Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actuals for 2023-
24, 2024-25, 2025-26 (expenditure incurred up to January 2026) and Budget 
Estimates of 2026-27; 
(viii) Focus Areas of the Ministry for 2026-27; 
(ix) Outstanding Audit Paras contained in the CAG Report and the action taken or 
proposed to be taken thereon; 
(x) NITI Aayog policy documents pertaining to the Ministry. 
5. The Committee’s examination encompassed six principal thematic dimensions: the overall 
financial architecture and its consonance with stated policy objectives; scheme-wise scrutiny 
of major programmes; a structured review of past demand versus fulfilment over three 
financial years; cross-cutting tests of budget realism, regional equity, port capacity utilisation, 
last-mile connectivity, efficiency-outcome linkage, and institutional governance; the green 
shipping transition and digital transformation; and a focused assessment of workforce 
development and legislative implementation readiness. The Committee further took oral 
evidence of the Secretary and senior officials of the Ministry on 25th February 2026. 
6. The Ministry, in its written submission to the Committee’s questionnaire, covered twenty-
two questions, spanning port modernisation, shipbuilding competitiveness, inland waterways, 
logistics cost reduction, digital initiatives, workforce development, environmental clearances, 
and the Maritime Development Fund. The reply disclosed, inter alia, that 145 out of 283 
berths at major ports are fully mechanised, handling 78 per cent of total cargo, with a target 
of 93 per cent by 2030; that cargo handling capacity has risen from 800.52 MTPA in 2013-14 
to 1,681 MTPA in 2024-25 (an increase of 110 per cent); that average turnaround time has 
improved from 93.6 hours to 49.5 hours (47 per cent reduction); that Indian shipyards face a 
25–30 per cent cost disadvantage relative to China, Korea, and Japan; and that 32 National 
Waterways are now operational, carrying 160.86 million tonnes up to December 2025. The 
Ministry’s depositional notes further recorded [Depositional Notes, Reply/Status] that only 5 
per cent of India’s EXIM cargo is carried by Indian-owned or Indian-flagged ships; that 
Indian-built ships account for merely 7.63 per cent of Indian-owned vessels; and that 
commercial shipbuilding capacity requires a forty-five-fold expansion from 0.1 million GT to 
4.5 million GT by 2047. These submissions have been examined in detail across Chapters 1 
through 5 and inform the Committee’s thirty-three observations and recommendations in 
Chapter 6. 
7. The OOMF for 2026-27 was examined with particular attention to the measurability of 
output and outcome indicators. The Committee note that both SbDS and SBFAS carry the 
designation ‘Target not amenable’ for all quantitative indicators in 2026-27, on the ground 
that the schemes are in their inaugural year and project identification is at an initial stage. The 
Jalvahak scheme targets 3,12,000 tonnes of modal-shift cargo and 16,800 tonnes through 20 
ICSL scheduled voyages. The IWT in NER programme targets 8 DPR/feasibility studies, 10 
vessels, and 2 terminals. These targets have been evaluated in the context of their adequacy 
relative to the allocations sought.

outcome accountability, maritime safety, equitable regional development, and workforce 
readiness at the centre of its assessment. The Committee’s thirty-three recommendations are 
framed in a spirit of constructive engagement and are intended to strengthen the planning, 
execution, and monitoring of the Ministry’s programmes.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
0.1.1 The total budgetary allocation under Demand No. 78 for 2026-27 is Rs. 5,764.80 crore 
(gross), comprising Rs. 4,464.88 crore under Revenue and Rs. 1,299.92 crore under Capital (net: 
Rs. 5,164.80 crore). The Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) of Rs. 12,702.94 crore 
bring the combined outlay to Rs. 17,867.74 crore. Three newly-approved schemes, SBFAS, 
SbDS, and MDF, command Rs. 1,765 crore (34 per cent of net GBS), notwithstanding their 
operational guidelines having been released only on 26th December 2025. 
0.1.2 The Ministry's depositional notes record that India ranks 17th in global shipbuilding, 
contributing less than 1 per cent to global capacity. Only 5 per cent of India's EXIM cargo is 
carried by Indian-owned or Indian-flagged ships. Indian-built ships constitute merely 7.63 per 
cent of Indian-owned ships. The sector carries an employment multiplier of 6.4 and an investment 
multiplier of 1.82. The Ministry's written submission to the Committee's questionnaire further 
disclosed that Indian shipyards face a 25-30 per cent cost disadvantage compared to major 
shipbuilding nations such as China, Korea, and Japan, attributable to higher financing costs, 
limited economies of scale, and gaps in advanced technology. The depositional notes further 
record that India's commercial shipbuilding capacity requires expansion from 0.1 million GT to 
approximately 4.5 million GT per annum by 2047, constituting a forty-five-fold increase. 
0.1.3 Against a BE of Rs. 3,470.58 crore for 2025-26, the RE was reduced to Rs. 2,899.11 crore 
(a contraction of 16.5 per cent), and actual expenditure as on 31st January 2026 stood at Rs. 
2,329.86 crore (80.4 per cent of RE). The OOMF lists 'Target not amenable' for virtually all 
quantitative indicators under SbDS and SBFAS, limiting outcome accountability in the inaugural 
year. Major Ports handled 854.86 MMT of cargo in 2024-25, with 8.22 per cent year-on-year 
growth. IWT cargo expanded from 18 MMT in 2013-14 to 146 MMT in 2024-25. Sagarmala has 
completed 277 of 839 projects (33 per cent) after approximately a decade. The SMFCL, now 
functioning as an NBFC (RBI licence dated 19th June 2025), has sanctioned Rs. 4,198.10 crore in 
lending. 
0.1.4 The Global Maritime India Summit 2025, held in October 2025 in Mumbai, was attended 
by 93 countries, and resulted in over 600 MoUs valued at approximately Rs. 12 lakh crore, 
signalling growing international engagement with India's maritime sector. 
0.1.5 This Report details thirty-seven observations and recommendations across seven thematic 
groups: financial management and budgetary discipline; port infrastructure, connectivity and 
capacity utilisation; shipbuilding, ship repair, recycling and dredging; inland waterways, cruise 
tourism and NW development; sector reforms and regulatory architecture; technology, digital 
governance and green transition; and workforce development, international connectivity and 
heritage.
