 Total Station, which are added to existing scientific methods of analysis such as radiocarbon (C 14) dating,
 thermoluminescence dating, archaeo-botany, archaeo-zoology etc. for obtaining objective inputs.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
16.       The Committee is surprised to note that its recommendations made in the context of Sarasvati Heritage Project
 the Department of Culture in its reply has not mentioned a single word about the Sarasvati Project or the irregularities
 pointed out by the Committee about the preparation of that project.  Our country has a rich and composite cultural
 heritage.  The Archaeological Survey of India is the custodian of that rich cultural heritage and as such its role to
 safeguard the cultural fabric of the country is of crucial national importance.  Therefore, the Committee reiterates that
 before undertaking any excavation of any such mythological projects like, Sarasvati Heritage Project, Archaeological
 Survey of India should made proper Scientific and technical appraisal and no extraneous factors should go into the
 decision making. 
 
VACANCIES AND STAFF STRENGTH IN ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
(Recommendation at Para 38)
 
17.       The Committee notes with concern that there are large-scale vacancies in various categories in the ASI, which
 has been hampering smooth and effective functioning of the Archaeological Survey of India.  The Committee also
 notes that the Government had been rather lax and inactive in completing the formalities for filling up many of the
 vacancies, as can be seen from the status furnished by the Archaeological Survey of India in respect of these vacancies. 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should take immediate steps to fill up the vacancies in the
 Archaeological Survey of India so that the works being undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India do not
 suffer.  The Committee also notes that there is an acute shortage of manpower for technical posts for which the
 Archaeological Survey of India had made proposals to create additional posts.  The Committee recommends that the
 Government should favourably consider the proposals submitted by the Archaeological Survey of India for creation of
 technical posts so that the Archaeological Survey of India is efficiently and smoothly able to carry out the voluminous
 work entrusted to it. 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNEMNT
 
18.       Continuous efforts are being made to fill up the vacant post in the ASI through convening the DPC meetings and
 also through the Union Public Service Commission and the Staff Selection Commission.  Additional requirement of
 technical manpower for the ASI is being worked out separately.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
19.       The Committee notes the reply.   The Committee however, would like to be apprised of the progress from
 time to time made in this matter.
 
NON-WRITING/PUBLICATION OF EXCAVATION REPORTS
(Recommendation at Para 46)
 
20.       The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on
 them goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological
 Survey of India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that
 despite its repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much. 
 However, the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the
 backlog in respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that
 the Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the
 excavation work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The
 Committee also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not
 transferred till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.

ENCROACHMENT AND SECURITY OF MONUMENTS/SITES
(Recommendation at Para 53)
 
25.       The Committee is concerned about the illegal encroachment of monuments/archaeological sites under the
 protection of Archaeological Survey of India.  In this context, the Committee would like to reiterate the
 recommendation made in its 85
th Report on Demands for Grants 2005-06 of Ministry of Culture which is as under:
"The Committee expresses its anxiety over the incidents of encroachment upon the land of Centrally Protected
 Monuments.  The Committee is more concerned about the inability of Archeological Survey of India to get back the
 land from encroachers.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that a complete assessment should be made
 regarding encroachment of monuments/sites under the protection of Archaeological Survey of India all over the
 country.  Prompt action ought be taken against the encroachers with the help of State Governments/Local
 Administrations and the matter should be pursued at the highest level.  The Committee also recommends that adequate
 budgetary provisions should be made for security arrangements and protection of monuments, as this is the most crucial
 aspect of preserving our cultural heritage and wherever possible modern gadgets like, electronic surveillance cameras
 should be installed in the monuments.  The Committee feels that security is a sovereign function.  Hence, it is the
 responsibility of Central Government to get the monuments and other important assets protected.  In view of this, the
 Committee is of the opinion that the Union Home Ministry should pay the bills towards the expenses incurred for
 paying the Central Security Agencies under this head.  Accordingly, the Ministry of Culture should pursue the matter at
 the highest level." 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
26.       As recommended by the Committee a complete assessment of the encroachment on centrally protected

 at Annexure.

 Directorate. The Superintending Archaeologist of the Archaeological Survey of India who is also vested with a power

 time frame.

            Over the past two decades, tourism has been identified as one of the world's largest industries with a growth rate
 of 5 per cent, per annum. The year 2003 saw tourism in our country emerging as a major sector of our economy,
 although it constitutes only a fraction of its vast potential.  A survey conducted by Conde Nast UK, the leading
 international travel magazine, ranked India amongst the top ten destinations of the world.  A poll conducted by Lonely
 Planet has ranked India as one of the top five destinations in the world. This Committee i.e. the Department-related
 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture discussed the kind of development that is taking

 place in the economy and particularly, in the aviation and tourism sectors where new priorities and initiatives have been
 actuated  and was of the view that the functioning of ITDC becomes very crucial in this kind of situation and

FORMATION AND OBJECTIVES OF ITDC
3.         The ITDC was established on the 1
st October, 1966 under the Company's Act, 1956 with the amalgamation of
 three undertakings namely Hotel Corporation of India Ltd., India Tourism Transport Undertaking Ltd. and India
 Tourism Corporation Ltd. into a unified Corporation.  The Corporation was incorporated with the sole objective of
 developing and expanding tourism infrastructure in the country thereby promoting India as a tourist destination.
 Subsequently, two Government companies namely the Ashok Hotels Ltd. and Janpath Hotel Ltd. were merged with
 ITDC on 20th March, 1970.  The mission of ITDC is to provide leadership and play catalytic role in the development of
 tourism infrastructure in the country and to achieve excellence in its strategic business units through professionalism,
 efficiency, value for money and customer focussed service.  Broadly, the main objectives of the Corporation are:
construction, management and marketing of hotels  and catering units.
providing tourist transport facilities and money changing facilities.
providing duty free shopping facilities to the tourists.
providing entertainment facilities to the tourists.
providing consultancy-cum-management services and training for tourism related projects.
production, distribution and sale of tourist publicity material.
promoting tourism through food festival, fairs and joint ventures in India and abroad.
ROLE OF ITDC
4.         The Committee was informed that ITDC is disseminating the benefits of its skills and experience for
 development of tourism in the country.  It is offering consultancy and management services both to private and public
 sectors and also undertaking the joint venture hotel projects in collaboration with the State Governments/State
 Corporations.  In addition, ITDC is popularizing Indian Cuisines abroad by participating in food-cum-cultural festivals. 
 Further, Corporation has diversified its activities by providing Management and Consultancy Services in collaboration
 with the Government both at Central and State levels, relating to tourism and engineering projects.  The Corporation
 has been playing a crucial and strategic role in ensuring proper dispersal of socio-economic benefits of tourism,
 promoting national integration and international understanding, helping removal of regional imbalances, generating
 employment opportunities, augmenting foreign exchange earnings and also acting as a catalyst in the development of
 tourism.  ITDC, thus, represents a major public sector effort towards the development of tourism within the country and
 abroad.      
5.         During the course of oral evidence, the Secretary, Department of Tourism has deposed before the Committee
 that:
"Sir, we entirely agree with the observation of the Committee that there has been a complete change, as a matter of fact,
 in the context in which the ITDC is now operating.  At this moment, everybody knows and recognizes that the economy
 has changed.  The economy has become very, very complex and has much more developed than it was in the early 50's
 or 60's.  The hospitality industry itself has grown beyond recognition. Remarkable growth has taken place in this sector
 and it is also poised for further growth in the years to come. At the same time, the private sector has come on its own. 
 Tourism industry in the private sector has established itself and, as a matter of fact, some of them have set world-class
 benchmarks for others in the world to emulate.  Besides, earlier, even the Department of Tourism itself was not very
 active.  Now the Department of Tourism has taken on itself the role of promoting tourism. The Department of Tourism
 is meant not only for the ITDC, but also for the entire tourism sector, which also includes the private sector in a major
 way, so, that is why, now it has been a Government effort, but driven by the private sector in a major way.  That is how
 the change is taking place."

17.       The Committee notes that ITDC has been playing active role, both as promotional and commercial for the
 development of tourism infrastructure spreading all over the country. The Committee also notes that ITDC has set-up a
 Tourism Task Force for promotion of camping and adventure tourism in the remote areas in collaboration with the local
 Governments/authorities.  The Committee finds that consequent upon the implementation of disinvestment policy, the
 presence of the Corporation in the country has shrunk and ITDC stopped  setting up of new hotels/resorts in the
 country.  The Committee feels that this has not only confined the activities of ITDC to metropolitan cities but also
 diminished the geographic spread of ITDC.  The Committee, however,  recommends that the geographic spread of
 ITDC should not be confined only to metro cities of the nation but it should further be expanded to rural areas and
 hinterlands to provide required logistics to foreign and domestic tourists and the Department of Tourism should provide
 all support/help to ITDC in this regard.  The Committee further recommends that Department of Tourism should
 consider the detailed project reports prepared by ITDC under Rural Tourism Development Scheme and release funds
 for execution of works.  The Committee also recommends that ITDC should monitor the execution under the Rural
 Tourism Development Scheme.   This will create infrastructure in the villages, which in turn will play catalytic role for
 attracting private investment there.

REASONS FOR LOW PERFORMANCE AND MEASURES TAKEN FOR IMPROVEMENT IN THE
 FUNCTIONING
23.       The Committee desired to know the reasons for low performance by the ITDC in earlier years and whether any
 measures have been put -in place for improvement of performance and future plans to meet such eventualities, the
 Department of Tourism in their written replies informed the Committee that Tourism scenario in the country was
 adversely affected by following national and international events/factors which resulted into low performance of ITDC
 :
Lower turnout of international business travellers due to following international and domestic reasons:
Terrorists attack in USA on 11
th Sept., 2001.
Conflict in Afghanistan.
Terrorists attack on Indian Parliament on 13
th Dec., 2001
Gujarat Riots
Tension on Indo-Pak Borders and advisories issued by a number of foreign countries against visiting India.
Media publicity on  ITDC disinvestment adversely affected business inflow into hotels from prospective clients and
 potential markets.
Lack of refurbishing/upgradation of hotel properties because of the process of disinvestment.
Uncertainty and psycho-fear created in employees due to disinvestment in ITDC.
Substantial increase in the license fee and royalty in respect of duty free shops payable to AAI.
Increase in availability of hotel rooms in approved sector resulting in cut-throat competition and price war.
24.       As regards measures taken for improvement in performance, the Committee was informed that ITDC
 management has been very conscious and concerned about the low performance in its profitability.  The following
 measures have been taken by the ITDC management to improve financial performance of the Corporation:
Aggressive marketing efforts including promotional schemes, special packages etc.
Consolidation in the existing facilities/services of the ITDC and sub-contracting some services.
To have strict control over wastage and pilferage.
Recovery of outstanding dues form public/private parties.
After the disinvestment of 18 ITDC hotels, ITDC has diversified and entered into new business activities such as Money
 Changing and Western Union Money Transfers, Consultancy and execution of tourism & engineering, projects, training
 consultancy in hospitality sector.  Even Management, Mounting of SEL Shows.
Leasing out of some business areas in few ITDC Hotels to private parties for generating fixed income.
Rationalisation of manpower through VRS and redeployment of manpower.
Reduction in wage bill by roll back of retirement age from 60 to 58 years.
Control of cost by exercising economy in expenditure.
Opening up of new Duty Free Shops at Hyderabad, Bangalore, Calicut and Ahmedabad.

 airports would decide to select Duty Free Operators in future.  However, AITD is confident that in a fair and

 by AAI.  The present five-year agreement and subsequent extension for operating duty free shops in Chennai, Kolkata,

th June, 2006.  AAI has floated a

 there prevails uncertainty in the operation of Duty Free Shops in these airports which contributed about 75% turnover
 of the Ashok International Trade Division (AITD).  However, the Committee notes that ITDC has been successful in
 securing and executing agreements with private management of Delhi and Mumbai Airports for extensions of licence
 for a further period of six months for operations of Duty Free Shops at these airports on the similar terms and
 conditions as was there with AAI previously.  The Committee feels that although the future status of AITD is uncertain
 and will much depend on the policy of the private managements in the selection of Duty Free operators but at the same
 time, ITDC can get the contract  with a mix of marketing strategies, right merchandising, competitive pricing and
 sustained product promotions.  The Committee is hopeful that given a fair and competitive environment, AITD will be
 able to secure the contract in these airports in the future besides operating Duty Free Shops in Chennai, Kolkata,
 Trivandrum, Goa, Calicut, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Bangalore airports.  The Committee recommends the
 Department to make all out efforts in securing the contract for operating Duty Free Shops in these airports.

 the issue of royalty has not been settled as yet.  The high incidence of rent/royalty to the tune of 40% of the turnover
 payable to the AAI is affecting product pricing, profitability and operational competitiveness of the business.  In
 addition, AAI has imposed a 12.2% service tax on rent from ITDC with retrospective effect and has claimed about
 Rs.9.00 crore.  ITDC has not acknowledged this liability and has taken up the matter with Service Tax Authorities.  The
 Division has made a submission against the contractual liability on account of royalty imposed by AAI amounting to
 Rs.28.34 crore for the business years 2001-02, 2002-03 and 2003-04 on the basis of the minimum guaranteed turnover
 because AAI could not fulfil its obligation to maintain the condition of the business i.e. ensuring projected tourist traffic
 flow for reasons already mentioned in the question.  The case is under mediation.

 were invited in November 2001 and again in January 2002, but there was no compliant bid for Ashok Hotel. 
 Subsequently, as per the decision taken by the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment in March 2002, Ashok Hotel, New

83.       As regards, impact of disinvestment, the Department submitted that ITDC started feeling the adverse impact as
 soon as the Government decided to disinvest ITDC Hotels.  Renovation schemes were put on hold rendering ITDC
 properties non-competitive. The psycho-fear created by uncertainty kept the morale of the employees very low
 affecting the services.  The business providers were hesitant to do business with ITDC due to the uncertainty.  Media
 publicity on ITDC disinvestment had also played a major role affecting business adversely.  In the initial stage itself,
 ITDC was directed by the Department of Disinvestment to avoid making any long-term commitment which resulted in
 drifting of its Conference Business as well as room bookings from prospective clients and potential market.  As a result
 of the impact of disinvestment, ITDC suffered losses during four consecutive years from 1999-2000 to 2002-03 leading
 to financial crunch in ITDC. After disinvestment of 18 hotel properties, the largest Hotel Chain of Ashok Group of
 Hotels was broken and ITDC's presence as a hotelier is now confined only to certain areas, its geographical spread
 achieved earlier stood diminished.
84.       The Committee is at pain to note that the role of ITDC was limited only upto providing
 information/data/material to the Advisor, Ministries of Disinvestment and Tourism and to implement decision of the
 Government for disinvestment of hotels.  The apex corporation in the field of tourism was not even given a reasonable
 opportunity for making presentation and defending its case before the Disinvestment Commission or pleading its case.
 The Committee strongly denounces the move of the Government for not giving any opportunity to the ITDC for being
 heard before disinvestment of its properties although it was performing well.  Further, by putting few other ITDC hotels
 in the disinvestments list for some years and subsequently removing those therefrom, also dampened the spirit of the
 employees working in these hotels and of the Corporation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a thorough
 probe in the matter of disinvestment of ITDC Hotels be undertaken by the Government to know the entire sequence of
 disinvestment of ITDC's properties and reasons for doing so by some independent agency. The probe should also
 include as to what was the end use of the money collected through disinvestments of ITDC properties.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS – AT A GLANCE
ROLE OF ITDC
            The Committee notes that with the transformation of Indian economy to keep pace with globalization, the ITDC
 is striving to achieve its objectives of developing and expanding tourism infrastructure in the country and promoting
 India as a tourist ­­­­­­­­­­­destination of the globe by providing all tourism related services under a single roof.  The
 Committee feels that  though ITDC is functioning on commercial lines it should also help in removing the regional
 imbalances by proper diffusion and uniform percolation of socio-economic benefits amongst  all stratas of the society. 
 The Committee feels that in this manner, it would pave the way for more employment generation in the tourism sector
 and act as a catalyst for development of Tourism across the country.                                   (Para 6)
BOARD OF DIRECTORS
            The Committee notes with concern that the re-constitution of the ITDC's Board of Directors with appointment of
 non-official part time Directors remains under consideration of the Department.  The Committee feels that presence
 of    non-official Directors on the Board will make the Board more professional.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the posts of part time non-official Directors on the Board of ITDC should be filled up by the
 Government from the concerned areas without fail.
                                                     (Para 12)
 GEOGRAPHICAL SPREAD OF ITDC
            The Committee notes that ITDC has been playing active role, both as promotional and commercial for the
 development of tourism infrastructure spreading all over the country. The Committee also notes that ITDC has set-up a
 Tourism Task Force for promotion of camping and adventure tourism in the remote areas in collaboration with the local
 Governments/authorities.  The Committee finds that consequent upon the implementation of disinvestment policy, the
 presence of the Corporation in the country has shrunk and ITDC stopped  setting up of new hotels/resorts in the
 country.  The Committee feels that this has not only confined the activities of ITDC to metropolitan cities but also
 diminished the geographic spread of ITDC.  The Committee, however, recommends that the geographic spread of
 ITDC should not be confined only to metro cities of the nation but it should further be expanded to rural areas and
 hinterlands to provide required logistics to foreign and domestic tourists and the Department of Tourism should provide
 all support/help to ITDC in this regard.  The Committee further recommends that Department of Tourism should
 consider the detailed project reports prepared by ITDC under Rural Tourism Development Scheme and release funds
 for execution of works.  The Committee also recommends that ITDC should monitor the execution under the Rural
 Tourism Development Scheme.   This will create infrastructure in the villages, which in turn will play catalytic role for

activities for enabling this nodal organization to compensate the loss already

 difficult for the Corporation to maintain even the present level of business. The Committee is also of the view that it is
 high time for making substantial investment in these properties for their revival. The Committee, therefore,

Phalguna 18, 1928 (Saka) Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture
 
                                                              
                          
 
 
 
 
 
* Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II, Section-2, dated 07.08.2006.
* *Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, No. 43442 dated 05.09.2006.
R E P O R T
The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 7 th August, 2006.  The Bill was
 referred to this Committee for examination and report.  Under the mandate, the Committee has examined the Bill and
 finalised the Report after hearing the views of various stakeholders, experts and Ministries/Departments.  The Bill seeks
 to enable the Government to regulate the foreign registered aircrafts which are being operated in India, to give powers
 to Government for the purpose of licensing of personnel engaged in air traffic control, certification, inspection and
 regulation of communication, navigation and surveillance and air traffic management, safeguarding civil aviation
 against acts of unlawful interference and to ensure civil aviation security and investigation of "incident" along with
 "accident". This Bill also proposes to give more powers to the Director General of Civil Aviation for performing safety
 oversight functions and to impose penalty for contravention of the provisions of the Chicago Convention. 
 
2.         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that a sea change has occurred in the aviation sector
 during the last two decades.   The Central Government are already exercising their control over the manufacture, use
 and operation of civil aircrafts under various provision of the Aircraft Act 1934 and also under various rules and
 instructions issued under that Act. The management and operation of domestic airports, navigation and communication
 facilities and air traffic control at all airports was transferred from Government to the National Airports Authority in
 1986.  The National Airports Authority was merged with the International Airport Authority of India w.e.f. 1
st April
 1995 to form a single entity named Airports Authority of India.  The Government opened the domestic air transport
 services to the private sector in 1994.  With drastic developments in the fields of technology, communication,
 navigation, surveillance etc. the air traffic management system is also switching over from ground based to satellite
 based technology in the near future.  With unprecedented growth of the civil aviation sector it has become all the more
 important to provide  safeguards for civil aviation security.
 
3.         The statement of objects and reasons further states that the safety and security provisions and international
 standards as mentioned in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is to be implemented in the present
 scenario and it also states that the various provisions of the Convention on International Civil Aviation popularly
 known as Chicago Convention are to be given effect. 
 
4.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation in their background note furnished on the 25
th September 2006 to the Committee
 have brought out the following points as reasons for the introduction of the Bill:- 
 
I           Regulation of Foreign Registered Aircraft
 
5.         The Aircraft Act 1934 is not having any provision for extending the applicability of the act to foreign registered
 aircrafts which may be for the time being in or over India.  There is no regulatory power with the Government over the
 foreign registered aircraft when they are operating in India.  However, Clause (b) of Sub-rule (2) of Rule 1 of the
 Aircraft Rules, 1937, which have been made in exercise of the powers conferred by Sections 5, 7 and 8 of the Act,
 provides that these rules shall also apply to all aircraft and to persons on aircraft for the time being in or over India.  In
 order to remove this anomaly, it is considered necessary to have a similar express provision in the Act, so as to exercise
 regulatory control on foreign registered aircraft operating in or over India.  It is, therefore, proposed to insert a new
 clause in sub-section (2) of Section 1 of the Act to make this point explicit and clear.

II          Accident and Incident
 
6.         Section 7 of the Aircraft Act deals with the investigation of an accident only.  However, the word ‘incident’ is
 mentioned along with ‘accident’ in annexure 13 of Chicago Convention and it has made a clear distinction between
 accidents and incidents.  An accident is said to have taken place when a person is fatally or seriously injured during a
 flight or the aircraft sustains substantial damage or structural failure or the aircraft is missing or is completely
 inaccessible.  An incident, on the other hand, is an occurrence other than an accident associated with the operation of
 the aircraft that affects or could affect the safety of operations.  Since the Parent Act is silent over the incident aspect,
 the present legislation proposes to include the word incident along with the word accident in Section 7 of the Act.
 
 
 
 
 
III   Supervisory control over ATM standards/ATC personnel
 
7.       The Government after the enactment of Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 , has entrusted the job of
 management of civil airports in the country to the Airports Authority of India which includes the air traffic control and
 navigational and communication facilities.  But the basic responsibility of ensuring air safety lies with the Government
 only and for that purpose it needs to exercise supervisory control on the airports and its ground aids, communication
 and navigation and management facilities etc.  The proposed amendment will give powers to the Government to grant
 license to the personnel engaged in air traffic control in order to maintain the desired standards and level of
 proficiency.  Annexure 1 to the Chicago Convention also provides for such licensing by States in the air traffic control.
 
IV  Civil aviation security
 
 8.    With the opening of Indian skies to the private players and arrival of a large number of foreign players in the civil
 aviation sector, the need for reviewing of civil aviation security is also emphasized.  The expression “safety of aircraft
 operations” mainly covers the maintenance and airworthiness aspects of the aircraft and the proficiency of flight crews,
 ground engineers, etc.   There is no mention about the threat due to unlawful acts of interference.  The International
 Civil Aviation Organization has recognized the distinct importance of safety and security and they have laid down
 separate standards for security of civil aviation against unlawful interference.  In this context, necessity arises to enlarge
 the scope of Section 5 of the Act to give more powers to the Central Government to make rules to safeguard civil
 aviation against unlawful acts thereby ensuring civil aviation security. 
 
V         Powers to DGCA
 
9.         Section 5A of the Aircraft Act speaks about the powers given to DGCA or any other Officer empowered by
 Government to issue directions from time to time in consistent with the provisions of the act and rules.  Clause (b), (c),
 (e), (f), (g), (h) and (m) of sub section (2) of Section 5 give powers of licensing, inspection of aerodromes, inspection of
 aircrafts, the conditions under which  aircraft may be flown, the licensing of persons employed in the operation or
 maintenance of aircrafts, the permission to fly on an air route.  However, the fast growing air traffic scenario and the
 past experience have shown that there is a necessity to enlarge the above powers to cover some grey areas.  As such it is
 proposed that the regulation of air transport services, prohibition of flight over specified areas and prohibition of
 slaughtering and flaying of animals within 10kms radius of the airports will be included in the section 5 (2) of the Act. 
 The proposed amendments in Clause 5A of the Bill will give more powers to the DGCA over the air traffic control and
 operation of CNS. 
 
VI        Safety Oversight Functions
 
10.       Safety Oversight is a function to ensure effective implementation of safety related Standards and Recommended
 Practices and associated procedures contained in the Annexure to the Convention on International Civil Aviation and
 related ICAO documents.  Section 4 of the Aircraft Act, 1934 provides power to Central Government to make rules to
 implement the Convention.  Safety Oversight function is currently being performed by DGCA but the Act does not

109th report of commitee on Transport,tourism & culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/109threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:16:50]
 specifically delegate this function to DGCA.  It is, therefore, proposed in the Bill to add a Section in the Aircraft Act to
 specifically provide for Safety Oversight functions to be performed by Director – General of Civil Aviation or any
 other officer specially empowered in this behalf by Central Government.
 
VII       Penalties for violations of provisions of the act
 
11.       The aircraft operators who are violating various provisions of the Act are punishable under Sub Section 1A of
 Section 10 of the Act.  This punishment includes imposition of fine and imprisonment.  These punishments vary
 depending upon the act or rule it is violating.  These penalties were laid down several decades ago and the quantum of
 fine or imprisonment in this Section has now become out dated and it will not have much deterrent effect on the
 operators.  As such it is inevitable to raise the quantum of punishment in the existing scenario. 
 
VIII      Quantum of punishment for rules framed under Chicago 
            Convention
 
12.       Section 4 of the Act gives powers to the Government to frame rules for the implementation of Chicago
 Convention.  However, the violation of Rules is not punishable under Sub Section 2 of Section 10 of the Act.  It is
 therefore, proposed to amend Sub Section 2 of Section 10 to make such violations punishable. 
 
13.       In its meeting held on the 6
th October, 2006 the Committee heard the views of Secretary, Ministry of Civil
 Aviation on the Bill.  The Committee decided to invite the views of experts/stakeholders on the subject. 
 
14.       In order to have wider consultations, the Committee had also decided to invite written memoranda containing
 suggestions/ views/ comments of individuals / institutions/ organizations interested in the subject matter of the Bill.
 
15.       Thereafter, the Committee heard the views of Employees Union of the Airports Authority of India in its meeting
 held on the 25
th January, 2007. The representatives of the Employees Union mainly opposed the Bill on the following
 grounds:-
(i)                  The enhancement of powers to the Government through the proposed amendments in various sections of
 Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 will directly result in the encroachment of Airports Authority of India Act,
 1994.  The powers of the Airports Authority of India will be taken over by the Government through these
 amendments.
 
(ii)
                Section 15 of Airports Authority of India Act as amended in 2003 gives the power to Airports Authority of
 India to award licence to airports.  However, the proposed amendment in clause 5 of Aircraft (Amendment)
 Bill will give more powers to Government for licensing of airports.  This will curtail the existing powers of
 Airports Authority of India.  The present legislation has created confusion by involving two institutions in
 the process of licensing of airports.  The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 clearly contravenes Airports
 Authority of India Act 1994 which empowers Airports Authority of India to award license to airports.
 
(iii)
               Section 55 and functional clause 12 (a) to (r) of Airports Authority of India Act 1994 gives various powers
 to Airports Authority of India for managing, inspecting and other all operational activities involved in the
 airports.  But the Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 if enacted will effectively make Airports Authority of
 India to sit on the side lines.
 
16.       The Committee also heard the views of representatives of Airports Authority of India, Centre for Asia Pacific
 Aviation, Jet Airways and Kingfisher Airlines and obtained their written comments on the subject.  After perusing all
 these, the Committee in its meeting on 20
th February 2007 considered the Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006 clause-by-
clause.
 
17.       The Clause wise recommendations of the Committee are as follows:-
           
CLAUSE 2
17.1     Clause 2 reads - " In section 1 of the Aircraft Act, 1934 (hereinafter referred to as the principal Act), in sub-

(i)                  in clause (a), the word “and” shall be omitted;
(ii)                  after clause (b), the following Clauses shall be inserted, namely:-
(c)        to, and to the persons on, aircraft registered outside India but for the time being in or over India; and
 
(d)        to an aircraft operated by a person who is not a citizen of India but has his principal place of business or
 permanent residence     in India.”.
 
17.2     This Clause intends to amend Section 1 of the Principal Act and proposes to expand application of the principal

 India.  The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation while briefing the Committee about the broad objectives of the Bill
 stated as under:-
 
“……. One important area, which I should have mentioned earlier and for which I apologise, is regulation of
 foreign registered aircraft, which is now becoming an important issue.  The Aircraft Act of 1934 does not have
 any explicit provision regarding the applicability of the Act to foreign registered aircraft, which may either be
 on our land or flying over our country.  A foreign aircraft that is using the Indian airspace is guided or given a
 certain route to fly over it.  The Aircraft Act does not really envisage the kind of a situation where it deviates
 from that route, and, it does not directly bind down that aircraft to follow the guidelines that the DGCA may
 issue for compliance.”
 
17.3.    The Committee feels that the opening of Indian skies to private players has resulted in expansion of aviation
 traffic and as a result thereof a large number of aircraft are operating over the Indian skies leading to heavy traffic over
 the Indian skies.   There is no regulation for the foreign registered aircrafts who are operating in India in the Parent Act.
 In view of this the Committee adopted this Clause without suggesting any change therein.

 as to who will be solely responsible to perform the safety oversight functions.  The Committee feels that with the

 civil aviation sector etc. in the proposed Bill. The proposed Bill should not leave any area uncovered pertaining to civil

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            At present the Central Government through various provisions of the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the rules made
 thereunder exercises control in respect of manufacture, possession, use, operation, sale, import and export of civil
 aircrafts and licensing of aerodromes.
            2. In the last two decades, significant developments have taken place in the civil aviation sector in India.  The
 domestic air transport services were opened to the private sector in 1994 and the management and operation of the
 airports, the navigation, communication facilities and the air traffic control at airports were transferred to the Airports
 Authority of India with effect from the 1
st April, 1995.  Now, with vast developments in technology, communication,
 navigation, surveillance and air traffic management are switching over from ground based to satellite based
 technology.  As a result of these developments, a need has arisen to lay down appropriate safeguards to ensure
 protection of civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference.
            3. Keeping in view the above aspects as well as standards laid down by the International Civil Aviation
 Organisation (ICAO) for safety and security of civil aviation and also to give effect to various provisions of the
 Convention on International Civil Aviation popularly known as Chicago Convention, certain amendments are proposed
 to be made to the Aircraft Act, 1934.
            4. The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006, inter-alia, seeks –
(a)
    to regulate foreign registered aircraft which is for the time being operating in or over India;
(b)   to empower the Central Government for –
(i)                  licensing of personnel engaged in air traffic control;
(ii)                certification, inspection and regulation of communication, navigation and surveillance
 and air traffic management;
(iii)               safeguarding civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference and to ensure civil
 aviation security; and
(iv)              investigation of incident along with accident.
(c)    to empower the Director General of Civil Aviation for performing safety oversight functions
(d)   to impose penalty for contravention of the provisions of the Chicago Convention;
(e)    to enhance quantum of existing penalties for violation of rules relating to carriage in aircraft of arms
 or explosives of providing false information or abetment of offences or non-compliance of directions
 with a view to achieve desired deterrent effect which would go a long way in raising the compliance
 level;
(f)     to enlarge the scope of the powers of Director General of Civil Aviation.
5. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and
 Tenth Report of the Committee on the Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006*.
 
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 18
th December, 2006. In pursuance of rules relating to the
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the
 Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, referred** the Bill to the Committee on the 26 th December, 2006 for examination and
 report.
 
3.         The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary, Department of Road Transport and Highways and Secretary,
 Ministry of Rural Development at its meeting held on the 9
th March, 2007.
 
4.         The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill and considered the draft Report on the Bill
 and adopted the same on the 19.03.07 .
 
5.         The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways for the assistance provided during deliberations on the provisions of the Bill.

The Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 18 th December, 2006. On
 26th December, 2006 Hon'ble Chairman Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha referred the
 Bill to the Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture for examination and Report.  Under the mandate, the
 Committee has examined the Bill and finalised the Report after hearing the views of the nodal Ministry, i.e. , Road
 Transport and Highways and the only stakeholder i.e., Ministry of Rural Development.  The Bill seeks to amend the
 Central Road Fund Act, 2000 which provides for levy and collection by way of cess, excise and customs duty on petrol
 and high-speed diesel oil for development and maintenance of National Highways, rural roads, State roads and
 improvement of safety at railway crossings.  Under Section 9 of the Act the Central Government has the power to
 administer the fund and allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary to the concerned departments
 responsible for the development and maintenance of rural roads.  Under section 10, the Central Government is
 responsible for allocation of fifty percent of the cess on high-speed diesel oil for the development and maintenance of
 National Highways, rural roads, State roads and construction of roads over or under railways.  The fund available under
 Section 10 is utilized for the provision of all-weather connectivity to rural habitations through centrally sponsored
 scheme “Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana”.  Under the Scheme, a target has been set to provide road connectivity to
 all rural habitations having a population of 1000 and above (500 and above in hilly and tribal areas) by 2009.  This will
 require an investment of about Rs.48,000 crores.  To bridge the funding gap, the Government intends to borrow
 Rs.16,500 crores over a period of four years. Since the Central Road Fund Act, 2000 does not have any provision for
 borrowing for rural roads and utilization of the proceeds of future cess for repayment of loans, the Central Road Fund
 (Amendment) Bill, 2006 seeks to amend the Parent Act to enable the Central Government to take such measures as may
 be necessary to raise funds for the development of rural roads, and it may use the share of the fund for the repayment of
 any loan taken for the purpose of development of rural roads in any State or Union territory.
2.         The Central Road Fund was in existence since 1929.  It was being governed by the Parliamentary Resolution of
 1977 according to which an amount not less that 3.5 paise per litre of petrol consumed was to be set apart out of the
 custom and excise duty levied on petrol for development of roads.  The amount was being distributed between the State
 and the Central Schemes at the ratio of 80:20 after defraying the cost of administration of the Fund.  The two Houses of
 the Parliament passed a revised Resolution in May 1988 according to which an amount not less than 5 per cent of the
 basic price of petrol and diesel was earmarked for the development of Road Sector.  However, this resolution could not
 be implemented due to reservations expressed by Ministry of Finance and difficult resources position.
3.         In recognition of the need for funds for the road infrastructure sector the Union Budget for 1988-89 provided for
 a levy of additional excise duty and additional customs duty of one Rupee per litre of petrol.  Subsequently, an
 additional duty of one Rupee per litre on imported and domestic high speed diesel was proposed in the Budget  for
 1999-2000.  The revenue from these two levies was to accrue to the dedicated Central Road Fund.  It was also decided
 that 50 per cent of the cess on diesel will be given to the Ministry of Rural Development for Rural Roads.  A legal
 instrument was necessary for administration of the Fund.  Accordingly, due to urgency of the matter the Central Road
 Fund ordinance was promulgated on 1.11.2000 for this purpose.  Subsequently the ordinance was replaced by the
 Central Road Fund Act, 2000.
4.         With regard to utilisation and apportioning of the fund, the Department of Road, Transport and Highways
 informed the Committee as follows:-

(A) Under Section 7 of the Act, the Fund shall be utilised for the
(i)                  Development and maintenance of National Highways
(ii)                Development of rural roads
(iii)               Development and maintenance of other State roads including roads of inter-state and
 economic importance
(iv)              Construction of roads either under or over the railways by means of bridge and erection
 of safety works at the unmanned rail-road crossings; and
(v)                Disbursement in respect of such proposals as may be prescribed.
(B)            According to Sub-Section (viii) of Section 10 of the Act, the money accrued to the Fund will
 be apportioned in the following manner.
(a)                Fifty per cent of the cess on high speed diesel oil for the development of rural roads in
 such manner as may be prescribed; and
(b)               The balance amount of fifty per cent of cess of high speed diesel oil and the entire cess
 collected on petrol is allocated as follows:-
(i)                  An amount equal to fifty seven and one half percent of such sum for the development
 and maintenance of National Highways.
(ii)                An amount equal to twelve and one half per cent for the construction of roads either
 under or over the railways by means of bridge and erection of safety works on un-manned
 rail-road crossing.
(iii)
               The balance thirty per cent on development of roads other than National Highways and
 out of this amount, ten per cent, that is three per cent of the total share of State roads shall
 be kept as reserve by the Central Government for allocation to States for implementation
 of ,State road schemes of inter-state and economic importance' to be approved by the
 Central Government.
            Under Section 9, the Central Government shall have the power to administer the Fund and shall -
(a)
                take such decisions regarding investment on projects of national highways and
 expressways as it considers necessary;
(b)               take such measures as may be necessary to raise fund for the development and
 maintenance of the National Highways;
(c)                allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary, to the concerned
 departments responsible for the development and maintenance of -
(i)                  National Highways;
(ii)                rural roads;
(iii)               State roads; and
(iv)              Construction of roads either under or over the railways by means of a bridge and erect
 suitable safety works at unmanned rail-road level crossings.
5.         The Department of Road, Transport and Highways further informed the Committee that Under Section 10 of the
 Act the Central Government provides fifty per cent of the cess of high speed diesel for the development of rural roads. 
 This allocation is utilized for provision of all-weather connectivity to rural habitations through centrally sponsored
 scheme "Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana." 'Bharat Nirman' Scheme has been announced as a time bound business
 plan for augmenting rural infrastructure.  Bharat Nirman has six components including rural roads.  Under this
 initiative, target has been set to provide road connectivity to all rural habitations having a population of 1000 and above

 (500 and above in hilly and tribal areas) by 2009.  66,802 eligible habitations are proposed to be provided new
 connectivity under Bharat Nirman.  This would involve construction of 1,46,185 kms of new link roads and
 upgradation of 1,94,130 kms of existing through routes.  This will require an investment of about Rs.48,000 crore. 
 Against this, the likely availability of funds will be Rs.16,000 crore from the Cess of High Speed Diesel (calculated at
 2% rate of annual increase over the 2005-06 receipts) and Rs.9000 crore from the credit/loan from the World Bank and
 the Asian Development Bank.  This leaves a funding gap of Rs.23,000 crore.
6.     In compliance with the decision taken earlier in January 2005 by the Cabinet, various funding options were placed
 for consideration before the National Committee on Rural Infrastructure (NCRI) under the Chairmanship of Hon'ble
 Prime Minister.  In its meeting held on 5th October, 2005, it was suggested by the NCRI that a separate window may be
 created in NABARD to fund the rural roads component of Bharat Nirman.  The Planning Commission constituted a
 Task Force to work out the modalities and procedures for creation of the separate window.  The Task Force
 recommended that a special window may be created under NABARD to borrow Rs.16,500 crore over a period of four
 years to bridge the funding gap under Bharat Nirman which would be repaid from out of the future cess allocation for
 the development of rural roads.  The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech on 28
th February, 2006 had announced
 opening of a separate window for rural roads with a corpus of Rs.4,000 crore during 2006-07.
7.         The Cabinet Note dated 27 th June, 2001 of the Ministry of Rural Development pertaining to the Pradhan Mantri
 Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) laid down the objectives, time frame, the level of investment and the institutional
 mechanism required for implementation of this programme.  It was brought out in the Cabinet Note that a total
 investment of about Rs.58,200 crore (say Rs.60,000 crore) was required to achieve total connectivity for all eligible
 habitations, by the end of the 10 th Plan Period.  The proposals were considered and approved by the Cabinet in its
 meeting held on 7th August, 2001.  The Cabinet Note, as approved, identified  the 50% share of the cess on high speed
 diesel as the readily available source of funding for the rural roads programme, and authorised the Department of Rural
 Development, in consulation with the Ministry of Finance, to generate additional financial resources, including
 borrowings from, inter alia, the World Bank and Asian Development Bank (ADB.)
8.   The initial data available from the States showed that there were 1,40,895 eligible habitations which were to be
 provided connectivity under PMGSY.  Based upon projected average distance of 1.26km. per habitation and a projected
 average cost of Rs.14.75 lakh per km, it was estimated that the total funds required to provide new connectivity to these
 habitations would be Rs.34,200 crore.  Upgradation of existing rural roads to prescribed standards was estimated to cost
 another Rs.24,000 crore.
9.         Subsequently, all the States were asked to prepare District Rural Roads Plans based on actual survey and identify
 a subset of the road network, referred to as Core Network, which ensures basic access to all the habitations and
 connectivity to market centres.  According to the Core network finalised by the States, there are 1,72,772 eligible target
 habitations which require new connectivity and 3.70 lakh kms of roads are required for connecting them.  Based on the
 actual cost of new road construction in 2003-04 under the programme, the total requirement of fund for providing new
 connectivity for the eligible unconnected habitations is estimated to be Rs.69,450 crore (say Rs.69,500 crore)
10.   According to the Core Network, the total road length required for upgradation/renewal of rural roads is 3.86 lakh
 km, of which 2.36 lakh km. are through routes.  The total financial requirement for upgradation of through routes and

 share for rural roads of the cess on High Speed Diesel imposed through the Central Road Fund Act, 2000. Additional

 US $ 400 million & US $ 750 million each) from 2004-05.  Another loan/credit of US $ 500 million is being negotiated
 with the World Bank.  Rural Roads component of Bharat Nirman will require an investment of about Rs.48,000 crore. 
 Against this, the likely availability of funds will be Rs.16,000 crore from the Cess on High Speed Diesel (calculated at

 the Asian Development Bank.  This leaves a funding gap of Rs.23,000 crore.  To bridge the funding gap, it has been

 borrow Rs.16,500 crore over a period of four years.  The Central Road Fund Act, 2000 does not have any provision for
 borrowing for rural roads and its repayment with the proceeds of future cess.

2009-2010                                                                         Rs.4000 crore

 Road, Transport and Highways and Rural Development on the subject. In the said meeting the Committee perused the
 provision of the Bill which reads as follows:-
15.       Clauses (2) and (3) of the Central Road Fund (Amendment) 2006
15.1 Clause (2) reads:-
" In the Central Road Fund Act, 2000 (hereinafter referred to as the principal Act), in
 section 9, sub-section (1), after clause (b), the following clause shall be inserted, namely:-
“(ba) take such measures as may be necessary to raise funds for the development of rural
 roads;”.
15.2 Clause (3) reads:-
"In section 11, of the principal Act, after sub-section (1), the following proviso shall be
 inserted, namely:-
            “Provided that the Central Government may use the share of the Fund under sub-
clause (a) of clause (viii) of section 10 for the repayment of any loan taken for the purpose
 of development of rural roads in any State or Union territory."
16.       During the discussion on the Bill, the Committee suggested that instead of introducing a separate Clause - (ba) -

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
The Central Road Fund Act, 2000 provides for levy and collection by way of cess, excise and customs duty on
 petrol and high-speed diesel oil for development and maintenance of National Highways, rural roads, State roads and
 improvement of safety at railway crossings.  Under section 9, the Central Government has the power to administer the
 fund and allocate and disburse such sums as are considered necessary to the concerned departments responsible for the
 development and maintenance of rural roads.  Under section 10, the Central Government is responsible for allocation of
 fifty percent of the cess on high-speed diesel oil for the development and maintenance of National Highways, rural
 roads, State roads and construction of roads over or under railways.  The allocation under section 10 is utilized for
 provision of all-weather connectivity to rural habitations through centrally sponsored scheme “Pradhan Mantri Gram
 Sadak Yojana”.  Under this, a target has been set to provide road connectivity to all rural habitations having a
 population of 1000 and above (500 and above in hilly and tribal areas) by 2009.  This will require an investment of
 about Rs.48,000 crores.  To bridge the funding gap it has been decided to borrow Rs.16,500 crores over a period of four
 years.
 
2.         Since the Central Road Fund Act, 2000 does not have any provision for borrowing for rural roads and utilization
 of the proceeds of future cess for repayment of loans, the Central Road Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2006 seeks to amend
 the Act to enable the Central Government to take such measures as may be necessary to raise funds for the development
 of rural roads, and it may use the share of the fund for the repayment of any loan taken for the purpose of development
 of rural roads in any State or Union territory.

5.      The Committee finds that despite its earlier recommendations on the aspect of funds utilization and the
 need for constant monitoring of projects, the Department of Road Transport and Highways has done precious
 little to improve the situation. This is evident from the reply of the Department with regard to non-utilisation of
 funds that the allocation for road sector is based on anticipated implementation of projects every year. The
 trend from the year 2002-03 onwards would reveal that the actual utilization has been more or less steady and
 consistent. The slippages occur when major projects do not get implemented for the years they are projected for
 implementation. For instance, allocations for programmes of NHDP Phase-III and SARDP-NE did not
 materialize fully because the approvals were not available in the time-frame projected. The Committee desires to
 know as to why approvals were not available in time and whether any responsibility has been fixed in the
 matter. The Committee observes that the budgetary allocation of the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was substantially increased from 2004-05 (revised estimates) of Rs. 8566.00 crore  to Rs. 13293.75
 crore during 2005-06 and for 2006-07 (budget estimates) the allocation has again been increased to Rs 15307.31
 crore. The Committee, therefore, re-emphasises that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should
 devise strategies, in such a way so that they are able to fully utilize the funds placed at their disposal. They
 should also evolve some mechanism to identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such
 hindrances in coordination with all the concerned agencies. This would also help them to avoid time overrun and
 consequential cost overrun of the projects to be executed by them.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.      The reason for non-utilisation  of funds cannot be solely attributed to the delayed implementation of projects. It is

63.    The Committee notes that against the total BE for 2006-07 of Rs 15307.31 crore for the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways, only an amount of Rs 814.38 crore  has been earmarked for the maintenance and
 repair of National Highways. The Committee feels that the proportion of the outlay for maintenance and repair
 of National Highways to the total outlay of the Department of Road Transport and Highways is not up to the
 desired level in view of the lengths of National Highways completed so far and proposed to be added in the
 current financial year. The Committee recommends that in view of the bad condition of various National
 Highways, which carry heavy traffic load, the Department should draw up a comprehensive list of high-density
 traffic National Highways which will enable it to utilize the available funds in a meaningful manner.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
64.    Requirement of funds as per norms for the year 2006-07 for maintenance and repair of National Highways was
 projected as Rs. 2012.00 crore, while funds provided in BE is of Rs. 814.38 crore. Funds provided for maintenance and
 repair of National Highways are generally about 40 per cent of the requirement of funds as per norms. The department
 has to maintain all NHs in traffic-worthy condition within the available financial resources. In view of this, spending
 money on high-density traffic corridor would render other National Highways in bad shape and thus, invite public
 criticism.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
65.    The Committee feels that is lack of understanding between different wings of Government when the
 Department of Road Transport and Highways projected the requirement Rs.2012.00 crore  for the year 2006-07
 for proper maintenance and repair of National Highways. However Planning Commission/Ministry of Finance
 allocated only 40 per cent of the required fund which certainly lead to a situation where the majority of high
 density traffic corridor will not be in traffic-worthy condition as the amount available as 40 per cent of the
 requirement. The Committee feels that National Highways which carry heavy traffic load are lifeline of the
 country and cannot be left in a bad shape. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation made
 earlier that in view of the bad condition of various National Highways, the Department should draw up a
 comprehensive list of high-density traffic National Highways which will enable it to utilise the limited funds in a
 meaningful way.
(Recommendation at Para 91)

 issuance of Pollution Testing Equipments has been simplified in the year 2006-07. It is proposed to procure them
 centrally in consultation with a technical agency after ascertaining requirement of the States. Instead of granting 75 per
 cent reimbursement to the States, equipment would be offered to them after procurement.

98.    The Committee notes that the Tenth Five Year Plan envisages the setting up of at least one Model Drivers’
 Training School in each of the five zones. The Committee feels that the functioning of Drivers’ Training Schools
 will have a direct impact on reducing the rate of road accidents and therefore is of the opinion that there is a
 need to setup at least one such School in each of the States/UTs in view of the increasing number of vehicles in
 the country. The Committee recommends that the Department should formulate suitable schemes to encourage
 the States/UTs to setup such Schools and that the procedure for setting up of such schools should be simplified
 and widely circulated. The Committee also recommends that the scheme should be liberalised to enlist the
 assistance of private sector also in this field in view of its direct impact on reducing the rate of road accidents.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
99.    This Committee’s recommendations are noted for appropriate incorporation while reformulating the Scheme for
 the Eleventh Five Year Plan.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
100.  The Committee considers this as an interim reply and hopes that recommendation made with regard to
 Model Drivers’ Training School in each of the five zones will be suitably incorporated in the scheme of the
 Eleventh Five Year Plan, which will be done this year.
(Recommendation at Para 134)
101.  The Committee is constrained to note that out of the allocation of Rs.4.85 crore for R&D in 2005-06, only
 Rs. 0.01 crore has been incurred upto December, 2005. The Committee is of the view that the R&D activities are
 imperative to enhance the sustainability of road projects being implemented in the country and to make them
 user friendly. The Committee feels that a non-utilisation of the budget provision during 2005-06 exemplifies the
 lack of efforts to bolster the R&D activities. The Committee also feels that there is a need to access the benefits
 derived from the R&D applications. The Committee expects that suitable institutional mechanisms will be
 developed to study the impact of R&D initiatives on specific projects so that the beneficial results can be
 replicated in similar conditions in future. The Committee also expects that adequate steps will be taken for the
 progressive installation of Advance Traffic Management Systems and Intelligent
 Traffic Systems on the National Highways. The Committee further recommends that the GIS based National
 Highways Information Systems should be completed and implemented in a time bound manner.

 of Rs 295.46 lakh was incurred.

 of sustainable road infrastructure of the country and fully shares with the concern expressed by the Committee.

 to the best in the world. The various components of this strategy are: improvement in design, modernization of

112.  The Committee is alarmed at the steep decline in the share of public transport vehicles in the total vehicles
 population from 11.1 per cent in 1951 to 1.1 per cent in 2003. The Committee is not aware of any concerted
 policy measure formulated to arrest this decline. In this context the Committee reiterates its
 observations/recommendations made in its 84th Report, which is reproduced below: -
“The Committee expresses its concern that in the absence of user-friendly public transports, the people
 in the country are resorting to excessive use of private vehicles and this has put the roads under undue
 pressure. The Committee observes that most of the investment on roads is being extracted from the
 public itself but the returns accruing to the users are not equitable. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the efforts of the Government should focus on developing public transport, which
 discourage excessive use of private vehicles. The Government should adopt a methodology, whereby, in
 the more densely populated states, the rich and the affluent are asked to pay more for keeping more
 than one vehicle.”
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
113. Constitutionally, road tax falls under the purview of the State Governments. The recommendation of the
 Committee has been circulated to the States vide letter dated 5.7.2006.

 recommendations may be obtained on priority and a detailed study on the response may be forwarded to the

115. The Committee understands that the Indian Railways has adopted an aggressive marketing strategy for
 increasing its share of freight traffic. The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why there is no initiative to
 upgrade the design parameters of the roads commensurating with the technological advancement in the load
 carriers enabling them to bear higher load capacities. The Committee is of the view that this has resulted in the
 flouting of provisions related to overloading. The Committee notes that the Department has held that the
 revenue likely to accrue on account of increase in Gross Vehicle Weight will be accrued to the State
 Governments and Central Government will not get any part thereof. Further, on the one hand it is submitted by
 them that the likely increase in revenue is not possible to assess, on the other hand it is claimed that the loss
 caused on account of the deterioration of roads would be much more than the revenue that would be gained by
 the State Governments. The Committee also feels that non-accrual of any revenue to the Central Government by
 way of road tax consequent on the increase in the permissible Gross Vehicle Weight should not be taken as an
 excuse to defer the decision on the suitable amendments to the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The Committee expects
 that the Department will either ensure the strict compliance of provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 or
 consider the amendment in the Act to help the carriage sector.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
116.  The Department held a meeting of technical experts regarding implications of revision of the Gross Vehicle
 Weight (GVW). Unanimous opinion of the experts was that any increase in GVW while keeping the road design
 parameters unchanged would have a disastrous consequence on the life and maintainability of road infrastructure. On
 the other hand, changing the design parameters of the road and increase in GVW is going to be unaffordable and
 expensive. Further, it also came out that GVW legislated in India is comparable to the rest of the world. The
 Department has, however, decided to commission a study through Central Road Research Institute (CRRI) for in-depth
 examination of all issues pertaining to overloading and possibility, if any, of revision of GVW.
(Recommendation at Para 147)
117.  The Committee is surprised to note that even though the Integrated Transport Policy was formulated in the
 year 2001, the National Road Transport Policy has not been finalised so far. The Committee further notes that
 the discussions on the draft National Road Transport Policy are still in preliminary stage and meetings with
 stakeholders are still to be held. Further, the agency to be entrusted the task of submitting a revised draft has
 not been finalised. In this scenario, the Committee is apprehensive that the National Road Transport Policy
 document will not be available by December, 2006 as envisaged. The Committee recommends that concerted
 efforts should be made to finalise the National Road Transport Policy expeditiously. In this context, the
 Committee had observed in its 84th Report that the absence of the right kind of modal-mix in the country is
 hampering optimum utilisation of all the resources. The Committee therefore reiterates its recommendations
 made in the same Report that the Government must come forward with an integrated transport policy to make
 optimum utilisation of the various transport facilities available in the country.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
118.  The Integrated Transport Policy comes under the purview of Planning Commission. This Department is in the
 process of finalization of an agency to assist the Department in drafting National Road Transport Policy. The National
 Road Transport Policy is expected to be ready by March, 2007. The same would be sent to the Planning Commission
 for incorporation in Integrated Transport Policy.

 perusal as and when it is finalised by the Department.

 the 33 per cent of the budgetary allocations could spent in the last quarter ending March. However, ceiling of the

REPORT
        The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the observations
 recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Third Report on Demands for Grants  (2006-07) (Demand No.
 20) of the Department of Culture, which was presented to the Parliament on  22nd May, 2007.
2.     Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on 15th January 2007 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:-
 (i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government:  
  Para Nos. 11, 15, 21, 29, 37, 55 and 61 Total-7
 (ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
 view of the Government replies:
 
  Para No. 65 Total-1
 (iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
 not been accepted by the Committee:
 
  Para Nos. 32 and 49 Total-2
 (iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
 are still awaited:
 
  Para Nos. 18, 24, 40, 44 and 71 Total-5
3.     The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as
 interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.     On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of the action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee contained in the One Hundred and
 Third, action taken thereon by the Government and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
THE APPROACH IN THE TENTH PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 11)
5.     The Committee is of the view that fixing of the Revised Estimates ceiling by the Ministry of Finance on the
 basis of the level of expenditure attained upto the month of September/October creates problem for the
 Department of Culture. The Committee observes that most of the cultural functions and festivals take place in
 the month of October and November, after the monsoon. The Archaeological Survey of India also incurres
 major expenditure after the monsoon. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government must review
 the budgeting procedure and evolve some mechanism to ensure that the Plan allocation for the Department of
 Culture is not reduced. The Committee recommends that if the review of the budgetary allocation is done in the
 month of December, instead of the month of September then the cut in the budgetary provision could be
 avoided. The Committee observes that the major allocation for conservation work is being done under Non Plan
 Allocation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that conversation activity should be brought under the Plan
 Head so that conservation is not affected for want of funds, which is causing problem to the Department of
 Culture who wish to increase the conservation activities, hence need more expenditure.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.     In pursuance of the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, budget provision for conservation
 will be brought under Plan heads while preparing the Budget Estimates for 2007-08 onwards.
7.     In Archaeological Survey of India, field officers are asked regularly to programme  the activities in such a manner
 that flow of expenditure is proportionately distributed in the months and 67 per cent expenditure is achieved by end of
 December. But as the conservation work of Archaeological Survey of India is seasonal in nature and in extreme
 summer and monsoon seasons, the pace of work and the flow of expenditure will be slow and the flow of expenditure
 will not strictly be proportionate every month. Archaeological survey of India is explaining the above to Planning
 Commission and Ministry of Culture every year to minimize the budget reduction on this ground.
8.     With regard to review of Budgetary  allocation in the month of December instead of September, the
 recommendations of the Committee have been forwarded to Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission for
